subject.detail: Measured 2026-09-03 (WE3) while adjudicating `an-effect-class-the-census-cannot-name-reads-as-no-effect.md`. That brief cites one requirement. The requirement axis is clean -- all 44 declare a class in `EFFECT_CLASSES` -- and the finding is on the axis nobody counted: 31 of the 49 cases that name a `witness.effect` name a class the vocabulary does not carry, and every one of the 31 is `oracle: effect-witness` at `status: pass`. machine-state 25 CASE-0366..0371, 0420..0426, 0470..0477, 0490..0493 file 2 CASE-0342, CASE-0386 notification 1 CASE-0441 os-record 1 CASE-0387 process 1 CASE-0440 ui-state 1 CASE-0346 WHY NOBODY SAW IT, and this is the half that makes it a defect rather than a chore. `campaign.py:702` DOES check the field, and its blocker line reads `40 effect-witness claim(s) with no recorder, no effect class, or a count of zero`. That 40 is 31 bad classes plus 9 missing recorders and counts, verified by replicating the loop. The report then caps its detail at twelve lines -- which on this campaign are twelve lines about four cases with missing recorders and null counts. **All 31 class findings are inside the 40 and not one of them is printed.** A reader of the campaign report cannot learn from it that any case names an unrecognised class, and the number reads as a recorder problem. WHY THE 31 ARE NOT REMAPPED HERE, deliberately and on the record. Some are a rename: `process` on CASE-0440, whose recorder is `Get-ScheduledTaskInfo`, is `subprocess`. Some are a harder question a rename would bury: `machine-state` on CASE-0423..0426 and CASE-0490..0493 is recorded over *"the router's own /servers listing, read over the control API"*, which is a recorder INSIDE the product -- whether those cases belong at the `effect-witness` rung at all is a judgement about the case, not about a word. Picking the nearest legal spelling for all 31 would turn 31 rows green while answering neither question, and every one of them belongs to the Windows waves rather than to this runner. `references/effect-boundary.md` is what settles them.
subject.title: 31 of the 49 cases naming a witness effect class name one the census cannot recognise, and campaign.py counts them into a 40 whose printed detail names none of them

cell.dataShape: two claims inside one renotify window

subject.note: R26. The throttle withholds a REPEAT and never an ESCALATION. The brief asks that a recurring error not generate alert spam, and the naive reading -- one alert per server per window -- swallows the one transition that matters. Four things make a notice due: nothing has been said yet, the KIND changed, the EXPIRY moved, or the window elapsed. E13 runs with `renotifyAfterMs` set to a year so nothing can go out on elapsed time, watches `expiring` become `expired` one millisecond past the boundary, and then asserts the repeat after it IS withheld -- so the arm is the escalation rather than the throttle being broken.

R26. Reading the report does not consume the notice; claiming it does. That is why there are two routes rather than one: folding them together would make `GET /upstreams/auth-expiry` spend the notification a caller was about to be shown, so opening a settings pane would silence the next alert. It is the same rule this repository enforces on its own gates -- a check that mutates the tree as a side effect of checking is not a check. E16 asserts it on the monitor and E24 through the routes; the lane asserts it as `count:2` after two GETs.

cell.dataShape: a credential record with no expires_in

subject.note: R26. THE VACUITY CASE, and the reason this item exists in the shape it does. A token whose stored record declares no lifetime has no derivable expiry, and the tempting reading -- it has not expired, therefore it is fine -- is the class this campaign keeps finding: a state that reads healthy because nothing measured it. `AuthExpiryRecord.state` has NO path from a missing number to `valid`; it returns `unknown` and the wire carries `unknownReason` saying which half is missing (`no-lifetime-declared` when `expires_in` is absent, `unreadable-authorized-at` when the stamp is). Asserted at both planes: E5/E6/E17/E21 in the suites, and the lane reads `state`, `unknownReason` and the ABSENCE of any invented `expiresAt` off a record it planted itself. Not `expiresAt: null` -- absent, so there is nothing there for a careless reader to round to fine.

cell.dataShape: an authExpiry block below the floor

subject.note: R26. A configured value the router will not take is REFUSED and reported with its key, its value as written, the floor that rejected it and its scope -- never clamped. A clamp invents a number nobody wrote, so the file says 500 and the behaviour is 60000 with nothing anywhere saying which is real. `warnWithinMs`'s floor is this item's own vacuity rule and ZERO IS NOT ACCEPTED: at zero a token passes straight from valid to expired and `expiring` is unreachable, which is R27's `tripAfter >= 2` one item earlier. E2 asserts that in both directions -- under a zero window a token one millisecond from death reads `valid`, and under the resolved policy the same token reads `expiring`.

cell.dataShape: a credential re-authorised between two claims

subject.note: R26. *Resolving authentication immediately clears the warning status* -- the brief's third bullet, and it is a CLEAR rather than an age-out. A server that stops deserving a notice has its delivery record DROPPED, so the next thing that goes wrong is reported at once instead of waiting out a six-hour window. The lane proves it against a wall clock: it re-authorises the record from outside, claims, breaks it again, claims again, and the notice arrives seconds later under the default six-hour renotify. A throttle that merely aged out could not produce that. The absence half is paired -- a SECOND server is broken in the same step, so 'the re-authorised one is gone' is read off a reply that carries another server rather than off an empty one.

cell.dataShape: no monitor, and the wrong verb, token and content type

subject.note: R26. With no monitor both routes answer 503 NAMING the missing capability, the shape `/harnesses`, `/extensions`, `/caches` and `/upstreams/health` use -- an empty report would be indistinguishable from a router holding no credentials at all. Beside it the wire refusals: 405 on the wrong verb for each path, 401 untokened, 415 with no content type, and a 404 rather than a 405 on `/upstreams/auth-expiryx`, because claiming a prefix collision would turn a typo into an answer that reads as 'the method is wrong'.

cell.dataShape: five upstreams, four planted records, one stdio server

subject.note: R26. THE PAIRED ABSENCE, and the load-bearing case. The claim is that the expiry is DERIVED from files the router already wrote rather than asked of the upstream, and half of that claim is an absence: nothing was spawned. An absence asserted alone is satisfied by a feature that does nothing, which is REQ-035's recorded lesson. So the lane never asserts it alone. It reads the daemon's child count off the process table -- zero, and zero running the stdio fixture's own script -- in the same run in which it REWRITES a planted credential record between two requests and requires the reported `expiresAt` and `state` to move with it. Zero children beside a report that follows the file is the claim; zero children alone is not.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=package not installed
subject.note: A real MSIX, built, deployed and removed, with a recorder at each step that is not the thing that wrote it. MakeAppx packs and .NET's ZipArchive reads the OPC container back - so the identity assertion is made against the PACKED ARTIFACT rather than against the file on disk that was handed to the packer. `winget validate` is the winget client applying a schema this repository does not own. Add-AppxPackage deploys and Get-AppxPackage reports: Fledgeling.MCPRouter_0.1.0.0_x64__facmrsw33693e. THE INSTALL ARM IS WHAT TURNS A FILE INTO A PACKAGE. A manifest can pack cleanly, validate cleanly, and be refused at deployment for a capability, an architecture or a signature - and every static check in the world passes right up to that point. 'CLEAN UNINSTALL RULES' IS THE HALF WORTH READING TWICE. UninstallGuidance promises that uninstalling preserves %USERPROFILE%\.claude\mcp-router. That is a promise about what SURVIVES, and a promise about survival cannot be checked by any amount of reading - only by an uninstall that actually ran. The lane plants a marker, installs, removes, and requires both that the deployment stack reports the package gone and that the marker is still there. WHAT THE LANE PUTS BACK: a self-signed certificate is added to LocalMachine\TrustedPeople so an unsigned developer package can deploy at all, and removed in a finally block however the run ends. Verified afterwards: zero Fledgeling.* packages, zero witness certificates. A lane that left a trusted publisher behind would have changed what this machine will install, silently and for every future run. NOT SETTLED: that anyone can obtain the package. Nothing publishes it, the winget InstallerUrl is a deliberate example.invalid placeholder, and this lane asserts the placeholder is PRESENT so the manifest cannot be mistaken for a shipping one. DEF-083 carries the publishing step, which needs a signing certificate and a pull request into a third-party repository.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=one capability queued
subject.note: The toast itself, in the Action Center, read by a process that cannot raise one. DEF-082 filed this as unmeasurable and gave a reason: UserNotificationListener's userNotificationListener capability is only grantable to a packaged application, and MCPRouter.Shell is WindowsPackageType=None, so the row was said to be downstream of WIN19's MSIX. THE REASON WAS WRONG, AND IT WAS WRONG BEFORE WIN19 LANDED. Measured on this host from an ordinary unpackaged Win32 console process with no package identity at all - Package.Current throws InvalidOperationException, which the lane asserts rather than assumes - UserNotificationListener.Current resolves, RequestAccessAsync returns Allowed with no consent prompt, and GetNotificationsAsync returns the toasts that are really there. On the first run those included three raised by win22-toast-witness the day before, carrying the exact strings NotificationPresentation writes. No MSIX, no capability, no packaged identity. WHAT IS STILL NOT AVAILABLE UNPACKAGED, and it bounds this case: every member of UserNotification.AppInfo throws NotImplementedException 0x80004001 for a caller with no package identity, so the listener can say what a notification SAYS and when it arrived and cannot say who raised it. Attribution here is the payload text, which the product owns, inside a time window this run opened - weaker than a publisher identity, and recorded as such. THE RECORDER IS NOT THE WRITER AND IS NOT EVEN THE SAME PROCESS: app/windows/MCPRouter.Witness.ActionCenter shares no code with the shell and cannot raise a notification. The shell's toast-probe.json is carried as the writer's self-report and graded by nothing. THE PRESENCE CONTROL is a removal: the matched notification is taken back out through the listener and the Action Center is read a third time, and the recorder is required to say no about it.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=one capability queued
subject.note: The COM activator the Windows notification platform wrote, read out of the registry by a process that did not write it. The writer is AppNotificationManager.Register() inside the shell; the recorder is HKCU through PowerShell's registry provider, and nothing of this repository's sits between them. Four arms. BASELINE requires the AUMID key to be ABSENT before the shell launches, so what the other three read is this launch. The three EFFECT arms read the key, the CustomActivator CLSID it names, and that CLSID's LocalServer32 - which came back as MCPRouter.Shell.exe carrying the platform's own ----AppNotificationActivated: argument, a string this repository does not write anywhere. THE ACTIVATOR IS THE ARM THAT CARRIES THE ITEM. A toast outlives the process that raised it; when somebody presses Review an hour later, Windows COM-activates the LocalServer32 registered for that CLSID. Without it the toast still appears and pressing it does nothing, which is the failure that looks most like success and exactly what a screenshot of a notification would have certified. WHAT THIS CASE DOES NOT SETTLE: that a toast is drawn, and that a press re-activates the app. Both need UserNotificationListener, whose capability is only grantable to a packaged application; DEF-082 carries them and is downstream of DEF-073. The shell's own report that the platform accepted a Show is carried in the evidence as writerSelfReport and is graded by nothing, because a process reporting its own effect is the shape of claim DEF-072 was about.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=no task registered
subject.note: The Windows task scheduler holding a task the product registered, read by an API that did not write it. The writer is MCPRouter.Shell.Live's LogonTaskSupervisor driving schtasks.exe with the Task Scheduler XML it builds; the recorder is Get-ScheduledTask, the ScheduledTasks module over the scheduler's WMI provider - a different API, a different process and a different vocabulary for the same facts. The XML says RunLevel LeastPrivilege and the recorder answers RunLevel Limited, and nothing in this repository translates between them. The scheduler also normalised the interval this run asked for, PT60S, into PT1M, which is the plainest available evidence that the read did not come back through anything this code wrote. EIGHT ARMS, AND TWO ARE ABOUT THE INSTRUMENT. BASELINE requires the recorder to report the task ABSENT before registration - without it, a task left behind by an interrupted run makes every other arm pass over a run that registered nothing. SILENCE requires it to report absence again after removal, which is what separates a reader from an echo: a recorder that always answered yes would satisfy the six product arms by construction. The other six read the three claims LifecyclePresentation prints to the operator - triggered at logon, un-elevated, restarting on failure - plus the executable and port this run asked for, plus presence and removal. WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE, and the reason it is one case rather than the whole of REQ-035: nothing here logs the user out, so the trigger has never been watched to fire, and nothing here starts or kills a daemon, so the restart has never been watched to happen. DEF-081 carries those two. This case settles that the registration the product performs produces, in the Windows task scheduler, a task carrying the properties the product's own UI describes - which before 2026-09-02 was unmeasured entirely, and which DEF-074 recorded as a supervision model nothing performed.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=a supervised process that dies
subject.note: The half of WIN23's supervision promise that had never been watched: a daemon the Windows task scheduler starts, loses, and starts again. DEF-081 filed it as unmeasurable and named the blocker as a missing Windows daemon binary; the blocker was real and is gone - app/windows/MCPRouter.Witness.Daemon is a harness process that starts, records its own start and waits to be killed, so there is something for the scheduler to supervise. WHAT THE MEASUREMENT FOUND IS NOT WHAT THE ROW EXPECTED. The registration the product wrote carried RestartOnFailure with a 60-second interval and a count of 3, and it did not restart the daemon at all. Killed, watched 150 seconds, on the unified scheduling engine and the legacy one, for a run started by a trigger and one started on demand: four registrations, no restart. The same block DID restart, three times at exactly 60 seconds, a task whose Command named a file that does not exist - so the instrument can see a restart, and RestartOnFailure governs a task that fails to LAUNCH rather than one whose action launched and later died. DEF-320 carries that, and the product now writes a Repetition on the trigger alongside MultipleInstancesPolicy IgnoreNew. THE RECORDERS ARE TWO AND NEITHER WROTE ANYTHING: Get-ScheduledTaskInfo for the scheduler's own account of its runs, and Get-CimInstance Win32_Process for the process identity, which is what makes 'it came back' a different process id rather than a report from the thing that came back. The daemon's own run log is carried and graded by nothing. EIGHT ARMS, THREE OF THEM ABOUT THE INSTRUMENT: BASELINE requires both tasks absent and no daemon running, so nothing below is inherited from an interrupted run; CLAIM.repetition and CLAIM.ignorenew read the product's own unmodified logon registration back through the WMI provider; SILENCE requires both recorders to say no once the tasks are gone. ONE SUBSTITUTION, SAID OUT LOUD: a trigger repetition does not apply to an on-demand start - measured, twice - so the live task carries a TimeTrigger where the product writes a LogonTrigger, because this lane must not log the machine out. Every Setting, the repetition interval, the principal, the action and the instances policy are the product's own document. That the trigger fires AT LOGON is still unwitnessed and DEF-081 keeps it.

subject.evidence: SettingsBoardModel holds RouterSettingsState in memory and has no store: no file, no registry key, no control-API call. Without it the target's 35 surface assertions are vacuous in a way that reads exactly like a product rendering no copy — DEF-029, where they were vacuous for ten consecutive runs. Armed three ways on 20 Aug 2026: renaming the symbol fails this case alone; mutating the call to `(false)` on a device created for the arm reads 53 failures across 36 tests, which is what proves the other 35 depend on it; and the first run ever taken on a device whose engine had never been live is clean, which proves the fix needs no warm-up on a fresh device. subject.note: ControlAPIRequest.isMutating is POST || DELETE || PATCH, ported from src/control.ts, and PUT is not in it. No route served PUT before this family, so nothing was ever exposed — but this family's write was written as a PUT, and an untokened PUT /profiles/x measured 200 while the rest of the suite was green. The write is a POST instead, because widening a ported gate that parity-manifest-check.sh derives from the reference in both directions is not a thing to do for a verb. The lane asserts the 405 on the wire and ControlProfileRoutesTests C6 holds the invariant over PUT, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE for whoever adds the next route here.

F5. The incremental scan. Scanning an unchanged file twice must yield the same events as scanning it once and must not open it the second time; a file that shrank must be re-read from zero and say so in filesReread. The corpus is 59,476 files and 19.5 GB (measured 2026-08-29), so the watermark is what makes the reader answerable inside a request rather than an optimisation.

subject.note: Added by G17. `filesystem-read` is a new value in this campaign's effect vocabulary — the five that existed were none, inbound-socket, outbound-socket, subprocess and filesystem-write, and none of them describes a route that reads a directory it was told about. The requirement itself is not new work: M19 and M30 both shipped against it and the campaign had no row for it, so the feature had no denominator and no case could have failed on it. Reach limit, stated rather than buried: the route serves only servers declaring a package directory and 0 of the 21 upstreams on this machine declare one (M30, planning/evidence/M30-reach.txt), so every case citing this requirement is measured against a CONSTRUCTED server. RECONCILED 2026-08-27. This row was allocated REQ-026 by G17 and G19 at the same time, off the same `main`. G19's REQ-026 keeps the number and states the WIRE contract: what GET /servers/:name/document serves and the exact refusal each rule names. This row keeps the half G19's does not carry -- that those documents are DRAWN in the Mac capability document panel, that a figure resolves from inside the package and nothing else is fetched, and that each refusal identifies itself on screen. Its cases are the swiftui lane's (CASE-0185..0190, CASE-0194) and they need a requirement to trace to; folding them into a router-daemon requirement would put a panel assertion inside a route's contract. G17's one WIRE case, CASE-0184, traces to REQ-026 instead, because that is the requirement its assertion is of. The two rows overlap on 'read out of the declared package directory' deliberately: neither text was rewritten, so the overlap is visible rather than resolved by editing delivered work. The `filesystem-read` effect class is left exactly as G17 declared it and is NOT in campaign.py's closed EFFECT_CLASSES -- `check` has flagged that since G17 landed and still does; G19's REQ-026 note records the same gap from the other side, having declined to name a class the vocabulary does not hold. Reconciling the vocabulary is the campaign owner's, not this renumber's. VOCABULARY RECONCILED 2026-08-29 by K4, which is the campaign-owner decision the paragraph above defers. `filesystem-read` is NOT added to the census vocabulary and this row no longer declares it as its `effect`. The list is the instrument's and it is closed: 24 copies of `campaign.py` and `vacuity-check.py` visible to this repository -- the `vendor/` pin and eleven cache versions from 0.9.3 to 0.16.0 -- carry the same nine-member tuple, `vendor/README.md` forbids editing the vendored copy ('a script that behaves one way in this repository and another way everywhere else stops being evidence of anything'), and upstream is a different repository. So the branch taken is the acceptance sketch's first: declare a class the census knows. THE CLASS IS `none`, AND `none` HERE MEANS `no representable class`, NOT `no external interaction`. The router does read the filesystem and the row still says so, in `effectUnrepresentable`, which `planning/test-campaign/bin/effect-class-census.py` reads and holds to a HARDER obligation than an ordinary row rather than a softer one: the named class must be outside the instrument's set, `effect` must be exactly `none` so the narrowing is stated rather than implied, and `provider` must RESOLVE against `campaign.json`'s `sourceRoot` through vacuity-check's own `resolve_provider`. Measured 2026-08-29 at `83e5380`: it resolves by path on `RouterCore/Control/ControlDocument.swift`, so deleting the read site reddens this row even though it has left the external-effect census. WHY NOT `inbound-socket`, which is the option a second reader picked. The route is served on the loopback listener and the class is defensible, but declaring it would trade one blocker for another and neither reader had the fact: `campaign.py`'s `unbacked_effects` (campaign.py:1078) blocks a requirement that names an external effect, is recorded `observed`, and has no passing case at the `effect-witness` rung. REQ-027's seven cases are structural, structural-visual, raster-visual and metamorphic; none is a witness, and the eight witnesses this campaign holds belong to other requirements. Choosing `inbound-socket` therefore means BUILDING a witness with a recorder, a non-zero count and a sabotage arm -- real engineering, and its subject would be the accept that CASE-0183 already witnesses for REQ-026. Recorded as the alternative it beat, with the axis it is better on: `inbound-socket` keeps the row inside the instrument's own external-effect denominator, where `none` moves that obligation into a repository-owned gate. WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE. The gate proves a provider exists in production source. That is the census floor, not a witness, and no case here observes a read at the boundary. The reach limit recorded above is unchanged.

The node costs the readme fidelity census nothing, because it is drawn only when a reference is refused and the M19 fixture's one image resolves. Check G17-P5. --- ARTIFACT CORRECTED by J3, on the same finding as CASE-0186 and from the other side of it. G17-P5 reads the `figure-refusal` node's own frame and requires under 1% figure colour, so the pixels are real and the picture was the whole frame the other two cases also cited. Refusal 1 of 3 — nothing served. A server declaring no cwd is refused noPackageDirectory on the wire, and the panel draws the designed state: 'g17-no-package has no package to read', and no figure. This is the state EVERY ONE of the 21 upstreams on this machine is in today, so the frame is a picture of the product as configured rather than of an edge case. Checks G17-W4, G17-R1. Picture: evidence/g17-document/refusal.nopackage.png. --- RUNG CORRECTED by J3, from `raster-visual`. The wire read is a real outcome and this case is the only home of it; the drawn half is structural. Neither opens `refusal.nopackage.png`, which stays cited as the frame the dump came from and is claimed as evidence of nothing.

Refusal 2 of 3 — too large. A read me of 600,012 bytes is over the 524,288-byte transport cap for one document; the route refuses `documentTooLarge` naming the file and the limit, and the panel draws 'README.md is too large to show here' with the 512 KB cap in its advice. Note the wire spelling: `documentTooLarge`, not `tooLarge` — the latter is the IMAGE refusal one level in, and a check written against the Swift enum's case name rather than against the wire would have passed on a router that refused nothing. Checks G17-W5, G17-R2. This frame is also DEF-060: it never names the capability it refuses. --- RUNG CORRECTED by J3, from `raster-visual`. Its checks are G17-W5 — `reason`, `file` and `limit` read off the router's own response — and G17-R2, which reads the state title and the `512 KB` string out of `refusal.toolarge.dump.json`. The wire read is a real outcome and this case is its only home; the drawn half is structural. Neither opens `refusal.toolarge.png`, which stays cited as the frame the dump came from.

STRUCTURAL AND PERMANENTLY SO, and the reason is not a missing instrument. Its subject is the correspondence between the capture manifest and the artifacts on disk — a property of the EVIDENCE RECORD rather than of the product, so there is no product state a change could move and no rung on the ladder it could climb to. It is counted against the strict total rather than dropped from it, because a campaign that hid its own record-keeping checks from the denominator would be scoring itself on a smaller suite than it runs. Capture lineage over this flow's own wall of pictures. The fifth, refusal.toolarge, cannot do this and is NAMED rather than counted as corroborated: G17-L2 fails if that set is ever anything other than exactly it. DEF-060. Checks G17-L1, G17-L2.

The flow's whole shape in one relation: one package, three tabs, three different documents. The three frames' drawn text is pairwise distinct and all three titlebars name the same package — so the tab is what changed and the subject is not. Check G17-P8.

subject.note: J2. `Held` and `All` are the two filter chips SURF-004 declares, driven off one loaded reading of the fixture. `Held` is asserted in both directions against `Skill.held?.wantsMore` — every row it draws has an update held, and every row it hid does not — and `All` is asserted as the RESTORATION, which is the assertion that fails if a segment latches. SURF-004 reaches 2 of 21 and the remaining four state-changing controls are recorded in `inventory.json` under `controlsUnactuatable` rather than left in the denominator unexplained: the build draws none of them. That is DEF-062, and it is the finding this case produced — `references/inert-ui.md`'s own stated limit is that no amount of testing the build reveals what the build lacks, and giving the surface a denominator is what made the four visible.

J2. `Accept the new text` is driven and the effect is read as the operation the client recorded: exactly `["approve"]`. Its twin, `Keep serving the old text`, is deliberately NOT claimed as actuated and is recorded in `inventory.json` under `controlsUnactuatable` with the reason: its whole promised effect is that nothing is sent, so the only available read is an absence, and an absence passes identically on a control that does nothing at all. The test asserts it anyway; the census does not count it.

N8. The inertness guard on the untrusted-input boundary, made capable of failing. M19 shipped `MarkdownSecurityTests.htmlIsInert` with four spellings that named `javascript:`, no scheme, or nothing, and two assertions -- no link, no `imageURL` -- that `MarkdownInline.sanitized` makes true of every input it touches. It could not go red. M30 wired `ControlAPICapabilityDocumentSource` into the shipped UI, so router-served third-party text now reaches this renderer in a Release build, and the guard on it measured nothing. MEASURED, not assumed: the platform parser does keep inline HTML inert -- under `MarkdownInline`'s own options it hands each tag back as characters and marks it `.inlineHTML`, an intent naming no destination, and it does so under all four combinations of `allowsExtendedAttributes` and `interpretedSyntax`. Swift 6.2, macOS 26.6.2 (25G83), Debug, `swift test`. So this was an evidence defect and not a live vulnerability, and the fix is the assertion rather than new sanitisation. Two `https` spellings were added, because `https` is the one scheme the allowlist keeps and therefore the only one that can carry an interpreted `<a>` through to the assertion; a presence control runs the same reader over the markdown twin of the same destination first; and two clauses were added that the old body did not have -- handed back verbatim, and no attribute beyond the `.inlineHTML` marker. That last clause also corrects the test's own claim: the parser DOES attach one attribute to inline HTML and `sanitized` carries it, so the old name -- `inline HTML acquires no attribute of any kind` -- was false as written as well as unfailable, which is why nobody found out.

subject.note: Nothing served — the three ways this route has nothing to give, each reachable and each NAMING ITS OWN RULE rather than a shared 404. `noPackageDirectory` (the server declares no cwd), `packageUnreadable` (it declares one that is not on disk) and `noDocuments` (the directory is there and publishes no README.md, CHANGELOG.md or CAPABILITIES.md). Nine assertions, three per refusal: the status is 404, the `reason` is the specific rule, and a human sentence rides along. The app maps each reason to different copy, so a shared code is a refusal the reader cannot act on. Run against BOTH implementations over a real socket: `dist/index.js serve` and the shipped `app/.build/debug/MCPRouterCLI serve`, each on 127.0.0.1:8981 with a scratch MCP_ROUTER_HOME. M30 already proves this route in process — `ControlDocumentRouteTests.swift` calls the handler and asserts on the string it returns — which is a different claim from this one: this lets the kernel carry the bytes and reads what a client actually receives, which is what the campaign asks of every other route on this lane. Observing only the TypeScript half would leave the SHIPPED router unobserved, so both are run and both pass.

Too large, and it names WHICH cap it hit. A README.md of 524,289 bytes — the 512 KiB documentBytes cap plus one — returns 413 with `cap: documentBytes`, `limit: 524288`, `actual: 524289` and `file: README.md`. Seven assertions. There are three caps on this route that can produce a size refusal, so 'too large' without a cap name tells a reader nothing they can act on. The fixture is built one byte over the boundary rather than comfortably over it, and the runner REFUSES TO START (exit 2) if the caps declared in src/document.ts have drifted from the three the fixture is sized for — a fixture sized past a cap that has since moved is a fixture that passes by never reaching the boundary at all. Run against BOTH implementations over a real socket: `dist/index.js serve` and the shipped `app/.build/debug/MCPRouterCLI serve`, each on 127.0.0.1:8981 with a scratch MCP_ROUTER_HOME. M30 already proves this route in process — `ControlDocumentRouteTests.swift` calls the handler and asserts on the string it returns — which is a different claim from this one: this lets the kernel carry the bytes and reads what a client actually receives, which is what the campaign asks of every other route on this lane. Observing only the TypeScript half would leave the SHIPPED router unobserved, so both are run and both pass.

M39. The denominator is the window the code was ISSUED for, not MacPairing.lifetime. One code minted with a fifty-second lifetime must still read 1 at issue, half at its own midpoint and nil at its own end -- the same three readings as CASE-0262 over a different window, which is what tells a window-denominated fraction from a constant-denominated one. PairingSessionModel.issue takes its lifetime from the service precisely so a shorter-lived code is described accurately, and a fraction read off the constant would draw a ring that starts one-sixth full and never empties.

R22. The needle floor, which is a correctness rule rather than a performance one. An env value of `1`, `true` or `dev` used as a scrub needle deletes every occurrence of that text from every log line in the bundle — the timestamps, the ports, the word `device`. The result READS as thorough redaction and is a corrupted document, and nobody looking at it can tell which.

WHERE THE AMBIENT STATE IS ACTUALLY ON SCREEN. SURF-041, the notification-area flyout, is the surface WIN11 describes and nothing in the build mounts it (DEF-380). This one is the pane footer the shell draws on every destination: two lines, ambient.status.title and ambient.status.detail, painted from the reading RouterStatusReader takes off the router's own /status every two seconds. It is in the pane rather than on a board because an ambient claim that appears on one destination is not ambient. It declares NO controls, and that is not an omission: it is a readout. Nothing on it can be pressed, so nothing on it belongs in an actuation denominator - the cases that read it carry no `actuates` for the same reason.
subject.title: Windows ambient status readout - the navigation pane footer

subject.note: Seven sections, measured on the automation plane rather than counted in the markup: settings.section.router, .harnesses, .sessionanalyst, .updates, .security, .ambientsurface, .advanced, each publishing a name. Three of them carry a switch; the other four carry WIN13's governance prose because this build has no harness settings, no session analyst and no update check. The switches publish as Button carrying TogglePattern - which is what a WinUI ToggleSwitch is on the plane, and what made DEF-076's first reading say there were none. SINCE DEF-087 ONE OF THE THREE REACHES THE MACHINE AND TWO ARE DISABLED. `Launch router daemon at sign-in` registers and removes WIN23's logon task, and the board seeds it from the Windows task scheduler rather than from its own memory; the state persists to %APPDATA%\MCPRouter\shell-settings.json. `Show status in notification area` places and removes a real notification-area icon (DEF-101), registered by GUID so that something other than this application can ask the shell whether it is there. `Confirm before removing a server` - narrowed from `Require confirmation on destructive operations`, which named a class of operations this build does not have - decides whether the Servers board asks before it sends the router the one destructive verb the shell speaks (DEF-102). Both were DISABLED with a reason until those two landed, and neither is any more: nothing on this board now moves a boolean that reaches nothing. `Copy the loopback endpoint` copies (DEF-088). The two disabled switches still publish a readable toggle state, so the census rows over them are unchanged.

subject.note: SURF-029's two SecondaryCommands, 'Export log' and 'Reset router', were enumerated and unreached: a CommandBar does not realise its overflow items while the overflow is shut, so the at-rest lane could only record an absence with its reason, and planning/registry-drop-gate.py reported the surface as uncovered for exactly that. This case opens the overflow through ExpandCollapsePattern.Expand and reads both commands back with their names and ControlType.Button, between a BASELINE and a SILENCE that both find them absent from the control view AND the raw view. The writer is not the reader: overflow-actuate.ps1 expands in its own process and writes only the ExpandCollapseState it saw, while every element reading comes from uia-dump.ps1 started separately. TWO FINDINGS FROM THE FIRST RUN, neither planted, both corrected in the manifest rather than in the assertion. (1) probe-expectation.json predicted that opening the overflow would cost the never-activated guarantee, and IT WAS RIGHT: the probe held the foreground at none of the three baseline samples and at all six effect and silence samples, so Expand activates the window and Collapse does not hand the foreground back. That cost is now DECLARED as `overflow.activationCost` and compared both ways, so the day WinUI stops activating, this arm reddens rather than quietly acquiring a guarantee nobody re-checked. Baseline stays a hard assertion. (2) each command resolves to TWO tree paths with the overflow open, because WinUI publishes the OverflowPopup subtree once through a Microsoft.UI.Content.PopupWindowSiteBridge child and once in place beneath the ApplicationBar. Both copies agree on name, controlType, className, isEnabled, isOffscreen, accessKey, patterns and bounding rectangle, so it is one control on two routes; the assertion now permits several matches only while they agree on everything a caller would act on, and plant (H) watches that a genuinely different control under one id still fails. WHAT THIS DOES NOT BUY. It is not at-rest coverage and does not close DESIGN.md section 11 rule 9 for these two commands. The product fix is a surface that realises them without an actuation, and that is DEF-340. Neither command is INVOKED, so both stay outside the actuation census with a stated reason on SURF-029; this arm's subject is realisation and vocabulary, not effect. And the subject is WIN20's probe rather than the MCP Router Windows client: it measures WinUI 3's automation behaviour on this machine.

subject.note: The toast's wire format, on both sides of the trip, checkable with no display. ToastPayloadCodecTests parses the XML the platform will parse - it is a toast, it carries the title and the 'Nothing has been installed' line, it offers exactly Review and Dismiss - and then drives every argument string in that document back through the reader a real click goes through, requiring Review to come back as OpenReviewSheet FOR THAT CAPABILITY. Without the capability travelling, the action is a navigation to a list and the operator has to go and find the item the toast was about. THE SAFETY RULE IS ASSERTED OF THE DOCUMENT RATHER THAN OF ITS OWN SENTENCE. WIN22 tested ToastSafetyRule by asserting the string contained its own words. Here every action's arguments must parse into a closed set of two, and six refusal rows require the reader to return null - not a default - for an empty string, a bare form with no scheme, another application's scheme, our scheme with no action, and an action outside the set. That last row is the one that matters: this process does not control what sits in the Action Center, and a reader that fell back to something that ACTS would be the defect the safety rule names arriving through the parser.

WIN3. The shell is ONE surface and its ten destinations are ten more, per the destination-collapse rule. The pane items are the shell's controls and the boards they open are ten other surfaces, which is why those cases carry `actuatesSurface: SURF-030` while staying filed against the board each one proves. The pane control is declared as `Nav`, its x:Name in ShellWindow.xaml, and not as the phrase "NavigationView pane" the case generator used to emit: that phrase appeared in no source file, so the row's provenance could not be checked against anything. Recorded while renaming it: the NavigationView carried NO AutomationProperties.Name of its own, unlike the ten items inside it, so from the automation plane the pane itself was addressable by AutomationId alone. That was DEF-089, fixed 2026-09-02 by wb2 - the NavigationView now declares AutomationProperties.Name="Destinations" and the live lane reads it back off the running tree.

DETECTOR DEFECT in test-campaign, measured 2026-08-27 (G29) against the vendored 0.9.2 and the machine's 0.15.0, which carry a byte-identical `tie()`. SURF-028's route is `app://mac/servers/{server}/document` -- a family of addresses, one per server. `bin/g17-document-flow.sh` rendered its frames against three of them and recorded each target honestly. `tie()` normalises scheme, host, port, query and fragment away and then asks for string equality or a suffix match, so `mac/servers/g17-capability/document` against `mac/servers/{server}/document` fails all three tests and the gate reports UNTIED -- 'the recorded target does not resolve to the subject's route'. Nothing was pointed at the wrong thing. `references/capture-lineage.md` says resolution is 'deliberately loose on the parts a harness legitimately varies'; a `{server}` segment is exactly such a part, and it is the one case the looseness does not cover. THE FIX BELONGS UPSTREAM, and is not applied here. `vendor/README.md` pins the tree by checksum so the gates can be re-run from a clone, and a `tie()` that behaves one way in this repository and another way everywhere else stops being evidence -- the same reasoning that keeps X7 and X8 open. Referred out of family (gpt-5.6-sol, high effort, 2026-08-27) and it reached the same conclusion independently: patch upstream, cut a release, re-vendor and re-pin, rather than forking the pinned copy. The patch is one function: treat a route segment of the form `{name}`, `:name` or `*` as matching exactly one non-empty target segment, leaving literal segments, the source-file refusal and the normalisation untouched, and leaving the seeded swap red. WHAT THIS REPOSITORY DID INSTEAD, and why it is not a workaround. The three served frames are published by the FLOW-006 steps that rendered them, each carrying the concrete route its own capture recorded, and SURF-028 publishes none. That is the registry becoming more accurate rather than less: the surface is a template and has no single portrait, while a step is that surface at one address and can name it. Every frame is now filed at the address the channel was pointed at. The detector limit is unchanged and is what this row records.
subject.title: The capture-lineage tie pass has no notion of a route template, so a parameterised surface's capture is reported as a wrong subject

The assertion is now the relation — an unreachable router WITHHOLDS the counts entirely and says why, rather than rendering 0 tools from 0 servers, which a reader cannot tell apart from a running-and-empty router. 1206x2622 off the simulator's display server, attributed to testEachTabRendersItsOwnSurface by xcresulttool rather than by filename. Distinct sha c3f1c31a.

The package lane's own instrument, and a relation across runs rather than a fact about one: the same source must give the same verdict on a loaded host and an idle one. It did not — `make test` reported 4 issues at a one-minute load average of ~700 and passed 1473 tests at load 46 minutes later (DEF-030). Every one of the four asserted after a fixed sleep or a 2–5 second deadline, so what they were measuring was the machine. Closed by replacing each deadline with a condition: `ShellTestSupport.waitUntil` and `ActivityReconnectTests.completes` keep a bound so a condition that never arrives fails rather than hangs, but at 30s rather than inside the noise; and `searchIsDebounced` waits for the debounce to fire and then holds a full debounce window of quiet, because the wait alone is satisfied by the first request and would pass against the one-per-keystroke defect it exists to catch. Armed 20 Aug 2026 three ways, each watched to fail with its own message — `.seconds(0)` on the shared waiter reads `no poll ran at all` and `five keystrokes issued 0 requests`, `.milliseconds(1)` on the completion bound reads `reconnect did not return while the feed stayed live`, and a `queryChanged()` inserted into the quiet period reads `a later request arrived`. The contention that triggered the original failure came from another project and is not reproducible on demand, so the arms are the proof rather than a repeat of the load.

The behaviour it names is covered at an effect rung by CASE-0138 (outcome, macos-glass), which reads the substitution off a running build, and by CASE-0131's relation, which reads it off two windows and requires the action set to be a function of the row. This case is kept rather than retired because its predicate is the one that fires in seconds on a source change, and it is counted against the strict total rather than disappearing from it — but its rung now says it reads text, so no future reader takes it for a rendered assertion one step from an effect. PREVIOUSLY: `prototype.html:961` puts `Read first…` **in place of** Inspect and Remove rather than beside them, and the substitution is the requirement rather than a layout preference: a removal left on that row is one click from a fact nobody has read yet. `theRowSwapsItsActions` takes the `CleanupBoardRow` declaration, finds the `if candidate.provenance != nil {` branch, and asserts Inspect and `Remove…` appear nowhere inside it. Source-level for the reason the suite's header already gives — the claim is about every flagged row in every state, and a rendered assertion over one row leaves the rest unchecked. It reads the declaration with every `//` line stripped, because the first `ShellDetailWidthTests` searched raw source for a modifier its own doc comment three lines above also named, and deleting the modifier left the assertion green: a predicate satisfied by the prose explaining it is not a predicate. `structural-visual`, and counted against the strict total, for CASE-0128's reason. Armed 20 Aug 2026 twice: renaming the button reads `draws no Read first…` plus the Inspect predicate firing, and adding `Remove…` back into the flagged branch reads `a flagged row still draws Inspect or Remove`.

PREVIOUSLY: The sheet `Read first…` opens is where REQ-007 was most at risk on this board, because the design's version of it is almost entirely invented. `prototype.html:1249` lists an owner at install (`@jbailey`), a default branch `force-pushed 11d ago`, an installed hash `a3f19c2 — no longer in history`, and `Its evals fail 5 of 8`. The router reports none of them, and one is not computable at all: `SkillProvenance` records in its own doc comment that the client's files carry a commit and never an owner, so `changed since you installed it` cannot be derived — which is why the sheet's date is labelled as the router's own first sighting and why `CleanupPresentation.provenanceLimit` says so on screen rather than leaving the reader to infer it. `theSheetReportsOnlyObservations` asserts the sheet renders all three fields `SkillProvenance` actually carries and states none of the four invented strings. The negative half enumerates them by name rather than being a blanket not-that predicate, so it fires on the specific thing that would regress. Armed 20 Aug 2026 twice: deleting the `firstSeenAt` field reads `never renders firstSeenAt`, and adding `field("Owner at install", "@jbailey")` reads `the sheet states 'Owner at install', which the router never reported`.

subject.note: REQ-019 where DEF-001 makes it matter: this build ships no pairing transport, and the sheet says so instead of drawing a code it cannot complete a pairing with. The AXSheet carries `Pair iPhone`, `Pairing is not available in this build`, and the sentence that keeps the reader from debugging their own network — `this build ships no way to listen for one. Nothing is wrong with your phone or your network.` The negative half is the one that would catch a regression: nothing in the window matches Crockford base-32 at the length REQ-015 specifies, checked by pattern rather than against a literal, so a code this predicate's author never saw would still trip it. This case does NOT make REQ-015 pass — CASE-0010 and CASE-0110 fail against it and keep failing. The sheet is honest about a capability that is missing; the capability is still missing.

THE ROWS ARE A REAL ROUTER'S, NOT A FIXTURE'S — and this is the only lane that can say so. ShellClientFactory makes a Debug build ALWAYS take a fixture, so no macos-glass capture is evidence about a real reading; every glass case above proves the board renders what the route's shape provides. Here the Swift router itself served GET /harnesses over loopback on 127.0.0.1:8975 under an isolated MCP_ROUTER_HOME. Four checks: the route answers with a harness list (7 rows); readAt is 0s old, so a reading taken now rather than a recording replayed; every row's `exists` flag agrees with stat(2) on THIS filesystem (7 of 7); and every traceable row's `entries` count is REPRODUCED by a reader that shares no code with the router, opening the same file itself — claudeCode=1, claudeDesktop=0, codexCLI=5, cursor=0, geminiCLI=20, grokCLI=3. One row is in a format that reader cannot parse and is reported untraceable rather than as agreeing.

THE HARD HALF, AND THE ONE NOBODY REACHES BY LAUNCHING THE APP. A board showing a stale figure as current looks exactly like one that is right, so this promise can only be proved by arranging the failing condition on purpose. The router that had been answering was killed while THIS SAME app instance kept running — a relaunch would reach `.failed`, which is a different state that renders differently — and the board was photographed again. It drew `3 tools from 3 servers · last reading, not current`. Four things are checked. The absence was arranged: the harness's own read of http://127.0.0.1:8955 at that shutter got nothing. The header says its reading is no longer current. No present-tense running count appears anywhere in the board — the check is for the absence of any digit in that position, never for a dash or a placeholder, because a placeholder is a figure of its own. And the sidebar readout withholds its own count too, which is a second absence over the same promise in code that does not share a line with the first: `ServersBoardHeader.subtitle()` draws one and `ReadoutCopy.accessibilityLabel` the other, and a guardrail that held in one place and not the other would pass a single-predicate check. The fifth check is the direction people forget: the servers that WERE read are still shown, 3 of them, the same number as while the router answered. A failed refresh is not evidence that the servers went away, and a board that cleared itself would satisfy every absence check above while destroying data no source said was gone.

subject.cell: execution-plane=daemon · state=a declared server with disabled: true
subject.note: A disabled server is declined on both probe paths, and the assertion is on the process table rather than on the reply. The lane gives the disabled server its OWN copy of the fixture script under a different name, so the reading is a count of children running THAT file: zero. Counting the shared script could not speak for it — the enabled servers run the same command line, so any statement about the disabled one would be arithmetic on a denominator that moves whenever the lane adds a server. A route that answered `declined` while spawning the child anyway would pass every status assertion above it. `disabled` means never spawned to be warmed or indexed, so a probe route that spawned one would be a hole in the switch rather than a health check.

subject.cell: execution-plane=daemon · data-shape=an env value of three characters beside a log line containing it
subject.note: The needle floor, which is a correctness rule rather than a performance one. An env value of `1`, `true` or `dev` used as a scrub needle deletes every occurrence of that text from every log line in the bundle — the timestamps, the ports, the word `device`. The result READS as thorough redaction and is a corrupted document, and nobody looking at it can tell which. So a value below 8 characters is not used as a needle, is named in `unscrubbable` with the reason, and is still withheld by layer 1. The assertion that bites is the positive one: `dev-server on port 3000` must survive intact. BOTH out-of-family reviewers proposed an entropy filter on top of the floor, to stop a value like `production` scrubbing that word out of the logs. Declined, and the reason is the direction of the error: an over-redaction announces itself in place as `<redacted:MODE>` and a reader can see exactly what happened; an under-redaction is silent. A second exclusion tuned by entropy moves values from the first class to the second on a judgement nobody can audit from the bundle.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - modality=process diagnostics - data-shape=one injected fault per launch
subject.note: Each of the shell's three top-level unhandled-exception handlers made to fire on purpose, and the line it wrote read back out of shell-startup.log by a process that did not write it, after the process that did had exited. THIS CASE EXISTS BECAUSE REGISTRATION IS NOT FIRING. DEF-079 was raised on sixteen launches that wrote no `unhandled:` line including eight that terminated at 0xC000027B, and it stayed open through the fix - two more handlers registered - because none of the three had been observed catching anything. App.xaml.cs takes `--fault <ui|appdomain|task|dispatcher>`, compiled out outside DEBUG and inert unless passed; win-shell-unhandled-witness.ps1 launches the shell once per kind. FOUR ARMS. BASELINE is a launch with NO --fault and requires its region of the log to hold `launched` and no `unhandled:` line, which is what makes the three EFFECT lines the injection's rather than startup's; and every arm reads only the bytes appended after its own launch, so a line an earlier run left behind cannot satisfy one. The three EFFECT arms then require, each after its own fault, `unhandled: [xaml]` for a throw on the UI thread inside XAML's dispatch of OnLaunched, `unhandled: [appdomain terminating=True]` for a throw on a non-UI foreground thread, and `unhandled: [unobserved-task]` for a faulted task nobody awaits after a collection and WaitForPendingFinalizers. And the injection is compiled out outside DEBUG, so this grades the Debug binary only. The shell's own `handlers:` line saying which handlers it attached is carried in runs[] as writerSelfReport and is graded by nothing. The command the lane ran is scripts/windows/uia/run-shell-lane.ps1; `actuates` carries the two band containers the surface declares, which is what control-census.py counts. subject.detail: prototype.html routes ?pane=evals and titles the board Evals; the running app's window title reads back Checks. Found by capture-lineage's tie pass, which refused a capture whose recorded target did not resolve to the surface's route. The rename went one way and the design of record was not followed.
subject.text: WITHDRAWN 20 Aug 2026 — this was not a product defect. It was recorded as "prototype.html routes ?pane=evals and titles the board Evals; the running app's window title reads back Checks". The second half is false. `prototype.html:600` declares the sidebar entry as `{id:'evals',t:'Checks',ic:'evals'}` — the route **id** is `evals` and the **title** is `Checks` — and the board's own header draws the selected suite (`pr-summariser · 8 cases`) rather than a board name at all. So the design of record titles this board Checks, the app titles it Checks, and there was never a rename to follow. WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED is a detector artefact, and it is worth keeping for that: capture-lineage's tie pass refused a capture whose recorded target did not resolve to the surface's title, and the target it held was the route id. An id and a title are different fields that the design is entitled to disagree on, so a tie pass that compares one to the other reports a rename wherever a route is not named after its board. Checked against the other seven boards: no second instance, because every other route id matches its title. Closed rather than deleted, so the next reader meets the artefact rather than rediscovering it.
subject.title: a route id was compared against a board title, and they differ in the design itself

subject.text: CAUSE FOUND AND FIXED 20 Aug 2026; this record replaces one that said the cause was unknown and named machine saturation as a candidate. The candidate was wrong. The process-wide accessibility engine was OFF, so SwiftUI's `_UIHostingView` built its accessibility container and vended an EMPTY element array — `accessibilityElements == []`, not nil — and every label assertion in the target read empty and reported its own honest verdict, `nothing was measured, so this proved nothing`. That is indistinguishable, from inside the suite, from a product that renders no copy. A probe settled it: calling `_AXSSetAutomationEnabled(true)` took the same hosted view's published element count from 0 to 1. THE ENGINE HAD BEEN ON BY ACCIDENT — something else on this machine had switched it on — which is why this suite was green for months while depending on ambient host state no file in this repo controls, and why it went red with no change to the branch. THREE CHANGES ARE THE FIX, and the third was found only because the first two were not enough. (1) `PhoneSurfaceTests` resolves `_AXSSetAutomationEnabled` out of `/usr/lib/libAccessibility.dylib` (falling back to `AccessibilityUtilities.framework`) via dlopen/dlsym and calls it once per process, before the first `host()`. (2) The walker reads `accessibilityElements` first, because SwiftUI publishes through the array and leaves `accessibilityElementCount()` at 0 — measured on iOS 26.5, where one hosted `Text` reported `accessibilityElements.count == 1` and `accessibilityElementCount() == 0` in the same breath, so reading only the indexed API walked past every element SwiftUI had. Those two took `make test-ios` from 52 failures to 0 — and then `make all`, run immediately afterwards on the same device, came back with 39. (3) THE STATE IS DEVICE-SCOPED AND THE CALL LANDS ON THE NEXT PROCESS, NOT THIS ONE. On a device left in the disabled state, the run that re-enables it fails a DETERMINISTIC set of 15 test cases — identical set, measured three times, verified with `comm` in both directions — and the run after it, with no change to anything, is clean. The 15 are exactly the cases that host a `ScrollView`; the tests that pass alongside them are geometry, counts and negative assertions, all of which an empty tree satisfies, so the green half of that run was vacuous too. `test-ios` therefore runs a throwaway single-test process before the graded one and discards its exit code. MEASURED END TO END: three consecutive runs with the call mutated to `(false)` drive `MCPRouter-Unit` into the disabled state (54 failures each, the whole suite red, which is correct for a dead engine); the very next `make test-ios`, with the warm-up in the recipe, is 36 tests and 0 failures in 1.4s. THE INSTRUMENT CHECK IS ITSELF INSTRUMENTED. `testTheAccessibilityEngineCanBeSwitchedOn` blocks on a probe that hosts `ScrollView { Text }` and reads it back through the same walk every other assertion uses, with a 20s deadline. Two narrower probes were built first and both were wrong in opposite directions, which is why the shape is stated rather than assumed: a bare `Text` read either way reports the engine live at t=0 of a run in which 15 cases went on to read empty, and a `ScrollView` read through the accessibility-container path alone reports the engine dead on a device where all 35 other tests pass. A probe that answers differently from the thing it stands for answers a different question. On a dead engine the deadline fires and the case fails with `no hosted Text published a label within 20s`, measured. ARMED THREE WAYS. (a) Renaming the symbol to `_AXSSetAutomationEnabledXXX` on a device whose engine is already live fails exactly one test — the instrument check — and leaves the other 35 green, which is correct for that arm and proves only the resolution assertion. (b) With the call mutated to `(false)`, the first run on `MCPRouter-Arm`, a device created for the arm, recorded 53 failures across 36 tests: that is what proves the other 35 depend on the engine. (c) The first run ever taken on `MCPRouter-Arm2`, a device whose engine had never been live, is 36 tests and 0 failures, so a fresh device needs no warm-up and only an explicitly disabled one does. Both arm devices were deleted afterwards; `make test-ios IOS_UNIT_DEVICE=<name>` recreates either. TWO HARDENING CHANGES from the investigation are kept and neither is the fix: `test-ios` creates and owns `MCPRouter-Unit` instead of sorting booted devices first — the exact picker DEF-020 condemned, still live in this recipe — and the walk retains every element it visits so `ObjectIdentifier` is unique among live objects as its use assumes. A third, waiting on a product surface's tree over a two-second deadline, was written, measured to change nothing, and removed: it cost 130 seconds a run and bought no measurement. The wait that IS kept differs from it in the one way that matters — it waits on a probe whose answer is known, so a timeout is a fact about the instrument rather than about the view. THE DEPENDENCY IS ON A PRIVATE SYMBOL, in the test target only, never linked into the app; the instrument check fails loudly if a future runtime renames it, so this target goes red rather than quietly empty. Carried as CASE-0126.
subject.title: the iOS unit lane read an empty accessibility tree because the engine was off

subject.text: Found 20 Aug 2026 by the vocabulary differential, which reported `Edit cases…` and `Run again` in-design-not-build on this board, and recorded here rather than fixed because bolting those two buttons on would be the wrong repair. The design's pane at `prototype.html:885-891` is **one subject's** eval suite: it heads `pr-summariser · 8 cases`, subtitles `Ran 2 minutes ago against 0.4.1 in a scratch checkout`, and lists eight named cases with a verdict each. The built board is **cross-subject**: every server and skill, one row apiece, a reachability verdict per row, a filter, and `CheckCopy.runAllLabel` = `Re-check all…`. Those are two different surfaces wearing one route id, and the actions follow the framing — `Run again` re-runs the one suite on screen, which is what `Re-check all…` already does across all of them, so drawing both would be two names for one act (the failure DEF-012 records). `Edit cases…` opens an editor for a collection the app does not model: there is no eval case anywhere in `EvalsBoardModel`, so the button would offer a reading of something that does not exist — the same reason `Read first…` is a stated gap in DEF-011 rather than a drawn control. The divergence itself is the finding, and it is a scope question rather than a defect fix: the design specifies a per-subject eval board with named cases and an editor, and the app ships a cross-subject reachability board. Which one this product wants is the owner's call, and it is written up as a brief rather than decided here. Not guarded by an assertion, deliberately: there is nothing to assert until that call is made, and a test pinning today's cross-subject board would make the divergence harder to close rather than easier.
subject.title: the Checks board is cross-subject where the design's is per-subject, so two of its actions have nowhere to go

subject.detail: CLOSED 2026-08-20. The cause was two independent framing errors, both invisible because the gate could not run to report them. The design references came from `obscura fetch --screenshot`, which captures at a fixed 1280x720 dpr1 viewport with no viewport flag, so every reference was clipped rather than merely small - the bottom row of one carried 578 non-background pixels of 640 sampled. And the build captures were 980x620 against the design's 1156x680 window, aspect 1.581 against 1.700, which no crop reconciles. Fixed by rasterising the design through CDP with `Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride` at 1280x900 dpr2 (readback asserted `[1280, 900, 2]` before any capture), re-photographing the eight Mac boards at the design's own 1156x680 with a setframe readback guard, and cropping both halves to the window's own content box. prescan goes from framingComparable 0/16 to 8/8, aspectRatioOfRatios 1.0 and scaleRatio 1.0 on every pair (evidence/runs/prescan-fidelity.json). Eight verdicts written: 2 pass, 5 fail, 1 unoracled.
subject.text: The campaign names design-review and be-my-witness as gates and has never run either, and the reason was never measured — it read as a skip. It is not. be-my-witness 0.2.0's deterministic prescan over all 16 pairs that hold both halves reports isEvidence 16/16, settled 16/16, framingComparable 0/16, proceed 0/16. Not a dead predicate: the scale ratios differ per lane (0.466x on the SURF-001 sidebar crop, 1.64x on the Mac boards, 0.942x on the phone) rather than returning a constant. Every reference was rasterised at a 1280x720 dpr-1 viewport, inside which prototype.html draws a fixed artboard rather than filling the frame, so rendering larger pads rather than enlarges. Re-rendering the reference does not fix it either: the design's Mac window is #win at 1156x680, aspect 1.700, and the build's is 980x620, aspect 1.581. The build half crops exactly — scale=(2096-1376)/(980-620)=2.0, margin=(2096-980*2)/2=68, content rect (68,68,1960,1240), precisely 2x the AX frame — but no crop reconciles two different window shapes. What would make them comparable is re-capturing the app at the design's window size, which means driving the app again and photographing a window shape the product does not use. Left unresolved deliberately: the structural and lexical differential in evidence/differential.md is the comparison that is valid here, and it ran.

subject.detail: `evidence/shots/captures.json` is the only manifest `capture-lineage.py --gate` reads, and two lanes write it: `capture-mac-glass.sh`, and `scripts/acceptance/name-glass-attachments.py`, which merges the iOS lane's rows up from `evidence/shots/ios/captures.json`. The Mac script wrote `json.dumps(rows)` — its own rows, whole file — so whichever lane captured last erased the other's lineage without saying anything. Measured 2026-08-20 on v0.9.1's new lineage plane: the parent held 16 Mac rows and none of the 9 iOS ones, and the gate reported 6 iOS captures UNSOURCED — 'the only thing binding this picture to SURF-012 is its filename', which is the correct verdict on a manifest that had been overwritten. The pictures were always right and their provenance was always recorded; it was recorded into a file that was then replaced. Fixed by merging on `path` in both writers, and the 9 rows were restored from the lane's own capture-time record rather than reconstructed.

subject.detail: `vacuity-check.py`'s blind pass reports `examined=1820 mutating=3 re-read-after=0 blind=3` over this test tree. All three read after the mutation: `restartIsIssuedBeforeTheStagingWrite` reads `WatchWorld.serverNames`, the log, `kicks.issued` and `WatchState.load`; `restartIsOwedBeforeTheWriteLands` reads `WatchState.load` inside the lock and `WatchWorld.serverNames` on both sides of the rename; `restartRechecksTheCamera` reads `model.entry.characters`. The heuristic looks for a read AFTER the last occurrence of a mutating verb, and in this product the verb `restart` is also the name of the thing being observed — `restartPending`, `restarted scratch-label` — so the last `restart` in the file sits inside the final assertion and nothing is textually after it. Recorded rather than acted on: the tests are correct as written, and rewording an assertion to satisfy a text heuristic would make the suite worse. The pass is still worth running; 3 of 1820 is a reviewable rate, and it is the check that would have caught 26 of 32 on the campaign it was built from. CAUSE CORRECTED 21 Aug 2026; the diagnosis recorded above was wrong. It said the mutator's name is the observable's name (`restart` inside `restartPending`). Measured against 0.9.2's actual patterns, that cannot happen: the mutator scan at vacuity-check.py:180 requires `(?<![A-Za-z0-9_])` + verb + `\w*\s*\(`, so `state.restartPending == false` never matches for want of the call parenthesis. The real cause is that the seven default readers are all snake_case -- list_, get_, read_, fetch_, sample_, count_, load_ -- and the nine default mutators mostly are too (stop_all, stop_runner, clear_, cancel_). This is a camelCase Swift codebase, so NEITHER side could fire. The pass examined 1657 test bodies and found 3 mutating, 0 re-reading and 3 blind: `blind=3` reads as almost nothing wrong, and meant almost nothing looked at. The denominator was printed and nobody read 3-of-1657 as the alarm it was. Fixed by declaring the project's own vocabulary, which 0.9.2 added for exactly this: campaign.json now carries `blindVocabulary` with 14 camelCase mutators and 13 readers, and the pass reports examined=1657 mutating=320 re-read-after=232 blind=88, with the vocabulary it used printed above the findings. Two of the three original findings resolved on their real reads (`WatchState.load(`, `WatchWorld.read(`). The third, restartRechecksTheCamera, stays flagged and correctly so for a verb heuristic: its only reads are property comparisons -- `model.step`, `model.entry.characters` -- which carry no verb at all. That is the ceiling of this instrument rather than a defect in the test, and it is why the 88 is a worklist and not a verdict: the vocabulary is hand-declared and unvalidated. Of the 21 findings the tool prints, 15 carry a @Test attribute and 5 are fixture helpers in dedicated client files that 0.9.2's per-file helper heuristic does not exclude, because it keys on a function being called more than once in its OWN file and these are called from their importers.
subject.title: the blind-test pass flags three tests that do read after mutating, because the mutator's name is the observable's name

subject.detail: The effect census over `app/Sources` with the test targets excluded finds no symbol that opens a connection to a paired device. REQ-016 — 'a pairing exchange actually contacts the other device and stores a record only after that contact succeeds' — therefore holds vacuously: the guarantee cannot be violated by a build that never contacts anything. This is DEF-001 (pairing transport unimplemented) reached from the effect side rather than from a failing assertion, and the two agree. Kept as its own row because the remedies differ: DEF-001 wants the transport built, and this row is the record that until it is, no test result about REQ-016 means what it appears to mean.

Discover: the design has install velocity and eval pills; the build prints 'No trend or velocity figure is shown. Measuring one needs a history of these indexes over time, which the router does not keep yet.' Checks: the design shows a graded eval run with per-case verdicts and a failed exchange; the build shows checks the router performed itself and states 'No model-graded evaluation exists in this product.' Servers: every design row carries a trailing evaluation pill; no build row does. The build is the correct half. ORCHESTRATOR.md's rule is that no number is displayed that the router does not observe, and the build obeys it on all four boards while explaining itself on three. The design of record predates the rule. Filed against the design rather than the build, and left open because which artifact gets changed - re-cut the mock, or annotate it as superseded - is the owner's call, not the campaign's.

subject.detail: The SURF-007 verdict of this campaign read 'the built board's rows carry no trailing controls at all' and 'the build also truncates the column that exists to explain'. Photographed at the design's own 1156pt, every Cleanup row carries `Inspect` and `Remove...`. The controls were outside the 980pt capture the verdict was written against. This is the failure mode the campaign already knows in a different costume: a picture that claims a subject it cannot support. The subject here was right and the frame was wrong, which is harder to see, because nothing about a correctly-named capture of a too-narrow window looks incorrect. The old verdict is kept and marked superseded rather than deleted. Fixed by photographing at the design's window size with a setframe readback guard that refuses to write a capture the window clamped.
