subject.detail: STILL PRESENT in 0.9.2, re-measured 21 Aug 2026 and the gap widened by one. witness-worklist.py reports `pairs=20 judgeable=17 WITHOUT a reference=3` and a comparable fraction of 85%, while capture-lineage.py --gate on the same registry reports `published captures: 16` and `JUDGED 16 of 16 judgeable (100%)`. Two gates in one skill version disagree about the judgeable denominator, 17 against 16, and neither names the other's population. CAUSE PINNED 21 Aug 2026. The disagreeing member is SURF-009, the Mac menu-bar popover, and it is the only one: witness-worklist's judgeable set and capture-lineage's judged set are identical apart from it. SURF-009 has a rendered design of record on disk (evidence/shots/mock/SURF-009.png), which is the sole condition witness-worklist tests, so it counts as the 17th judgeable pair. It has NO build capture at all — the popover cannot be opened without activating MCPRouter, which this campaign never does — so it never enters capture-lineage's population, which is built from published captures. capture-lineage therefore reports 'JUDGED 16 of 16 judgeable (100%)' on a registry holding 17 judgeable surfaces. That is the defect's whole shape, and it is the campaign's own first failure mode occurring INSIDE a gate written to prevent it: a denominator built from what was captured rather than from what was enumerated reads 100% precisely when a surface was never photographed. The direction is the dangerous one — an uncaptured surface raises the percentage instead of lowering it. Nothing is concealed in this campaign's own record: SURF-009 carries a shotNote naming the constraint, its three cases (CASE-0004, CASE-0006, CASE-0109) are n/a with the reason, and evidence/shots/pairs.json carries shot:null. The defect is that a reader of the gate line alone would not know to look for any of it. Remains open-detector: the fix is in the skill's scripts, which are not edited from this repo.
subject.note: DETECTOR DEFECT, recorded so its number is not published as a product finding. `witness-worklist.py:90` is `judgeable = [p for p in pairs if p.get("reference")]` -- it tests the reference half and never the shot half. SURF-009 (Mac menu-bar popover) has `shot: null` and an explicit `reason: build half uncaptured` in pairs.json, and is still counted, so the script reported `pairs=20 judgeable=17 comparable fraction: 85%` where the honest figure is 16 of 20, 80%. The script already defends the mirror-image failure and its own comment says why: a campaign reported 20 judgeable pairs whose references were all unrendered .html paths, and it now demotes those to unjudgeable with a named reason. The shot side has no equivalent test. Consequence here is one point of over-report and no false verdict, because capture-lineage.py computes judgeable from captures that exist and reported JUDGED 16 of 16 -- the two gates disagree by exactly this surface, and the disagreement is what found it. A campaign relying on the worklist alone would carry an uncompared surface inside a comparable fraction. Filed against the skill's script rather than this repo, so it is not fixed here.
subject.text: witness-worklist.py counts a pair as judgeable on the reference alone, so a surface with no build capture inflates the comparable fraction.

` at line 521 renders `[c for c in cases if state_of(c.get('status')) == 'fail']` -- failing CASES -- and the nav counter at line 305 is `counts['fail']`, the same population. So the page's Defects section counts 3 (the failing cases CASE-0010, CASE-0040, CASE-0110) while inventory.json holds 11 open defects, and the two numbers are about different things. MEASURED against the regenerated 124100-byte evidence.html: of the 11 open defects, 8 appear ZERO times -- DEF-008, DEF-040, DEF-041, DEF-042, DEF-043, DEF-047, DEF-048, DEF-051. The 3 that do appear are there by accident of prose: DEF-001 in two failing case notes and one passing one, DEF-033 and DEF-049 each inside a single PASSING case's note, rendered by the per-case table rather than by the Defects section. The peer reported 11 invisible; the true figure is 8, because writing a defect id into a case note is a convention doing a gate's job and it happened to fire three times. `campaign.py check` also exits 0 with all 11 open, so no gate holds on the registry either. This is the skill's own first-named failure mode -- covering a subset and reporting it as the whole -- arriving in its publisher: the gated half of the campaign is sound and the ungated half is the half people look at. The fix belongs in the installed skill (render inv['defect'], and count open defects in the nav), not in this repo; recorded rather than patched, precedent DEF-048 and DEF-051. Its header line is sharper than an omission -- it prints `73 pass . 3 fail . 0 skip . 4 n/a . 0 open . armed 73/73`, where `0 open` is the count of open CASES, on a campaign holding 12 open defects. subject.detail: Measured 2026-08-21, test-campaign 0.9.2. `ledger.md`'s header line reads `80 cases` and `73 pass · 3 fail · 0 skip · 4 n/a`; its table carries 72 rows. The eight absent cases are CASE-0145, 0146, 0147, 0148 (lane router-daemon) and CASE-0151, 0152, 0153, 0154 (lane swiftui). All eight pass. MECHANISM, exact. The writer at campaign.py:1218-1241 buckets every case with `by_surface.setdefault(c.get('surface', '—'), [])`, so a case whose `surface` is absent lands under the literal key `'—'`. It then emits rows with `for s in inventory['surface']: for c in by_surface.get(s['id'], [])`. `'—'` is not a surface id, so that bucket is never visited and its contents are never printed. Nothing warns; the count in the header comes from a different code path than the rows beneath it, which is why the two disagree without either being flagged. WHAT IS LOST. CASE-0145 through CASE-0148 are this campaign's four `effect-witness` cases — the rung that required building a recorder outside the product, and the most expensive evidence in the run. They are absent from the ledger entirely. A reader of ledger.md cannot learn that the campaign has an effect-witness rung at all. DIRECTION. The eight dropped are all passes, so the table under-states the work rather than over-stating it. That makes it the safer direction, and it does not make it safe: a reader counting 72 rows against a stated 80 meets an unexplained gap of exactly the kind this campaign is written to make impossible, and the campaign's own rule is that every sweep prints its denominator. SCOPE. Ledger-specific. evidence.html renders all eight (5 to 11 references each, measured by grep), so the HTML page is correct and only the markdown artifact is affected. Distinct from DEF-052, which is about the defect registry being absent from BOTH artifacts; this one is about cases, in one artifact, via a different mechanism. NOT FIXED FROM HERE: campaign.py lives in the installed skill cache, not this repo.

subject.detail: Measured 2026-08-21. `.gitmodules` vendors `.claude/plugins/fledgeling-plugins` at `main`, and `planning/features-to-triage/LEDGER.md`'s allocation notes state the reason: 'a runner reads mockup-fidelity, mac-craft, design-craft and ux-craft at a repo-relative path rather than depending on the machine.' For test-campaign that is not what happens. The submodule (HEAD baaf79a, branch main, clean) carries `plugins/test-campaign` at version 0.5.0, whose `skills/test-campaign/scripts` holds five files: attach-shots.py, campaign.py, evidence-page.py, strict-check.py, witness-worklist.py. It has no `vacuity-check.py` and no `capture-lineage.py`; `grep effect-witness strict-check.py` returns nothing and `grep -c blindVocabulary vacuity-check.py` cannot run because the file is absent. Every gate this campaign reports ran from `~/.claude/plugins/cache/fledgeling-plugins/test-campaign/0.9.2/`, on the machine. The vacuity census, the effect-witness rung, the blind-mutation pass, the capture-lineage ratchet and the strict score of 65 all come from code the submodule does not contain, four minor versions ahead of it. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PIPELINE, and it is the reason this is filed rather than noted: DEF-051, DEF-052, DEF-054, DEF-055 and DEF-056 are defects in 0.9.2's scripts. None of that code is in this repo at any path, so no ship-feature runner working in an mcp-router worktree can fix them. They are upstream work in github.com/fledgeling-co/fledgeling-plugins, and closing them requires a change pushed to that repo plus a submodule bump here — a different repo and an outward-facing action. Separately, a fresh clone that follows the documented `git submodule update --init --recursive` gets 0.5.0 and would reproduce none of this campaign's numbers. Not fixed here: which version the submodule should track, and whether the campaign should run from it rather than the cache, is the owner's call.

subject.text: Found while building R22's redactor, filed rather than fixed. `Describe.row` emits `command` and `args` RAW, and `ControlHandler.gate` reads the token only for POST/DELETE/PATCH, so the complete command line of every stdio upstream is readable by anything that can open the loopback port. The same function is careful in the adjacent case — it emits `envKeys` and `headerKeys` and never a value, with B10's reasoning attached — so argv is the one credential-carrying position on that route that is published whole. It matters because argv IS a credential channel: `--token=`, `--api-key=` and a connection string with an inline password are ordinary MCP server invocations, and R22 scrubs args for exactly that reason. The exposure predates R22 and is not made worse by it: the bundle's args go through the value scrub, and this route's do not. NOT FIXED HERE, and the reason is a parity decision rather than effort. `GET /servers` is reference-diffed — `control-servers-get` in planning/parity/surface.tsv, verdict `proven` — so redacting args moves a surface R4 compares byte for byte, and the ungated GET is itself a ported defect this repository records rather than silently repairs. Closing it means changing both routers or declaring a divergence, and that is the owner's call. 2026-10-19 — FIXED IN BOTH ROUTERS by merge 74d15306 (Merge ai/argv-redact), whose subject records that GET /servers stops publishing secret-bearing argv. Unit evidence: ArgvRedactionTests (app/Tests/RouterCoreTests/ArgvRedactionTests.swift) and test/argv-redact.test.ts, with parity vectors in argv-redact.json. Verified 2026-10-19: the `ArgvRedactionTests` suite passed under `swift test`, and `node --test` on test/argv-redact.test.ts passed. Status is fixed · in-test. No campaign re-run is recorded against this row.

subject.text: FOUND BY ARMING, not by reading. The status remap on this branch first synced `defects.in.json` to `inventory.json` wholesale, and the sync moved three rows that have nothing to do with vocabulary: DEF-002 `open` -> `closed`, DEF-040 `open-instrument` -> `fixed · in-campaign`, DEF-063 `open · measured` -> `open`. Those are adjudications, not spellings, so the sync was reverted and only the six unclassifiable SHAPES were rewritten in place. THE STANDING FACT: `reckon.read_campaign` reads defects from `inventory.json` and from nowhere else, so `defects.in.json` is a hand-edited source that no reckoning reads. Three of its 24 rows say something different from the file that is read, and nothing compares them. A reader who opens the source file gets a different answer about DEF-002, DEF-040 and DEF-063 than the ledger gives. WHAT IS NOT SETTLED, and why this is open rather than fixed: which of the two files is right about each of the three is an adjudication somebody has to make by reading the defect, and a runner remapping words is the wrong person to make it. `defect-status-vocabulary-gate.py` reads both files, so a NEW unclassifiable word is caught in either; it has no opinion on whether two files that both classify agree with each other.

subject.detail: **The recorded cause was wrong, and this replaces it.** It said the shutter fired during a board transition and named the fix as a settle in `capture-mac-glass.sh`. Measured 20 Aug 2026 from the accessibility dumps the same script already writes, one per board, beside the pictures: | board | window | AXSplitGroup | clipped | |---|---|---|---| | Servers, Activity, Cleanup, Inbox, Settings | 980pt | 980pt | — | | Checks | 980pt | 988pt | 8pt | | Skills | 980pt | 1044pt | 64pt | | Discover | 980pt | 1119pt | 139pt | Every window in the run is the same 980x620 and every capture is the same 2096x1376, so no capture rect is wrong and no shutter is early. What differs is the shell **inside** the window: on three boards `NavigationSplitView` lays out wider than the window and centres the excess — the split group's origin moves left by exactly half the overflow in all three cases (180→148 for 64pt, 180→110.5 for 139pt, 180→176 for 8pt), which is what makes the clipping symmetrical. That is why the sidebar's section headers read `unning` and `brary` while the nav rows beside them are whole: the headers sit at a smaller leading inset and fall off first, and the header's trailing controls — `Manage marketplaces.`, `Review 2.3.0…` — fall off the right by the same amount. So this is a product defect on three boards rather than a lane defect on two captures, and it is worse than recorded: Checks overflows too, by 8pt, which is small enough that nobody reading the picture saw it. The app declares no minimum window width anywhere, so nothing stops a user reaching this state — the campaign's 980pt window is an ordinary size, not a stress case. The consequence that made it a defect stands unchanged and is now better founded: a clipped capture is admissible for what it shows and silent about what it cut, so a reader cannot tell an absent control from a cropped one. Both witness verdicts that depend on these captures say in their method field that the right-hand controls were read from the accessibility dump instead. `capture-mac-glass.sh` now prints `board width: examined=14 overflowing=3` every run, with a line naming each board and its excess. Reported rather than enforced, because three boards overflow today and a known red in `make all` either blocks unrelated work or gets its assertion softened. NOT FIXED, and the fix is a decision rather than a repair. Either the shell declares a minimum window width at least as wide as its widest board — one line, guarantees nothing ever clips, and costs users on small screens a window they cannot shrink — or the three boards compress, which keeps small screens usable and is per-board column work across all three. Discover at 1119pt is the one that decides how much that costs. PARTLY CLOSED 20 Aug 2026, on `ai/x4`, and the part that is not closed is named rather than left to look finished. The mechanism turned out to be a chain rather than a board: each row's fixed columns report a hard minimum width, the detail pane sums them, `NavigationSplitView` reports that as its own minimum, and nothing ever reads it back — this app opts into no minimum window size and `windowResizability` defaults to `.automatic` — so the window proposes 980pt and SwiftUI **places** the oversized child with default centre alignment. The symmetry was the tell. Referred to the xAI lane (grok-4.6, xhigh) with the measured table; it named the propagation as the bug, called both listed fixes second-best, and its Q3 answer — placement plus `.automatic` resizability rather than any documented split-view overflow mode — is what the one-line fix then confirmed. FIXED: `ContentZone` carries `.frame(minWidth: 0, maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)`. Measured on the rebuilt app through the same accessibility channel: all eight boards read `split=980` inside a `window=980`, overflowing 0 of 8, where the same probe on the previous build read 3 of 8. The sidebar is whole again — `Running`, `Library` and the footer readout all render in full where they were `unning` and `brary`. The leading alignment is the deliberate half: it decides who loses when the content still does not fit, and the answer is never the navigation. STILL OPEN: the boards' content is still wider than the detail pane on those three, so the trailing chrome is cut at the pane's right edge — Discover's search field reads `Search the regis` and a body sentence loses its last word. That is one-edge clipping where it was two, and it is the conventional behaviour of a too-narrow window rather than a split view eating its own sidebar, but it is still content going missing without saying so. Closing it needs the three boards' columns to flex, which is a design decision about what Discover looks like compressed and is the owner's rather than mine. GUARDED two ways, and the two see different things. `capture-mac-glass.sh` now **fails** on any board whose split group exceeds its window, and refuses to pass on `examined=0`; all three arms were exercised on 20 Aug 2026 — red at 3 of 14, green at 0 of 14, and exit 1 with no dumps at all. `ShellDetailWidthTests` asserts the modifier in `ShellWindow`'s detail column so a revert is red in `make test` rather than on the next glass run. That test's own first version was a detector defect found by arming: it searched the raw source slice, and the modifier it looks for is named in the doc comment three lines above it, so deleting the modifier left the assertion green. Comments are stripped before matching now, and both halves were re-armed separately. CLOSED 20 Aug 2026, and the second half corrected the first half's diagnosis of *which* content was too wide. The brief written from the split-group numbers said three boards' table columns needed to flex. A pane-level probe — every leaf's right edge against the window's, read from the same dumps — says otherwise, and it says so only after the probe itself was fixed: the first version read the frame's **y** where it meant **x** and reported clipping on seven of eight boards, which the pixels flatly denied. The Settings capture is whole, and looking at it is what caught the field offset. A frame's last five fields are x, y, w, h and a flag; the split-group gate only ever compared widths, which is why it was right while the leaf probe was wrong. Corrected, the drivers are: - **Discover**: content wants 823pt against a 684pt pane. Not the table — cutting `nameColumn` from 216pt to 96pt moved the number by **zero**. It is the controls row: a `.fixedSize()` segmented picker measuring 567pt beside a search field pinned at 240pt. - **Skills**: 748pt against 684pt, same shape — a 516pt fixed picker and a 216pt pinned field. - **Checks**: not a content defect at all. Its real content ends at 1152pt inside a 1160pt pane; the only thing past the edge is `KeyClaimProbe`, the `#if DEBUG` test surface A21 names, overhanging by 4pt. It is absent from any build a user runs, and it is what the whole 8pt split-group excess on this board was. FIXED by giving each board a `searchMinWidth` of four units and declaring the field `minWidth:idealWidth:maxWidth:` rather than `width:`. The picker cannot give a point back — that is what `.fixedSize()` means, and it is right, because a segmented control has nowhere to put a truncated label — so the field is the only control in the row that can. It renders at its full width wherever there is room and shows about eight characters at the narrowest window this app is used at, which is less than anyone wants and more than nothing: it still takes focus, accepts a query and submits. Measured after: every board reads `split=980` in a `window=980`, and the only leaf past the pane edge on any of the eight is a 1pt scrollbar — plus the Debug key probe's 4pt on Checks. Before, Discover's rows and footnote sat at 1283pt against an edge of 1160. GUARDED by a second test in `ShellDetailWidthTests`, armed 20 Aug 2026: restoring `.frame(width: DiscoverBoardMetrics.searchWidth)` reddens all three of its assertions. It names the two boards rather than looping over every file, because those are the two the measurement covers — a third board growing this problem is a new measurement, not a case this test silently already made.

subject.detail: Measured 2026-08-27 by G15, while enumerating SURF-025. The committed glass evidence under planning/test-campaign/evidence/ax was last written by commit cef3729 on 20 Aug. M22 then added two destinations and RENUMBERED four accelerators, and nothing re-took the pictures. Running bin/capture-mac-glass.sh against the current build turns four previously-passing cases red, and in every one of them the PRODUCT is right and the recorded evidence is stale: 1. THE MENU MAP. Committed SURF-001.menu.txt binds Cmd-4 to `Discover`; the running app binds Cmd-4 to `Harnesses`, exactly as Destination.swift's selectionDigit declares (activity 1, servers 2, skills 3, harnesses 4, discover 5, inbox 6, evals 7, cleanup 8, insights 9). glass-assert.py's SURF-001 `menu` dict is the pre-M22 map, so CASE-0001 asserts five bindings the shipped build does not have. 2. SETTINGS IS NOT A SIDEBAR ROW. M15 made Settings a Scene and removed the case from Destination, and capture-mac-glass.sh still does `axkit select Settings`. That select now fails — `axkit: no sidebar row starting 'Settings'` — the app stays on Cleanup, and the script photographs the CLEANUP board and files it as SURF-011. CASE-0016 and CASE-0111 fail against it. THE CAMPAIGN'S OWN INSTRUMENTS CAUGHT BOTH, WHICH IS THE ONE GOOD PART. The capture manifest's readback records that picture as target `app://mac/cleanup` under subject SURF-011, contradicting its own filename — the exact mechanism the script was rebuilt around. Independently, glass-assert.py --discriminate reports LEAK SURF-007 wrongly accepted 1 of 8 foreign board dumps: SURF-011 — because SURF-011's dump IS the Cleanup board. Two instruments, one cause. WHY THIS IS THE SAME FINDING AS G14'S, ONE LAYER DOWN. G14 found the surface LIST had not grown since it was written. This is the EVIDENCE not having been re-taken since the build moved. In both cases a completeness gate reported clean because the thing it measured was a stale artefact rather than the product. NOT FIXED HERE, DELIBERATELY. G15's remit is the Harnesses enumeration, and correcting glass-assert.py's menu map or the Settings navigation would be editing an assertion to restore a green — even though the product is right, that is the move this campaign forbids, and the stale assertion is the instrument that found this. subject.detail: DETECTOR DEFECT in test-campaign 0.9.2, found 21 Aug 2026. attach-shots.py iterates every image under evidence/shots and assigns `hit['shot'] = rel` on each match, last write wins, with no preference for a build capture over a design render. This campaign keeps six directories under evidence/shots (16 root, 8 design-size, 16 fidelity, 9 ios, 17 mock, 11 mock-hidpi), so for SURF-001 the candidates in iteration order are SURF-001.build.png, SURF-001.shell.png, mock/SURF-001.png, mock-hidpi/SURF-001.full.png -- and the last one wins. MEASURED for SURF-001, SURF-002 and SURF-006: `--apply` would repoint each surface's `shot` from its build capture to `evidence/shots/mock-hidpi/SURF-00N.full.png`, which is the render of the DESIGN, not the build. That is the skill's own headline failure mode -- publishing a picture of one thing under the name of another -- arriving in a sibling of the plane built to prevent it, and it would do so while every other gate stayed green, because capture-lineage.py gates the 16 captures cited by CASES and the surface wall is a different population. The report compounds it: the UNCORROBORATED block prints surface ids (SURF-001 ... SURF-011) rather than the file each verdict is about, so a reader sees eleven surfaces apparently lacking provenance when in fact each surface's ACTUAL `shot` field points at a corroborated build capture and the complaint is about a mock render nobody intended to attach. Distinguishing the two costs a re-derivation of the matcher by hand. Recorded rather than patched, precedent DEF-048, DEF-051, DEF-052 and DEF-053. The campaign's standing refusal to run `--apply` here predates this and was based on the DEF-006 mis-wire; it now has a measured mechanism behind it. Separately closed while investigating: this campaign's design-size captures carried their provenance in a second manifest, evidence/shots/design-size/captures.json, in a different schema ({captures:[...]} against the root's bare list) that no gate reads. Its 8 entries were merged into the root manifest with `target` derived from the root's declared target for the same subject and corroborated by each capture's own windowTitleReadback -- Servers, Activity, Skills, Discover, Inbox, Checks, Cleanup, Settings, every one matching -- recorded at capture time, and each carries `targetDerivedFrom` saying so. That was the campaign's own inconsistency and is fixed here; it was not the cause of the 11. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-27 (G21) after `evidence/shots/captures.json` was made a derived file. The uncorroborated count is 12 and stays 12: SURF-001..011 and SURF-022. Eleven of them are this defect -- `mock-hidpi/` sorts last, so it is the row that decides each surface's `shotProvenance`. The mock rows in the manifest deliberately carry NO `target`; the address the channel was pointed at is recorded in full as `renderedFrom`, with an `attachHazard` field naming this defect. Measured both ways on this tree: writing that address as `target` instead drops the uncorroborated count from 12 to 1 and DISARMS `--apply`'s refusal, because `attach-shots.py` only checks the field is present and never compares it to the subject's route -- which is item 5 of X8's work order. So the report going quiet would have been this defect getting worse while looking fixed. The twelfth, SURF-022, is not this defect: see DEF-061.

subject.detail: Measured 2026-09-03 (WE3) on LUKESFF, Windows 11, CPython 3.13, console codepage 1252. `campaign.py`'s loader is `return json.loads(p.read_text())` with no `encoding=`. `Path.read_text()` defaults to `locale.getencoding()`, which is cp1252 here. This campaign's `inventory.json` holds em dashes and middots, so: $ python vendor/test-campaign/.../campaign.py check planning/test-campaign UnicodeDecodeError: 'charmap' codec can't decode byte 0x9d in position 284168 exit 1 It is a traceback rather than a verdict, and `exit 1` is the same code the gate uses for 'not ready to report'. A caller reading the exit status alone cannot tell a campaign that failed its checks from one the checker could not open. `PYTHONUTF8=1` makes it run; with that set it reaches its checks and reports normally, which is how the rest of this session's `campaign.py` measurements were taken. SCOPE. Windows hosts only -- macOS and most Linux default to UTF-8, which is why the campaign never met this on the Mac. It is not confined to `campaign.py`: `vacuity-check.py`, `strict-check.py` and `attach-shots.py` in the pinned 0.9.2 read and WRITE with the same bare calls, so on this host `attach-shots.py --apply` would write `inventory.json` back in cp1252 and mangle every em dash in the register. That one is a data-loss path rather than a crash, and it is the reason this is filed at detector severity rather than as a nuisance.
subject.title: campaign.py reads the registry with no encoding, so on a Windows console it dies on the first non-ASCII byte and checks nothing

subject.detail: Found 20 Aug 2026 while building R8's gate against both routers. Against a fixture returning `-32603` with the message `Internal error: Authentication required`, the reference records `MCP error -32603: Internal error: Authentication required` and the Swift router records `[-32603] Internal error`. The upstream's own message is gone. CAUSE, cited exactly: modelcontextprotocol/swift-sdk 0.12.1, `Sources/MCP/Base/Error.swift:217-240`. The decoder reads the server's `message`, then maps the code — `-32700`, `-32600`, `-32601` and `-32602` each pass `unwrapDetail(message)`, and `-32603` alone passes `unwrapDetail(nil)`. `unwrapDetail(fallback)` returns `data.detail` when present and the fallback otherwise, so a server that answers -32603 with a message and no `data.detail` has its message discarded, and `Error.swift:91` renders `"Internal error" + (detail.map { ": \($0)" } ?? "")` as the bare canonical name. -32603 is the code servers use for an arbitrary application error, so it is the one that loses the most. TWO consequences: for the whole class of -32603 upstream errors the Swift router tells the user strictly less than the reference does; and R8's Swift half cannot detect a credential refusal at all, because there is no text left to match. This is a coverage gap in the parity suite as much as a defect in the SDK — no parity scenario had ever exercised a JSON-RPC error carrying a detailed message, which is why 82 proven rows never saw it. Remedies, none taken: report upstream and take a fixed release; pin a patched fork; or read the JSON-RPC error before the SDK types it, which needs a seam below the client.
subject.title: the Swift MCP SDK discards an upstream's error message for code -32603, so the router reports less than the reference does

The claim is that the expiry is DERIVED from files the router already wrote rather than asked of the upstream, and half of that claim is an absence: nothing was spawned. subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=package not installed
subject.note: A real MSIX, built, deployed and removed, with a recorder at each step that is not the thing that wrote it. MakeAppx packs and .NET's ZipArchive reads the OPC container back - so the identity assertion is made against the PACKED ARTIFACT rather than against the file on disk that was handed to the packer. `winget validate` is the winget client applying a schema this repository does not own. Add-AppxPackage deploys and Get-AppxPackage reports: Fledgeling.MCPRouter_0.1.0.0_x64__facmrsw33693e. THE INSTALL ARM IS WHAT TURNS A FILE INTO A PACKAGE. A manifest can pack cleanly, validate cleanly, and be refused at deployment for a capability, an architecture or a signature - and every static check in the world passes right up to that point. 'CLEAN UNINSTALL RULES' IS THE HALF WORTH READING TWICE. UninstallGuidance promises that uninstalling preserves %USERPROFILE%\.claude\mcp-router. That is a promise about what SURVIVES, and a promise about survival cannot be checked by any amount of reading - only by an uninstall that actually ran. The lane plants a marker, installs, removes, and requires both that the deployment stack reports the package gone and that the marker is still there. WHAT THE LANE PUTS BACK: a self-signed certificate is added to LocalMachine\TrustedPeople so an unsigned developer package can deploy at all, and removed in a finally block however the run ends. Verified afterwards: zero Fledgeling.* packages, zero witness certificates. A lane that left a trusted publisher behind would have changed what this machine will install, silently and for every future run. NOT SETTLED: that anyone can obtain the package. Nothing publishes it, the winget InstallerUrl is a deliberate example.invalid placeholder, and this lane asserts the placeholder is PRESENT so the manifest cannot be mistaken for a shipping one. DEF-083 carries the publishing step, which needs a signing certificate and a pull request into a third-party repository.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=one capability queued
subject.note: The toast itself, in the Action Center, read by a process that cannot raise one. DEF-082 filed this as unmeasurable and gave a reason: UserNotificationListener's userNotificationListener capability is only grantable to a packaged application, and MCPRouter.Shell is WindowsPackageType=None, so the row was said to be downstream of WIN19's MSIX. THE REASON WAS WRONG, AND IT WAS WRONG BEFORE WIN19 LANDED. Measured on this host from an ordinary unpackaged Win32 console process with no package identity at all - Package.Current throws InvalidOperationException, which the lane asserts rather than assumes - UserNotificationListener.Current resolves, RequestAccessAsync returns Allowed with no consent prompt, and GetNotificationsAsync returns the toasts that are really there. On the first run those included three raised by win22-toast-witness the day before, carrying the exact strings NotificationPresentation writes. No MSIX, no capability, no packaged identity. WHAT IS STILL NOT AVAILABLE UNPACKAGED, and it bounds this case: every member of UserNotification.AppInfo throws NotImplementedException 0x80004001 for a caller with no package identity, so the listener can say what a notification SAYS and when it arrived and cannot say who raised it. Attribution here is the payload text, which the product owns, inside a time window this run opened - weaker than a publisher identity, and recorded as such. THE RECORDER IS NOT THE WRITER AND IS NOT EVEN THE SAME PROCESS: app/windows/MCPRouter.Witness.ActionCenter shares no code with the shell and cannot raise a notification. The shell's toast-probe.json is carried as the writer's self-report and graded by nothing. THE PRESENCE CONTROL is a removal: the matched notification is taken back out through the listener and the Action Center is read a third time, and the recorder is required to say no about it.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=one capability queued
subject.note: The COM activator the Windows notification platform wrote, read out of the registry by a process that did not write it. The writer is AppNotificationManager.Register() inside the shell; the recorder is HKCU through PowerShell's registry provider, and nothing of this repository's sits between them. Four arms. BASELINE requires the AUMID key to be ABSENT before the shell launches, so what the other three read is this launch. The three EFFECT arms read the key, the CustomActivator CLSID it names, and that CLSID's LocalServer32 - which came back as MCPRouter.Shell.exe carrying the platform's own ----AppNotificationActivated: argument, a string this repository does not write anywhere. THE ACTIVATOR IS THE ARM THAT CARRIES THE ITEM. A toast outlives the process that raised it; when somebody presses Review an hour later, Windows COM-activates the LocalServer32 registered for that CLSID. Without it the toast still appears and pressing it does nothing, which is the failure that looks most like success and exactly what a screenshot of a notification would have certified. WHAT THIS CASE DOES NOT SETTLE: that a toast is drawn, and that a press re-activates the app. Both need UserNotificationListener, whose capability is only grantable to a packaged application; DEF-082 carries them and is downstream of DEF-073. The shell's own report that the platform accepted a Show is carried in the evidence as writerSelfReport and is graded by nothing, because a process reporting its own effect is the shape of claim DEF-072 was about.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=no task registered
subject.note: The Windows task scheduler holding a task the product registered, read by an API that did not write it. The writer is MCPRouter.Shell.Live's LogonTaskSupervisor driving schtasks.exe with the Task Scheduler XML it builds; the recorder is Get-ScheduledTask, the ScheduledTasks module over the scheduler's WMI provider - a different API, a different process and a different vocabulary for the same facts. The XML says RunLevel LeastPrivilege and the recorder answers RunLevel Limited, and nothing in this repository translates between them. The scheduler also normalised the interval this run asked for, PT60S, into PT1M, which is the plainest available evidence that the read did not come back through anything this code wrote. EIGHT ARMS, AND TWO ARE ABOUT THE INSTRUMENT. BASELINE requires the recorder to report the task ABSENT before registration - without it, a task left behind by an interrupted run makes every other arm pass over a run that registered nothing. SILENCE requires it to report absence again after removal, which is what separates a reader from an echo: a recorder that always answered yes would satisfy the six product arms by construction. The other six read the three claims LifecyclePresentation prints to the operator - triggered at logon, un-elevated, restarting on failure - plus the executable and port this run asked for, plus presence and removal. WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE, and the reason it is one case rather than the whole of REQ-035: nothing here logs the user out, so the trigger has never been watched to fire, and nothing here starts or kills a daemon, so the restart has never been watched to happen. DEF-081 carries those two. This case settles that the registration the product performs produces, in the Windows task scheduler, a task carrying the properties the product's own UI describes - which before 2026-09-02 was unmeasured entirely, and which DEF-074 recorded as a supervision model nothing performed.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=a supervised process that dies
subject.note: The half of WIN23's supervision promise that had never been watched: a daemon the Windows task scheduler starts, loses, and starts again. DEF-081 filed it as unmeasurable and named the blocker as a missing Windows daemon binary; the blocker was real and is gone - app/windows/MCPRouter.Witness.Daemon is a harness process that starts, records its own start and waits to be killed, so there is something for the scheduler to supervise. WHAT THE MEASUREMENT FOUND IS NOT WHAT THE ROW EXPECTED. The registration the product wrote carried RestartOnFailure with a 60-second interval and a count of 3, and it did not restart the daemon at all. Killed, watched 150 seconds, on the unified scheduling engine and the legacy one, for a run started by a trigger and one started on demand: four registrations, no restart. The same block DID restart, three times at exactly 60 seconds, a task whose Command named a file that does not exist - so the instrument can see a restart, and RestartOnFailure governs a task that fails to LAUNCH rather than one whose action launched and later died. DEF-320 carries that, and the product now writes a Repetition on the trigger alongside MultipleInstancesPolicy IgnoreNew. THE RECORDERS ARE TWO AND NEITHER WROTE ANYTHING: Get-ScheduledTaskInfo for the scheduler's own account of its runs, and Get-CimInstance Win32_Process for the process identity, which is what makes 'it came back' a different process id rather than a report from the thing that came back. The daemon's own run log is carried and graded by nothing. EIGHT ARMS, THREE OF THEM ABOUT THE INSTRUMENT: BASELINE requires both tasks absent and no daemon running, so nothing below is inherited from an interrupted run; CLAIM.repetition and CLAIM.ignorenew read the product's own unmodified logon registration back through the WMI provider; SILENCE requires both recorders to say no once the tasks are gone. ONE SUBSTITUTION, SAID OUT LOUD: a trigger repetition does not apply to an on-demand start - measured, twice - so the live task carries a TimeTrigger where the product writes a LogonTrigger, because this lane must not log the machine out. Every Setting, the repetition interval, the principal, the action and the instances policy are the product's own document. That the trigger fires AT LOGON is still unwitnessed and DEF-081 keeps it.

Without it the target's 35 surface assertions are vacuous in a way that reads exactly like a product rendering no copy — DEF-029, where they were vacuous for ten consecutive runs. Armed three ways on 20 Aug 2026: renaming the symbol fails this case alone; mutating the call to `(false)` on a device created for the arm reads 53 failures across 36 tests, which is what proves the other 35 depend on it; and the first run ever taken on a device whose engine had never been live is clean, which proves the fix needs no warm-up on a fresh device. subject.cell: execution-plane=in-process · state=a server with a probe interval that is not live
subject.note: A scheduled sweep observes; it does not create the thing it is observing. `UpstreamHealthMonitorTests` H16 stages a server with a 60-second interval that the pool reports as not live, runs one sweep, and asserts on the PROBER rather than on the record: the thing that would spawn a child was never called, and the record says so with a reason rather than a failure. subject.evidence: vacuous
subject.note: HISTORICAL FINDING (2026-08-29, source revision 83e5380): the following absence finding describes that revision, not the current production transport. I5 measured neither side implements a transport; the phone stores a paired-Mac record for a Mac it never contacted. RE-CLASSED `contradicted` -> `vacuous` on 2026-08-29 by K4, per references/effect-boundary.md SS2: contradicted means the product does the thing and does it differently from the document; vacuous means the product does not do the thing at all, so there is nothing for the constraint to be true or false about. The two want different remedies and reading them as one sends a missing subsystem to the place that fixes a wrong one. SS3 names this row's exact shape -- a requirement whose declared effect class has no provider in production source is vacuous at phase 1, before any test is written. MEASURED AT `83e5380`, and the narrow true thing rather than the general one (SS7: absence is a fact about this commit). `PairingService` has exactly ONE conformance in production source, `public struct FixturePairingService: PairingService`, `app/Sources/MCPRouterKit/Pairing/PairingService.swift:31`; the shipped shell wires it by default, `pairing: any PairingService = FixturePairingService()`, `app/Sources/MCPRouterUI/Phone/PhoneShell.swift:63`. No `URLSession`, `NWConnection`, `NWListener` or `Network.NW` symbol appears anywhere under `app/Sources/MCPRouterKit/Pairing/` (9 files); the fourteen files in `app/Sources` that do hold one are OAuth, control-plane, registry and loopback-server code, none of it reachable from the pairing path. The protocol's own docstring states the decision rather than leaving it inferred: 'No live implementation ships in this item, and that is a decision rather than a gap.' SO THE CLAIM IS NOT BOUND, AND THE `provider` FIELD STAYS EMPTY DELIBERATELY. There is no symbol that opens the socket to bind it to. `vacuity-check.py --gate` therefore continues to report REQ-016 as uncensused, correctly, and that finding is a dispositioned expectation rather than a silence: it is the vacuity, visible. What the re-class buys is that `campaign.py check` stops counting REQ-016 as an effect somebody failed to witness -- `unwitnessed_effects` excludes `vacuous` (campaign.py:1099) -- and starts reporting it as the product gap it is. The remedy is to build the transport (I5, DEF-001) or to withdraw the requirement; neither is K4's.

subject.note: J2. Every sidebar row is selected in turn and the effect is read in the RESTORATION STORE, which is a different channel from the one that struck: `ShellModel.selection`'s `didSet` calls `store.save(destination:)`, so a real selection leaves a value in a scratch `UserDefaults` suite that nothing in the test wrote, and that a relaunch reads. `model.selection == .servers` after `model.select(.servers)` was deliberately NOT used — it reads the property the call just wrote, which is the actuation side of the vacuous assertion (`references/inert-ui.md`, `detector-defects.md` §11). Each row is approached from a DIFFERENT destination, because `didSet` guards on `oldValue != selection` and a loop starting where the model boots would have the first row write nothing at all. The destination-collapse relation is asserted as a count rather than as seven separate greens: seven presses, seven DISTINCT persisted values, so a shell whose rows all led to one place fails on the cardinality. A second model built on the same store comes up where the last row left it, which is the read-back a relaunch actually performs. `Settings` is the eighth control and is not a destination: M15 moved it to a scene of its own, so the effect read is the installed opener firing exactly once AND the console's persisted destination not moving. Both halves, because an implementation that opened the scene and also selected a board would pass the first alone. LIMIT, stated rather than left implicit: a persisted destination proves the selection took. It does not prove a different board was DRAWN — SwiftUI's view tree is opaque to a SwiftPM test and `ContentZone`'s switch is unreachable from here. That half is CASE-0001's, on glass, and it is FAILING (DEF-058, DEF-059), so it counts nothing. This is the in-process half and says which half it is.

J2. `Remove` is driven with the history checkbox both ways and the effect is read as the operation the client recorded — `remove(keepHistory)` then `remove`. The sheet closing and the selection dropping are the app's own report that it worked and are deliberately not the observable: `references/inert-ui.md` §3 is exactly a handler that changes a banner and does nothing else.

K3. `Install` is driven at `DiscoverBoardModel.install` and the effect is read as the DECLARATION THE CLIENT RECORDED — name, command and args, checked against the row that was pressed rather than against the function that built them. Two entries are staged with different install blocks and both are pressed, so a handler that declares a fixed payload, or the row it happened to have selected, fails on the second press; one press and one assertion cannot tell those apart. The read refused is `board.rows[0].installed == true`. `markInstalled` writes that from the board's own copy of the response, so it is true whether or not anything reached the router — the app's report that it worked, which is what the arm leaves standing.

N8. The inertness guard on the untrusted-input boundary, made capable of failing. M19 shipped `MarkdownSecurityTests.htmlIsInert` with four spellings that named `javascript:`, no scheme, or nothing, and two assertions -- no link, no `imageURL` -- that `MarkdownInline.sanitized` makes true of every input it touches. It could not go red. M30 wired `ControlAPICapabilityDocumentSource` into the shipped UI, so router-served third-party text now reaches this renderer in a Release build, and the guard on it measured nothing. MEASURED, not assumed: the platform parser does keep inline HTML inert -- under `MarkdownInline`'s own options it hands each tag back as characters and marks it `.inlineHTML`, an intent naming no destination, and it does so under all four combinations of `allowsExtendedAttributes` and `interpretedSyntax`. Swift 6.2, macOS 26.6.2 (25G83), Debug, `swift test`. So this was an evidence defect and not a live vulnerability, and the fix is the assertion rather than new sanitisation. Two `https` spellings were added, because `https` is the one scheme the allowlist keeps and therefore the only one that can carry an interpreted `<a>` through to the assertion; a presence control runs the same reader over the markdown twin of the same destination first; and two clauses were added that the old body did not have -- handed back verbatim, and no attribute beyond the `.inlineHTML` marker. That last clause also corrects the test's own claim: the parser DOES attach one attribute to inline HTML and `sanitized` carries it, so the old name -- `inline HTML acquires no attribute of any kind` -- was false as written as well as unfailable, which is why nobody found out.

subject.note: R22. The requirement is written as an honesty guardrail rather than a behaviour because the load-bearing half is a promise about what is NOT in the output, and this campaign's own history is that such a promise is satisfied trivially by producing nothing. Every case under it therefore pairs its absence with a presence: a public canary in the same log line, the key names, and a non-zero `occurrencesRemoved`. R25 (server configuration profile export with safe secret redaction) is the sibling and had NOT landed when this was built — checked at LEDGER.md, status To Do — so the redactor is new here rather than a second one. It is deliberately a general component under RouterCore/Diagnostics rather than private to the bundle, so R25 reuses it instead of writing a third.
subject.text: One action exports the router's recent log, every declared upstream with its live state and cached tool surface, and the recent tool calls — and no credential value leaves in it. A secret-bearing field is never placed in the document; every known secret value is removed from every string that does survive, in its literal, percent-encoded and base64 forms; a value too short to be scrubbed from free text is named rather than used; and the untokened preview carries counts and no content.

subject.note: R22. Every CONFIGURED credential is absent from the bundle, and the document that omits it is a real one. The absence alone is the easiest unfailable assertion in this repository: it holds over an empty document, over a 404, and over a gatherer that never read the config. So it is asserted beside three things that must be PRESENT — a public canary planted in the same log line, the env key name, and the header key name — and beside `"value":"present"`, which proves a decision was taken about the value rather than the whole server having been skipped.

R22. Layer 2, and the channel layer 1 structurally cannot reach. A credential arrives in a diagnostics export by more routes than the field it was configured in: an upstream that rejects a call and quotes the token back in its error text, a command line carrying `--token=`, a log line somebody wrote by hand. Those are strings the bundle has every reason to carry, and the only thing distinguishing the secret inside one is its VALUE.

R22. The needle floor, which is a correctness rule rather than a performance one. An env value of `1`, `true` or `dev` used as a scrub needle deletes every occurrence of that text from every log line in the bundle — the timestamps, the ports, the word `device`. The result READS as thorough redaction and is a corrupted document, and nobody looking at it can tell which.

R22. A secret does not always reach a log line as itself. It reaches it percent-encoded when it travelled in a URL and base64-encoded when it travelled in a `Basic` credential, and a scrubber that knows only the literal reports a clean bundle over both. Both out-of-family lanes raised this independently and it is the one addition of theirs taken wholesale.

R22. The preview is a GET and GET is UNGATED in this router — `ControlHandler.gate` reads the token only for POST/DELETE/PATCH, matching the reference, recorded there as a ported defect rather than quietly fixed. So the preview is written to one rule: it discloses nothing `GET /servers` does not already disclose. Category names, counts, key names, and the redaction plan.

R22. The verb IS the gate, and it is not describing a mutation. The bundle changes nothing. It is a POST because stage 2 of `ControlHandler.handle` gates the token on POST/DELETE/PATCH only, so the verb is the only thing deciding whether this router hands its whole diagnostic corpus — log lines included — to any unauthenticated caller that can open the loopback port, which per `ControlToken` includes a web page the user merely visits.

subject.note: SURF-029's two SecondaryCommands, 'Export log' and 'Reset router', were enumerated and unreached: a CommandBar does not realise its overflow items while the overflow is shut, so the at-rest lane could only record an absence with its reason, and planning/registry-drop-gate.py reported the surface as uncovered for exactly that. This case opens the overflow through ExpandCollapsePattern.Expand and reads both commands back with their names and ControlType.Button, between a BASELINE and a SILENCE that both find them absent from the control view AND the raw view. The writer is not the reader: overflow-actuate.ps1 expands in its own process and writes only the ExpandCollapseState it saw, while every element reading comes from uia-dump.ps1 started separately. TWO FINDINGS FROM THE FIRST RUN, neither planted, both corrected in the manifest rather than in the assertion. (1) probe-expectation.json predicted that opening the overflow would cost the never-activated guarantee, and IT WAS RIGHT: the probe held the foreground at none of the three baseline samples and at all six effect and silence samples, so Expand activates the window and Collapse does not hand the foreground back. That cost is now DECLARED as `overflow.activationCost` and compared both ways, so the day WinUI stops activating, this arm reddens rather than quietly acquiring a guarantee nobody re-checked. Baseline stays a hard assertion. (2) each command resolves to TWO tree paths with the overflow open, because WinUI publishes the OverflowPopup subtree once through a Microsoft.UI.Content.PopupWindowSiteBridge child and once in place beneath the ApplicationBar. Both copies agree on name, controlType, className, isEnabled, isOffscreen, accessKey, patterns and bounding rectangle, so it is one control on two routes; the assertion now permits several matches only while they agree on everything a caller would act on, and plant (H) watches that a genuinely different control under one id still fails. WHAT THIS DOES NOT BUY. It is not at-rest coverage and does not close DESIGN.md section 11 rule 9 for these two commands. The product fix is a surface that realises them without an actuation, and that is DEF-340. Neither command is INVOKED, so both stay outside the actuation census with a stated reason on SURF-029; this arm's subject is realisation and vocabulary, not effect. And the subject is WIN20's probe rather than the MCP Router Windows client: it measures WinUI 3's automation behaviour on this machine.

subject.cell: execution-plane=off-glass - data-shape=one queued capability
subject.note: The toast's wire format, on both sides of the trip, checkable with no display. ToastPayloadCodecTests parses the XML the platform will parse - it is a toast, it carries the title and the 'Nothing has been installed' line, it offers exactly Review and Dismiss - and then drives every argument string in that document back through the reader a real click goes through, requiring Review to come back as OpenReviewSheet FOR THAT CAPABILITY. Without the capability travelling, the action is a navigation to a list and the operator has to go and find the item the toast was about. THE SAFETY RULE IS ASSERTED OF THE DOCUMENT RATHER THAN OF ITS OWN SENTENCE. WIN22 tested ToastSafetyRule by asserting the string contained its own words. Here every action's arguments must parse into a closed set of two, and six refusal rows require the reader to return null - not a default - for an empty string, a bare form with no scheme, another application's scheme, our scheme with no action, and an action outside the set. That last row is the one that matters: this process does not control what sits in the Action Center, and a reader that fell back to something that ACTS would be the defect the safety rule names arriving through the parser.

subject.cell: execution-plane=daemon · data-shape=one stdio upstream declared
subject.note: The router spawning a child process, seen by two parties that are not the router. `bin/witness-effects.sh` runs `MCPRouterCLI index --force` against a scratch home holding one stdio server, and records the pid the shell launched (`$!`) beside the pid the CHILD reports for its own parent through `getppid()`. The child writes that into a file whose path arrives in its environment and which the router never reads back, so neither record passes through the product. They agree: shell launched 30913, child 30920 names 30913. A ps(1) sample runs alongside and usually misses, because the index verb spawns, handshakes and exits inside one scheduling quantum; two earlier versions of this witness depended on ps alone and could report only that the child had A parent, not whose child it was. Armed: against a config declaring no servers the same recorder reports count=0, and against the populated one count=1 with the parents agreeing.

The half of REQ-028 the app's own menu will answer for. `scripts/acceptance/menu-reason-plane.sh` launches the Debug build with `open -g`, never activates it, and reads its real menu bar off the accessibility plane: 220 menu items, 11 of them carrying a reason ShellMenuReasons wrote, and every sentence one MenuCommandAvailability declares — the vocabulary is derived from the source file at run time rather than copied, so the two cannot drift. WHAT THIS DOES NOT CLAIM: it does not read the badge. SwiftUI does not publish an NSMenuItem's badge to this plane and this app's menu bar is SwiftUI's, which the same lane asserts and `menu-badge-lane.sh` measured first on a fixture. The badge's CONTENT follows from the reason through MenuReasonBadgePairingTests, which proves one reason never appears beside two badges; the badge as DRAWN is CASE-0197 and is unoracled. Armed: `menu-reason-plane-selftest.sh` hands each of the five assertions a doctored dump and requires it to fire, then requires none of them to fire on the dump today's platform produces.

subject.cell: execution-plane=daemon · data-shape=one stdio upstream that answers and one whose command does not exist
subject.note: The health probe becoming a real child process, seen by two parties that are not the router. `bin/witness-health-probe.sh` drives `POST /servers/witness-fixture/probe` over the DAEMON's own socket — a production entry point, not the prober called from a test — and records the pid the shell launched beside the pid the child reports for its own parent. They agree: the shell launched the daemon as one pid, the child names that same pid, and ps(1) shows the row. The route reported the upstream healthy in the same breath, so the reading and the effect agree rather than one standing in for the other. THE LANE IS THE PORTABLE FLOOR AND SAYS SO: a real spawned process writing a sentinel the witness then reads. There is no bpf, no eslogger and no root here, so the kernel bar is not available and is not claimed. ONE MORE READING on the same run, and it is the one this feature is arranged around. Before any probe the report says every upstream is `unprobed` and the process table holds no fixture child — REQ-001 is that at rest there are zero child processes, and a health check that cold-started every server would invert it.

subject.cell: execution-plane=daemon · data-shape=a server whose health block is out of range in two keys
subject.note: A configured value the router will not take is REFUSED and reported, never clamped in silence. The lane's `r27-refused` server writes `tripAfter: 1` and `probeIntervalMs: 10`; the report carries both refusals with the value as written, the floor that rejected it, and a `scope` saying which block to fix, while `policy` reports the value actually in force. The `tripAfter` floor of 2 is this item's own version of the vacuity rule: with a threshold of 1 the first failure trips, `degraded` is unreachable, and the guarantee that an upstream is flagged degraded before it is tripped would hold only because nothing can enter the state it names. Refusing rather than clamping is the other half — a clamp reports 2 over a file that says 1, and the operator's next reading of their own file disagrees with the router for a reason neither can see.

subject.cell: execution-plane=daemon · data-shape=the same credential quoted back inside a router log line
subject.note: Layer 2, and the channel layer 1 structurally cannot reach. A credential arrives in a diagnostics export by more routes than the field it was configured in: an upstream that rejects a call and quotes the token back in its error text, a command line carrying `--token=`, a log line somebody wrote by hand. Those are strings the bundle has every reason to carry, and the only thing distinguishing the secret inside one is its VALUE. The scrub runs over the value tree ONCE, as the last step, so every string goes through it by construction rather than because each site remembered to call it — the property that survives the next person adding a section. Object keys are scrubbed as well as values. `occurrencesRemoved` is asserted non-zero, because a scrubber that ran and a scrubber that had something to do read as the same clean bundle and only one of them is evidence.

subject.cell: execution-plane=daemon · data-shape=an env value of three characters beside a log line containing it
subject.note: The needle floor, which is a correctness rule rather than a performance one. An env value of `1`, `true` or `dev` used as a scrub needle deletes every occurrence of that text from every log line in the bundle — the timestamps, the ports, the word `device`. The result READS as thorough redaction and is a corrupted document, and nobody looking at it can tell which. So a value below 8 characters is not used as a needle, is named in `unscrubbable` with the reason, and is still withheld by layer 1. The assertion that bites is the positive one: `dev-server on port 3000` must survive intact. BOTH out-of-family reviewers proposed an entropy filter on top of the floor, to stop a value like `production` scrubbing that word out of the logs. Declined, and the reason is the direction of the error: an over-redaction announces itself in place as `<redacted:MODE>` and a reader can see exactly what happened; an under-redaction is silent. A second exclusion tuned by entropy moves values from the first class to the second on a judgement nobody can audit from the bundle.

subject.cell: execution-plane=daemon · data-shape=the same credential percent-encoded and base64-encoded in log lines
subject.note: A secret does not always reach a log line as itself. It reaches it percent-encoded when it travelled in a URL and base64-encoded when it travelled in a `Basic` credential, and a scrubber that knows only the literal reports a clean bundle over both. Both out-of-family lanes raised this independently and it is the one addition of theirs taken wholesale. JSON escaping is DELIBERATELY NOT a third variant, and that is where this departs from both reviews. They are right that a token containing a quote appears in the SERIALISED document as `\"` and would survive a needle search over the finished bytes. The scrub does not search the finished bytes: it walks the value tree before serialisation, where every string is still unescaped. Scrubbing earlier removes the whole class rather than enumerating its members.

subject.cell: execution-plane=daemon · data-shape=an untokened GET against a router holding a planted secret
subject.note: The preview is a GET and GET is UNGATED in this router — `ControlHandler.gate` reads the token only for POST/DELETE/PATCH, matching the reference, recorded there as a ported defect rather than quietly fixed. So the preview is written to one rule: it discloses nothing `GET /servers` does not already disclose. Category names, counts, key names, and the redaction plan. The assertion that makes this a real constraint rather than a restatement of `no secret leaked` is the canary one: the preview must NOT contain the public log canary either. A preview carrying no secret is satisfied by a preview that carries the whole log with the secret scrubbed out; a preview carrying no log LINE is not.

subject.cell: execution-plane=daemon · data-shape=the bundle path asked three ways: untokened POST, GET, tokened POST
subject.note: The verb IS the gate, and it is not describing a mutation. The bundle changes nothing. It is a POST because stage 2 of `ControlHandler.handle` gates the token on POST/DELETE/PATCH only, so the verb is the only thing deciding whether this router hands its whole diagnostic corpus — log lines included — to any unauthenticated caller that can open the loopback port, which per `ControlToken` includes a web page the user merely visits. All three answers are pinned — 401 untokened, 405 on GET, 200 on a tokened POST — so a later tidy-up that makes the verb 'correct' goes red rather than silently opening the route. The 200 is asserted beside the other two so they read as refusals rather than as an absent route.

Does every committed piece of macos-glass evidence name the build it was taken from, and is that build the one this lane is being read against? `bin/glass-build-gate.py` binds each artifact to the git blob identity of the Mac app's own build inputs -- the set `scripts/acceptance/build-freshness.sh` compiles from, read out of that file rather than copied, so a Mac input added there and missed here fails as INPUT DRIFT instead of quietly narrowing every verdict below it. Blob ids are line-ending normalised, so the verdict is identical on macOS and on Windows for one commit; this row was produced on Windows. --- FAILING, and the finding is true: all 56 artifacts the lane cites are stale, in 7 capture groups spanning 20-29 Aug, and `app/Sources/MCPRouterKit`, `app/Sources/MCPRouterUI` and `app/Package.swift` have all moved since the newest of them. This is DEF-058 with an instrument on it. It goes green when a macOS host re-runs `bin/capture-mac-glass.sh`, and not before -- there is no edit to this repository that should turn it green.

Can every published glass capture be shown to have been written AT THE SHUTTER rather than afterwards? A manifest that post-dates its capture records what somebody believed, not what the channel did, so it is not lineage -- which is the finding `capture-lineage.py`'s RECONSTRUCTED pass raised against SURF-028 and which `bin/capture-manifest.py` closed on the derivation side. This is the ordering side: the gate requires each published row to carry `capturedAt`, `conditions.windowTitleReadback` and `conditions.cgWindowID`, none of which can be recovered after the fact, or an explicit `provenanceGap` saying that it cannot. WHAT IT DOES NOT PROVE, stated rather than folded in: it establishes that the row COULD only have been written by something standing at the shutter, not that it was. Only the capture channel writing its own row does that, which `bin/capture-mac-glass.sh` does and which no reader can verify from the artifact alone.

subject.note: DEF-084, the live rung. The lane actuates Discover through the plane, waits for the registry search to publish rows, scopes a ListItem sweep to each band by its automation id and reads every row's Name and AutomationId out of process. THE ASSERTION IS NOT "the name is non-empty": the defect published "MCPRouter.Shell.Views.DiscoverRow" for every row, which is non-empty, so a presence check would have passed on it. What is required is that no name is the type name and that the names are pairwise distinct within the band - the two properties that actually failed. Read 2026-09-02: 60 rows in each band, 60 distinct names, 60 distinct ids, none of them the type name. The command the lane ran is scripts/windows/uia/run-shell-lane.ps1; `actuates` carries the two band containers the surface declares, which is what control-census.py counts. WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE: that the sentence is a good one to hear read aloud, and that an id is unique across BOTH bands - an entry in both carries the same id in each.

subject.detail: Found by auditing the other reads once DEF-009 was fixed, not by a failing test — so no case watched it fail and it earns no arming credit. `usageSummary()` returned the recorded four-server summary for every scenario, and it is the only call CleanupBoardModel makes. Under `.empty` the Cleanup board therefore offered four never-used servers to cull on a router with nothing declared. Fixed the same way as DEF-009: `.empty` returns no servers and keeps `since` from the recording, because a router that has been counting since a moment and has nothing to report is a different statement from one with no window at all. Audit result for the record: of the seventeen methods, seven do not branch on the scenario and six of those are writes, where a read-scenario legitimately does not apply and guardFailure() already covers offline/unauthorized/error. The seventh is `server(named:)`, which answers about a server the caller has already named and has no meaningful empty form; no surface calls it.
subject.title: the fixture client's usageSummary ignored the scenario, so Cleanup had no empty state

subject.detail: prototype.html:716 puts 'Reset history…' in the Activity header's right slot, outside the rows conditional, so the design specifies it in both the empty and the populated state. The built board draws no control there at all. Not an honesty guardrail: the router can reset its call history, and the Cleanup board carries 'Reset call history', so the capability exists and only this entry point is missing.
