subject.detail: DETECTOR DEFECT, recorded so its numbers are not published as product findings. `vacuity-check.py`'s `blind` pass asks whether any READER appears after the last MUTATING call in a test body, both matched by name prefix. Run with the shipped defaults it reports `examined=1820 mutating=3 blind=3` — and all three are false: DEFAULT_READERS is snake_case (`load_`, `get_`, `read_`, `list_`) while this is a camelCase Swift codebase, so NO Swift reader can ever match, and the three `mutating` hits matched the token `restart` in their own function names. Both flagged WatchRestartTests cases read extensively after the mutation. Run with a hand-derived camelCase verb list it reports `examined=1834 mutating=258 re-read-after=158 blind=100`. Two of the flagged real tests were read in full and BOTH re-read: `undoRestoresTheItem` calls `queue.all()` three times after `model.remove(...)`, and `resetReindexesAnIndexFailure` reads `client.calls` after `board.reset(...)`. Neither `all` nor `calls` was in the list. Of the 20 findings the script prints, only 6 are `@Test` functions at all; the other 14 are test doubles and helpers, because the population is every `func` in any file with `test` in its path. CONCLUSION: on this codebase the pass measures the verb list rather than the suite, and no verb list derived by hand is evidence of anything. It is recorded, not published, and the campaign claims no blind-mutation number. The pass's other two arms — `unclassed` and `uncensused` — are exact and are kept. ADDRESSED UPSTREAM in 0.9.2, confirmed by running it 21 Aug 2026. Commit 28ecd67 (`the blind-mutation check was measuring itself`) fixes four detector defects that each RAISED the blind count, and the pass now prints the vocabulary it used above its findings -- `vocabulary: defaults + campaign.blindVocabulary — 22 mutator(s), 20 reader(s)` followed by the reader list -- which was this defect's complaint: a number published without saying what configuration produced it. The denominator also moved, 1841 to 1657, because fixture helpers are no longer counted as tests. Left open rather than closed: the residual named on DEF-040 sits in the same pass. SUPERSEDED 21 Aug 2026 by DEF-055. The specific claim here — snake_case DEFAULT_READERS against a camelCase Swift codebase, giving examined=1820 mutating=3 blind=3 with all three false — was resolved by declaring campaign.json's blindVocabulary, which 0.9.2 reads. The general claim, that no hand-derived verb list is evidence of anything, is not resolved; it is now MEASURED rather than asserted. DEF-055 carries that measurement (7 of 7 sampled findings false, four named mechanisms, a two-way arm) and is the entry to read. Recorded as superseded rather than closed: the finding was real and its successor is open.
subject.title: test-campaign 0.9.1's blind-mutation pass is dominated by its own verb configuration on this codebase, in both directions

subject.note: `#expect(result.tools != nil, ...)` at ShellTests.swift:133. `ReindexResult.tools` is a non-optional `Int` (MCPRouterKit/Control/Models.swift:263), so the comparison could not fail. The Swift compiler emitted `comparing non-optional value of type 'Int' to 'nil' always returns true` on every build of the test target; it was the only such warning in the suite. The intent was stated in the comment directly above it -- `.success` is distinguished from `.populated` by `a reindex that comes back with no error and a tool count` -- so the assertion was one character from doing its job. Repaired to `result.tools == 14`, the value FixtureControlAPIClient+Writes.swift:33 overrides for `.success`, which discriminates against the base `reindex-failure.json` fixture it starts from (`{"tools":0,"error":"fetch failed"}`). Armed in evidence/arming/CASE-0152.arming.log: with the override changed to 0 the assertion goes red (`(result.tools -> 0) == 14`), and the log records that the pre-repair form would have stayed green under the same mutation.

subject.detail:
DETECTOR DEFECT in test-campaign 0.9.1, found 20 Aug 2026 by the concurrent session at uds:/tmp/cc-socks/9881.sock and confirmed here against the artifact rather than against a model of it. The string `defect` does not appear as a registry key anywhere in evidence-page.py; measured with grep, zero occurrences. Its `

Defects

` at line 521 renders `[c for c in cases if state_of(c.get('status')) == 'fail']` -- failing CASES -- and the nav counter at line 305 is `counts['fail']`, the same population. So the page's Defects section counts 3 (the failing cases CASE-0010, CASE-0040, CASE-0110) while inventory.json holds 11 open defects, and the two numbers are about different things. MEASURED against the regenerated 124100-byte evidence.html: of the 11 open defects, 8 appear ZERO times -- DEF-008, DEF-040, DEF-041, DEF-042, DEF-043, DEF-047, DEF-048, DEF-051. The 3 that do appear are there by accident of prose: DEF-001 in two failing case notes and one passing one, DEF-033 and DEF-049 each inside a single PASSING case's note, rendered by the per-case table rather than by the Defects section. The peer reported 11 invisible; the true figure is 8, because writing a defect id into a case note is a convention doing a gate's job and it happened to fire three times. `campaign.py check` also exits 0 with all 11 open, so no gate holds on the registry either. This is the skill's own first-named failure mode -- covering a subset and reporting it as the whole -- arriving in its publisher: the gated half of the campaign is sound and the ungated half is the half people look at. The fix belongs in the installed skill (render inv['defect'], and count open defects in the nav), not in this repo; recorded rather than patched, precedent DEF-048 and DEF-051. SECOND PUBLISHER, same root cause, measured here: `campaign.py`'s own ledger writer (campaign.py:1210-1240) loads `inventory` and never reads `inventory['defect']` either, so ledger.md names zero defects across its 83 lines. Its header line is sharper than an omission -- it prints `73 pass . 3 fail . 0 skip . 4 n/a . 0 open . armed 73/73`, where `0 open` is the count of open CASES, on a campaign holding 12 open defects. A reader who takes that line at face value reads a campaign with nothing outstanding. ledger.md is generated rather than hand-kept, so it cannot be corrected in this repo: a fix that patched only evidence-page.py would leave the ledger short, and both publishers need to read the registry.

subject.text: Measured by R27 on 2026-08-29 against the daemon on a scratch home. A server whose command exists and exits immediately (a shell that returns 17) is acquired for the full startupTimeoutMs and then reported as 'did not initialize within Nms': with the budget at 3000ms the probe took 3.15s wall clock. A server whose command does NOT exist fails in 0.01s, because the spawn itself throws. So the cost is specific to a child that spawns and dies, and the reason is that the handshake races connect() against a timer with no third branch for 'the process exited' - nothing watches the child's termination during startup. NOT FIXED HERE, and the reason is a boundary rather than effort. The race lives in StdioUpstreamTransport, which is the reference-diffed startup path R2 owns and R4 compares; adding an exit branch would change how this router reports a failure the reference reports differently, which is a parity decision and not a health-check one. R27's own bound is deliberately narrower - probeTimeoutMs covers the tools/list request so that 'the child never started' and 'the child answered too slowly' stay different answers - which means the budget that governs this arm is the upstream's startupTimeoutMs, and that is stated on the record rather than hidden. WHAT IT COSTS TODAY: a manual probe of a crash-looping stdio upstream blocks for the default 60s, and the caller has no way to shorten it except by setting that server's startupTimeoutMs. scripts/acceptance/r27-health.sh sets 1500 on its flaky fixture for exactly this reason, and says so. 2026-10-19 — FIXED IN BOTH ROUTERS by merge 02d764b0 (Merge ai/stdio-exit). A child that exits before initializing now fails at once, naming its status, instead of waiting out startupTimeoutMs. Unit evidence: RealProcessStartupTests (app/Tests/RouterCoreTests/RealProcessStartupTests.swift) and test/stdio-exit.test.ts. Verified 2026-10-19: the `Real child processes — startup` suite passed under `swift test`, and `node --test` on test/stdio-exit.test.ts passed. Status is fixed · in-test. No campaign re-run is recorded against this row, and the R27 wall-clock probe has not been run again against it.
subject.title: A stdio child that starts and then exits is not noticed, so acquisition waits out the whole startup budget

subject.text: Found while building R22's redactor, filed rather than fixed. `Describe.row` emits `command` and `args` RAW, and `ControlHandler.gate` reads the token only for POST/DELETE/PATCH, so the complete command line of every stdio upstream is readable by anything that can open the loopback port. The same function is careful in the adjacent case — it emits `envKeys` and `headerKeys` and never a value, with B10's reasoning attached — so argv is the one credential-carrying position on that route that is published whole. It matters because argv IS a credential channel: `--token=`, `--api-key=` and a connection string with an inline password are ordinary MCP server invocations, and R22 scrubs args for exactly that reason. The exposure predates R22 and is not made worse by it: the bundle's args go through the value scrub, and this route's do not. NOT FIXED HERE, and the reason is a parity decision rather than effort. `GET /servers` is reference-diffed — `control-servers-get` in planning/parity/surface.tsv, verdict `proven` — so redacting args moves a surface R4 compares byte for byte, and the ungated GET is itself a ported defect this repository records rather than silently repairs. Closing it means changing both routers or declaring a divergence, and that is the owner's call. 2026-10-19 — FIXED IN BOTH ROUTERS by merge 74d15306 (Merge ai/argv-redact), whose subject records that GET /servers stops publishing secret-bearing argv. Unit evidence: ArgvRedactionTests (app/Tests/RouterCoreTests/ArgvRedactionTests.swift) and test/argv-redact.test.ts, with parity vectors in argv-redact.json. Verified 2026-10-19: the `ArgvRedactionTests` suite passed under `swift test`, and `node --test` on test/argv-redact.test.ts passed. Status is fixed · in-test. No campaign re-run is recorded against this row.

subject.evidence: `PREVIOUS = "HEAD:planning/test-campaign/bin/control-census.py"`. The arm's whole claim is a DIFFERENCE - six plants that redden this branch's census and are silent on the one it replaced, and two DECLARED SILENCES where the old census is red and the new one is deliberately not. That holds while the new census is UNCOMMITTED, which is the state wd3 wrote and watched it in, and it reported 8/8 correctly. Once the commit that earns it lands, `HEAD:` resolves to the NEW census and the arm compares the file with itself. Measured on the merged tree at 07d347c7 before the fix: all six EFFECT plants read `previous census exit 1 red`, the three that were the point - DEF-131's own exhibit among them - stopped being differences, DEF-420's given-up coverage read as no loss, and the arm exited 1 reporting its own collapse.

subject.evidence: `discover()` reads the git INDEX through `git ls-files` and separately walks the DISK through `os.walk` + `os.path.relpath`, then names the difference as briefs the gate did not read. `git ls-files` prints POSIX separators on every platform; `os.path.relpath` prints the platform's. On Windows the two sets therefore never intersect and the difference is the WHOLE corpus. Measured before the fix on this branch: the same run printed `brief discovery read 226 items of the git index ...; kept 219` and, four lines later, `219 brief(s) on disk are NOT in the index and are outside this verdict`, listing ten of them and `... and 209 more`. Both sentences cannot be true. The verdict and the partition were correct throughout - it is the accounting sentence above them that was false.

That is the script's own standing rule rather than a new one — it already declines to substitute a picture for the pairing sheet and the status item, and its header records the run that filed the Inbox board as SURF-010. The title and the dump are still written from what the app is really showing, so the failure stays visible downstream; what is withheld is the photograph, because a misattributed picture is the one artefact nothing downstream can correct. STILL OPEN, and deliberately not fixed here: 1. SURF-011 has no route to the Settings SCENE. It needs Cmd-comma or the app menu, not a sidebar select that cannot succeed. CASE-0016 and CASE-0111 fail until it does. 2. THE MENU MAP IS PRE-M22. Committed SURF-001.menu.txt binds Cmd-4 to `Discover`; the running app binds Cmd-4 to `Harnesses`, exactly as Destination.selectionDigit declares (activity 1, servers 2, skills 3, harnesses 4, discover 5, inbox 6, evals 7, cleanup 8, insights 9). glass-assert.py's SURF-001 `menu` dict is the old map, so CASE-0001 asserts five bindings this build does not have. Correcting it is editing an assertion to restore a green, which this campaign forbids — it is owed as its own item, from Destination.selectionDigit rather than by hand. WHY IT IS THE SAME FINDING AS G14'S, ONE LAYER DOWN. G14 found the surface LIST had stopped growing while the product did. The Settings capture it overwrote is restored to `SURF-011.build.png` from `cef3729`, TOGETHER WITH ITS MANIFEST ROW from the same commit -- the last commit where those bytes and that row agreed (sha 3b5a26ef, `target: app://mac/settings`, readback `Settings`, 2026-08-20T11:32:58Z). Restoring the pair from one commit is a recovery of a capture-time record; restamping the row against the new bytes would have been the manifest-after-the-fact defect. What is NOT closed is the cause: `axkit select Settings` still fails, so the campaign still has no Settings capture newer than 2026-08-20 and the glass script still declines to take one. THE CAUSE NOW HAS A READER, 2026-09-02 (wa5). `axkit select Settings` still fails, and the campaign still has no Settings capture newer than 2026-08-20 -- unchanged. subject.detail: parity-gate.sh, 20 Aug 2026 on main at e5755d0. The suite lane's citation run of scripts/acceptance/parity-oauth.sh exited non-zero and recorded `control-auth-post-http fail — the Swift router never reached the token endpoint`. The dedicated oauth lane, later in the same gate, ran the same script and recorded ok over 21 checks. The gate reported the row DIVERGED and printed 81 of 83. WHY IT IS UNEXPLAINED, established 21 Aug 2026 from disk without re-running anything. The run survives as evidence/runs/parity-gate-2026-08-20-oauth-flake.log, written 20:39:30. Its line 163 is the whole of what the citation run reported: `FAIL scripts/acceptance/parity-oauth.sh the gate reported findings`, and the next line is the following `ok` row. The script itself does not fail that quietly -- its failure branch (parity-oauth.sh:308-329) prints the POST /auth status, the browser hop, the tail of the router log and the first 20 requests the provider saw. Every one of those bytes existed and was discarded by the caller: `parity-suite.sh`'s `run_script` sent both streams to /dev/null at the time. So this defect is not a run that left no diagnostic, it is a run whose diagnostic the harness threw away, and no amount of re-reading the log can recover it. The instrument was repaired in commit 21d559b at 20:41:28 -- one minute and 58 seconds after this log was written, in the same commit that recorded the defect -- so `run_script` now keeps the log and prints its last 20 lines inline. A recurrence would therefore arrive with the cause attached. That is what closes this: the next occurrence, not more thought about this one. It stays open because there is still no cause and no reproduction; what changed is that the reason it could not be diagnosed is now known and no longer true. One candidate mechanism examined and NOT adopted. The R9 lane reported (21 Aug 2026, via uds:/tmp/cc-socks/9881.sock) that a stale $TMPDIR/mcp-router-parity.lock had made a gate fail its manifest-check for a non-real reason. That is a different symptom -- a manifest-check failure before the comparison, against this defect's completed run that reached `control-auth-post-http` and recorded a row -- and parity-oauth.sh takes that same lock at line 126 and preflights every port at 143-145, so the two lanes inside one gate could not have overlapped. Recorded as ruled out rather than left unmentioned, so the next reader does not spend the lead twice.
subject.text: Observed once, in one of two whole-gate runs, and not reproduced by: a standalone run of `parity-oauth.sh`, a second standalone run of it immediately afterwards (which exercised the same port-reuse wait, 9s and 12s), a standalone run of `parity-suite.sh`, or a second whole `parity-gate.sh` on the same tree. The second gate reported 82 of 83, 0 DIVERGED, and its suite lane reported the citation clean. **What it is not.** The lane distinguishes an environment failure from a finding on purpose, and this was the finding branch: `record control-auth-post-http fail` at `parity-oauth.sh:329`, reached only when the reference side completed an authorization and the Swift side did not. An unbindable port exits 2 through `wait_for_ports_bindable` and records `blocked`, not `fail`, so the port-reuse race is ruled out by the code path that fired. **Why it went undiagnosed, and what changed.** `parity-suite.sh`'s `run_script` sent both streams to `/dev/null` and printed `the gate reported findings` — a verdict with no evidence under it. The bytes naming which guard failed had already been thrown away by the time anyone read the gate's summary. `run_script` now keeps the log, prints its last 20 lines inline and names the file it kept, armed 20 Aug 2026 against a deliberately failing citation. A recurrence will say which of the 21 checks went red. **Why the duplicate run stays.** `control-auth-post-http` is proven on the wire by its own lane and also cites the script, so the gate runs it twice. That is now documented in `parity-suite.sh` rather than deduplicated, because the duplicate is what caught this: a single run would have reported a clean 82 of 83 and nobody would have known. Both record under the same row id and a `fail` wins. **Burn-in, 20 Aug 2026: 8 standalone runs of the lane, all green, 21 checks each.** Three immediately after the failure and five consecutively afterwards, plus one clean whole gate. One failure in roughly ten whole-lane executions, cause unrecoverable because that invocation's stdout was discarded. A green burn-in does not close this: the original failure is uninspectable, so the runs measure only that the lane is not reliably broken. What would close it is a captured reproduction, or a stated gate met — several consecutive whole gates including the cold port-reuse path — decided as its own question rather than inferred from a streak, which is the `install-launchd-watch` mistake this repository already paid for once (G1: name a fix per term and fix a bound IN ADVANCE, never a green streak). Not a UI defect and not a blocker on the cutover count — CASE-0036's measurement is the second run — but it is an unexplained non-determinism in the router or the lane, and it is recorded rather than absorbed.
subject.title: the OAuth parity lane failed once inside a full gate and has not reproduced

subject.detail: The lane built with CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO, so the app carried no keychain access group and SecItemCopyMatching returned -34018 errSecMissingEntitlement rather than errSecItemNotFound. PairingRecordStore maps the two apart correctly, so the phone's Settings surface rendered "Can't read this phone's pairing" on a device that had simply never been paired. That was recorded as DEF-X2-b, a suspected product defect. It is a lane defect: built with CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY=- the same assertion passes and the test proceeds 54 lines further. The Makefile now carries a SIGNED variable used by test-ios-glass alone, with the measurement in a comment beside it. The general lesson is the one the campaign keeps relearning — a harness flag can manufacture a finding that reads exactly like the product's own.

subject.note: F7. `Analyse now` actuated, and the outcome read on a channel the press did not write. The board posts once and then draws what a SECOND `GET /insights` returned; the staging client answers that read differently before and after, so “the board redrew from the router” and “the board did nothing” are not the same picture. The same-channel reads declined are the button's own callback returning and `analysing` falling back to false. Both survive an empty body — which is exactly the control this item replaced.

F7. The same control from the router's side, and the strongest reading of it: `POST /insights/analyse` through `ControlHandler.handle`, then a separate `GET /insights` that reports the run. The POST's own 200 is not the oracle — the later GET is, and it is a different request through a different arm of the dispatch table.

F7. The three configuration menus the design draws and the build replaced with an empty state — `Analyst model`, `Second-opinion model` and `Analyst cadence`. Each patches exactly one member and leaves the other two nil, which is what stops a press on the cadence menu from re-asserting a model the user did not touch. Asserted as the three patch payloads the client received, in order.

F7. What the analyst read and what it refused to say. The corpus reports a positive `linesRead`, a named discard count and every store it did not open with the reason — including Cursor's, which is enumerated and deliberately unread. A recommendation naming an entry outside the candidate list, or a signal the run never counted, is rejected and COUNTED rather than dropped, so an engine that discarded everything is distinguishable from one that was handed nothing.

parity-gate.sh on main at e5755d0, 20 Aug 2026: **82 of 83 rows proven (4 of them by suite only, not by wire comparison), 0 DIVERGED, 1 blocked.** REQ-014's contract is the owner's cutover target of 82 of 83 with `fixture-registry-search` a standing exclusion, and that is what was measured. The two rows that stood between 80 and 82 closed the same day: `install-launchd-watch` by ai/p8, which made the `reran` term attributable — it had read yes on 2 of 6 decoy trials where no stimulus could reach the watched path — and `control-auth-post-http` by ai/p7, which built a real OAuth client and now agrees with the reference across the discovery cascade, the registration bytes, the PKCE parameters, the token exchange, the callback page, the credential file and the re-authorization branch. **The gate exits 1 and that is not this case failing.** It exits 1 while any row is blocked, deliberately, and the one blocked row is the standing exclusion the requirement names. The gate prints the distinction itself: `82 proven is at or past the target of 82. That is a count, not a licence`. Read as a pass on the requirement, not as a licence to flip the installer — that is the owner's call on R4-C's evidence, which this case does not make. **Armed, and one arm was not planned.** The mechanical arm is `parity-lane-selftest`, which runs every lane against a deliberately broken Swift router and requires each to go red; it ran green in the same `make all` that carried this tree, printing `every new lane went red against a broken router. The lanes can fail.` The unplanned arm is the first whole-gate run of the day, kept at `evidence/runs/parity-gate-2026-08-20-oauth-flake.log`: the same script on the same tree reported `81 of 83 rows proven … 1 DIVERGED … This is NOT a pass`, so the aggregate verdict is live rather than a constant. That run's cause is unexplained and is recorded as DEF-033 rather than absorbed into this note.

subject.note: WHAT THIS ROW SPEAKS FOR, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It measures the NODE reference only. `swift` and `xcodebuild` are absent on this machine, so nothing here is a Swift test result and this case must not be read as coverage of `AuthRoutes.promote`; the Swift side of REQ-019 is still carried by `ControlApproveDispatchTests` and this campaign has not run it. Three arms over the shipped `handleControl` out of `dist/`: a writable home answering 200 with `pending` gone from disk; the same call with the save's temp path occupied by a directory, answering 500 with the errno message and `pending` still on disk; and the occupation removed, answering 200 again. The denial is the filesystem's own `EISDIR` at exactly the step that makes the change durable - not a mocked `FileSystem` - and the lock sidecar and the manifest read are left working on purpose, because a denial that also stopped the lock would produce a 500 carrying the LOCK's sentence and prove nothing about the save. ACLs were tried first and are recorded in the lane's header as a control that did not arm: `icacls <file> /deny <user>:(D,WD,AD,WEA,WA)` and `icacls <dir> /deny <user>:(DC)` both apply, read back as DENY aces, and `renameSync` over the target succeeds anyway on this machine. An ACL that is set and does not bite produces a green arm that never armed, which is why the temp-path occupation replaced it. What it found: the reference answers 500, so Swift's pre-R21 200 was a divergence and R21's change closed it (DEF-442), while the error BODIES still differ (DEF-441). `deps.liveReload` and `deps.manifest` are stubs - they are the announcement collaborators the 200 path calls after the write - and the route, the lock, `loadManifest` and `saveManifest` are the shipped ones.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=no task registered
subject.note: The Windows task scheduler holding a task the product registered, read by an API that did not write it. The writer is MCPRouter.Shell.Live's LogonTaskSupervisor driving schtasks.exe with the Task Scheduler XML it builds; the recorder is Get-ScheduledTask, the ScheduledTasks module over the scheduler's WMI provider - a different API, a different process and a different vocabulary for the same facts. The XML says RunLevel LeastPrivilege and the recorder answers RunLevel Limited, and nothing in this repository translates between them. The scheduler also normalised the interval this run asked for, PT60S, into PT1M, which is the plainest available evidence that the read did not come back through anything this code wrote. EIGHT ARMS, AND TWO ARE ABOUT THE INSTRUMENT. BASELINE requires the recorder to report the task ABSENT before registration - without it, a task left behind by an interrupted run makes every other arm pass over a run that registered nothing. SILENCE requires it to report absence again after removal, which is what separates a reader from an echo: a recorder that always answered yes would satisfy the six product arms by construction. The other six read the three claims LifecyclePresentation prints to the operator - triggered at logon, un-elevated, restarting on failure - plus the executable and port this run asked for, plus presence and removal. WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE, and the reason it is one case rather than the whole of REQ-035: nothing here logs the user out, so the trigger has never been watched to fire, and nothing here starts or kills a daemon, so the restart has never been watched to happen. DEF-081 carries those two. This case settles that the registration the product performs produces, in the Windows task scheduler, a task carrying the properties the product's own UI describes - which before 2026-09-02 was unmeasured entirely, and which DEF-074 recorded as a supervision model nothing performed.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=a supervised process that dies
subject.note: The half of WIN23's supervision promise that had never been watched: a daemon the Windows task scheduler starts, loses, and starts again. DEF-081 filed it as unmeasurable and named the blocker as a missing Windows daemon binary; the blocker was real and is gone - app/windows/MCPRouter.Witness.Daemon is a harness process that starts, records its own start and waits to be killed, so there is something for the scheduler to supervise. WHAT THE MEASUREMENT FOUND IS NOT WHAT THE ROW EXPECTED. The registration the product wrote carried RestartOnFailure with a 60-second interval and a count of 3, and it did not restart the daemon at all. Killed, watched 150 seconds, on the unified scheduling engine and the legacy one, for a run started by a trigger and one started on demand: four registrations, no restart. The same block DID restart, three times at exactly 60 seconds, a task whose Command named a file that does not exist - so the instrument can see a restart, and RestartOnFailure governs a task that fails to LAUNCH rather than one whose action launched and later died. DEF-320 carries that, and the product now writes a Repetition on the trigger alongside MultipleInstancesPolicy IgnoreNew. THE RECORDERS ARE TWO AND NEITHER WROTE ANYTHING: Get-ScheduledTaskInfo for the scheduler's own account of its runs, and Get-CimInstance Win32_Process for the process identity, which is what makes 'it came back' a different process id rather than a report from the thing that came back. The daemon's own run log is carried and graded by nothing. EIGHT ARMS, THREE OF THEM ABOUT THE INSTRUMENT: BASELINE requires both tasks absent and no daemon running, so nothing below is inherited from an interrupted run; CLAIM.repetition and CLAIM.ignorenew read the product's own unmodified logon registration back through the WMI provider; SILENCE requires both recorders to say no once the tasks are gone. ONE SUBSTITUTION, SAID OUT LOUD: a trigger repetition does not apply to an on-demand start - measured, twice - so the live task carries a TimeTrigger where the product writes a LogonTrigger, because this lane must not log the machine out. Every Setting, the repetition interval, the principal, the action and the instances policy are the product's own document. That the trigger fires AT LOGON is still unwitnessed and DEF-081 keeps it.

THE FIGURES ARE A REAL ROUTER'S, AND THIS IS THE FIRST MAC CAPTURE THAT CAN SAY SO. CASE-0166 records the reason none before it could: `ShellClientFactory` made a Debug build ALWAYS take a fixture, so every glass capture proved the board renders a JSON file in this repository. J5 gives the Debug branch a live choice — `MCPROUTER_SCENARIO=live` with `MCP_ROUTER_URL` naming a loopback router — and `bin/forced-state.sh` uses it. The reference router was started on http://127.0.0.1:8955 under a scratch `MCP_ROUTER_HOME` declaring 3 servers whose names carry this run's nonce, the Debug app was launched against it, and the Servers board was photographed from outside without ever being activated. The board drew `3 tools from 3 servers · 1 running` and the sidebar drew `1 of 3 declared servers running`. Every one of those figures is checked against `curl http://127.0.0.1:8955/servers`, taken by the harness itself at the shutter in a different process from the one that drew the board — tools 3, servers 3, running 1, each recomputed from the router's own response rather than read from a field the app also reads. Two further checks close the direction a matching figure cannot: every server the router declared is drawn, and no name matching this lane's nonce pattern is drawn that the router did not declare. A shell that had fallen back to the shipping endpoint — because the endpoint variable was refused, or because another router happens to be listening on this machine — would fail there rather than pass against the wrong world.

K3. `Rescan` promises a FRESH READING, and a board that redrew the answer it already had is indistinguishable from one that re-read and got the same thing. So the client stages a second answer that DIFFERS — a Mac whose harnesses were unwired between the two reads — and the row set is the observable rather than the round trip. The request count is asserted too, and is deliberately not sufficient on its own: the arm leaves the request going out and throws the answer away, so a case built on the count alone would stay green over a board frozen on its first reading. The empty second answer is also checked to be a READING rather than a failure, because a board that went stale on a router that answered perfectly well would satisfy the row assertion by accident.

subject.note: R22. The requirement is written as an honesty guardrail rather than a behaviour because the load-bearing half is a promise about what is NOT in the output, and this campaign's own history is that such a promise is satisfied trivially by producing nothing. Every case under it therefore pairs its absence with a presence: a public canary in the same log line, the key names, and a non-zero `occurrencesRemoved`. R25 (server configuration profile export with safe secret redaction) is the sibling and had NOT landed when this was built — checked at LEDGER.md, status To Do — so the redactor is new here rather than a second one. It is deliberately a general component under RouterCore/Diagnostics rather than private to the bundle, so R25 reuses it instead of writing a third.
subject.text: One action exports the router's recent log, every declared upstream with its live state and cached tool surface, and the recent tool calls — and no credential value leaves in it. A secret-bearing field is never placed in the document; every known secret value is removed from every string that does survive, in its literal, percent-encoded and base64 forms; a value too short to be scrubbed from free text is named rather than used; and the untokened preview carries counts and no content.

subject.note: R22. Every CONFIGURED credential is absent from the bundle, and the document that omits it is a real one. The absence alone is the easiest unfailable assertion in this repository: it holds over an empty document, over a 404, and over a gatherer that never read the config. So it is asserted beside three things that must be PRESENT — a public canary planted in the same log line, the env key name, and the header key name — and beside `"value":"present"`, which proves a decision was taken about the value rather than the whole server having been skipped.

R22. Layer 2, and the channel layer 1 structurally cannot reach. A credential arrives in a diagnostics export by more routes than the field it was configured in: an upstream that rejects a call and quotes the token back in its error text, a command line carrying `--token=`, a log line somebody wrote by hand. Those are strings the bundle has every reason to carry, and the only thing distinguishing the secret inside one is its VALUE.

R22. The needle floor, which is a correctness rule rather than a performance one. An env value of `1`, `true` or `dev` used as a scrub needle deletes every occurrence of that text from every log line in the bundle — the timestamps, the ports, the word `device`. The result READS as thorough redaction and is a corrupted document, and nobody looking at it can tell which.

R22. A secret does not always reach a log line as itself. It reaches it percent-encoded when it travelled in a URL and base64-encoded when it travelled in a `Basic` credential, and a scrubber that knows only the literal reports a clean bundle over both. Both out-of-family lanes raised this independently and it is the one addition of theirs taken wholesale.

R22. The preview is a GET and GET is UNGATED in this router — `ControlHandler.gate` reads the token only for POST/DELETE/PATCH, matching the reference, recorded there as a ported defect rather than quietly fixed. So the preview is written to one rule: it discloses nothing `GET /servers` does not already disclose. Category names, counts, key names, and the redaction plan.

R22. The verb IS the gate, and it is not describing a mutation. The bundle changes nothing. It is a POST because stage 2 of `ControlHandler.handle` gates the token on POST/DELETE/PATCH only, so the verb is the only thing deciding whether this router hands its whole diagnostic corpus — log lines included — to any unauthenticated caller that can open the loopback port, which per `ControlToken` includes a web page the user merely visits.

Seven sections, measured on the automation plane rather than counted in the markup: settings.section.router, .harnesses, .sessionanalyst, .updates, .security, .ambientsurface, .advanced, each publishing a name. subject.text: On Windows the router daemon is supervised by a Scheduled Task registered against the user's own logon: it starts in the interactive user session so it can reach local browser instances for OAuth and per-user harness configuration, it runs un-elevated, and it is restarted by the scheduler if it fails.

DETECTOR DEFECT in test-campaign, measured 2026-08-27 (G29) against the vendored 0.9.2 and the machine's 0.15.0, which carry a byte-identical `tie()`. SURF-028's route is `app://mac/servers/{server}/document` -- a family of addresses, one per server. `bin/g17-document-flow.sh` rendered its frames against three of them and recorded each target honestly. `tie()` normalises scheme, host, port, query and fragment away and then asks for string equality or a suffix match, so `mac/servers/g17-capability/document` against `mac/servers/{server}/document` fails all three tests and the gate reports UNTIED -- 'the recorded target does not resolve to the subject's route'. Nothing was pointed at the wrong thing. `references/capture-lineage.md` says resolution is 'deliberately loose on the parts a harness legitimately varies'; a `{server}` segment is exactly such a part, and it is the one case the looseness does not cover. THE FIX BELONGS UPSTREAM, and is not applied here. `vendor/README.md` pins the tree by checksum so the gates can be re-run from a clone, and a `tie()` that behaves one way in this repository and another way everywhere else stops being evidence -- the same reasoning that keeps X7 and X8 open. Referred out of family (gpt-5.6-sol, high effort, 2026-08-27) and it reached the same conclusion independently: patch upstream, cut a release, re-vendor and re-pin, rather than forking the pinned copy. The patch is one function: treat a route segment of the form `{name}`, `:name` or `*` as matching exactly one non-empty target segment, leaving literal segments, the source-file refusal and the normalisation untouched, and leaving the seeded swap red. WHAT THIS REPOSITORY DID INSTEAD, and why it is not a workaround. The three served frames are published by the FLOW-006 steps that rendered them, each carrying the concrete route its own capture recorded, and SURF-028 publishes none. That is the registry becoming more accurate rather than less: the surface is a template and has no single portrait, while a step is that surface at one address and can name it. Every frame is now filed at the address the channel was pointed at. The detector limit is unchanged and is what this row records.

THE ROWS ARE A REAL ROUTER'S, NOT A FIXTURE'S — and this is the only lane that can say so. ShellClientFactory makes a Debug build ALWAYS take a fixture, so no macos-glass capture is evidence about a real reading; every glass case above proves the board renders what the route's shape provides. Here the Swift router itself served GET /harnesses over loopback on 127.0.0.1:8975 under an isolated MCP_ROUTER_HOME. Four checks: the route answers with a harness list (7 rows); readAt is 0s old, so a reading taken now rather than a recording replayed; every row's `exists` flag agrees with stat(2) on THIS filesystem (7 of 7); and every traceable row's `entries` count is REPRODUCED by a reader that shares no code with the router, opening the same file itself — claudeCode=1, claudeDesktop=0, codexCLI=5, cursor=0, geminiCLI=20, grokCLI=3. One row is in a format that reader cannot parse and is reported untraceable rather than as agreeing.

Raised off `structural` by reading the board ACROSS its readings instead of within one. Nothing here presses `Rescan` and nothing needs to: the Debug shell reads a fixture, so a second read returns the same bytes and a green 'it refreshed' would be indistinguishable from a button wired to nothing — that claim is still declined. What relation `SURF-025/controls-track-reading` asserts instead is that the control set is COMPUTED. Across the populated, empty and failed readings the two header controls are invariant — Rescan drawn enabled and Reconcile all… drawn disabled in all three — while the per-harness controls number 10 where harnesses were returned and 0 in both readings that returned none. A board drawing a fixed column fails that, and so does one whose header controls come and go with the list.

THE HARD HALF, AND THE ONE NOBODY REACHES BY LAUNCHING THE APP. A board showing a stale figure as current looks exactly like one that is right, so this promise can only be proved by arranging the failing condition on purpose. The router that had been answering was killed while THIS SAME app instance kept running — a relaunch would reach `.failed`, which is a different state that renders differently — and the board was photographed again. It drew `3 tools from 3 servers · last reading, not current`. Four things are checked. The absence was arranged: the harness's own read of http://127.0.0.1:8955 at that shutter got nothing. The header says its reading is no longer current. No present-tense running count appears anywhere in the board — the check is for the absence of any digit in that position, never for a dash or a placeholder, because a placeholder is a figure of its own. And the sidebar readout withholds its own count too, which is a second absence over the same promise in code that does not share a line with the first: `ServersBoardHeader.subtitle()` draws one and `ReadoutCopy.accessibilityLabel` the other, and a guardrail that held in one place and not the other would pass a single-predicate check. The fifth check is the direction people forget: the servers that WERE read are still shown, 3 of them, the same number as while the router answered. A failed refresh is not evidence that the servers went away, and a board that cleared itself would satisfy every absence check above while destroying data no source said was gone.

NO PICTURE IS FILED HERE, AND THE REASON IS A MEASUREMENT RATHER THAN A SHRUG. `screencapture -x -l<CGWindowID>` against this window returns whatever surface the window server last composited, and against a LIVE launch that is behind everything that is nothing: window chrome, a title, and not even the sidebar. It exits 0 while doing it. The first two runs of this lane filed those frames. The cold and stale pictures came back byte-identical to each other — sha 84a469099e7c, 267622 bytes both — while their accessibility trees differed by 26 rows, so the pictures agreed about a state the app was not in and nothing in the capture channel said so. That is the defect `bin/capture-mac-glass.sh` already refuses in its own form, one plane over. The cause is measured. A FIXTURE launch photographs correctly, because `FixtureControlAPIClient` has its data at the first render and the first paint therefore carries the board — which is why nine years of this campaign's glass captures had never met this. A live launch does not, and the window never recovers: watched for 16 seconds at 2-second intervals, the same dump that reports a 980x620 window reports its sidebar at y=-537 with a height of 1964 on every single sample. Hide-then-unhide, a navigate-away-and-back reselect and a resize were each tried and each left the surface byte-identical. So `bin/paint-check.py` refuses the frame — the sidebar's rectangle is not inside the window's, which is an exact invariant of a laid-out window rather than a threshold — and the harness deletes it and records why. The state itself is not unmeasured: CASE-0197 holds it in the AX plane, over the same run. What is missing is the evidence that it reached the SCREEN, and that is stated rather than substituted.

THE OTHER HALF OF REQ-005: the router is not running, and it never has been. Arranged by NOT starting it, over a port the harness proved free first — a cold state cannot be arranged while something is listening, so `bin/forced-state.sh` refuses to run at all if http://127.0.0.1:8955 answers before it begins. Nothing has ever loaded, so `ServerStateTracker` is `.failed` rather than `.stale`, and the board may claim nothing at all. Five checks, four of them absences: the board draws `The router isn't running` — `ControlAPIError`'s own wording, not a paraphrase; it states no tools/servers total; it states no running count; the sidebar readout states nothing; and no server name is drawn for a router that has never answered. The last one is the one a fabricated zero would survive: `0 tools from 0 servers` is a figure nobody measured, and the header's three-case `Reading` exists precisely because a boolean once rendered it on every cold start. THIS CASE IS IN THE AX PLANE ONLY. The cold frame was refused by `bin/paint-check.py` for the reason CASE-0198 records in full, so there is no photograph of this state and none is claimed.

subject.cell: execution-plane=daemon · data-shape=the same credential quoted back inside a router log line
subject.note: Layer 2, and the channel layer 1 structurally cannot reach. A credential arrives in a diagnostics export by more routes than the field it was configured in: an upstream that rejects a call and quotes the token back in its error text, a command line carrying `--token=`, a log line somebody wrote by hand. Those are strings the bundle has every reason to carry, and the only thing distinguishing the secret inside one is its VALUE. The scrub runs over the value tree ONCE, as the last step, so every string goes through it by construction rather than because each site remembered to call it — the property that survives the next person adding a section. Object keys are scrubbed as well as values. `occurrencesRemoved` is asserted non-zero, because a scrubber that ran and a scrubber that had something to do read as the same clean bundle and only one of them is evidence.

subject.cell: execution-plane=daemon · data-shape=an env value of three characters beside a log line containing it
subject.note: The needle floor, which is a correctness rule rather than a performance one. An env value of `1`, `true` or `dev` used as a scrub needle deletes every occurrence of that text from every log line in the bundle — the timestamps, the ports, the word `device`. The result READS as thorough redaction and is a corrupted document, and nobody looking at it can tell which. So a value below 8 characters is not used as a needle, is named in `unscrubbable` with the reason, and is still withheld by layer 1. The assertion that bites is the positive one: `dev-server on port 3000` must survive intact. BOTH out-of-family reviewers proposed an entropy filter on top of the floor, to stop a value like `production` scrubbing that word out of the logs. Declined, and the reason is the direction of the error: an over-redaction announces itself in place as `<redacted:MODE>` and a reader can see exactly what happened; an under-redaction is silent. A second exclusion tuned by entropy moves values from the first class to the second on a judgement nobody can audit from the bundle.

subject.cell: execution-plane=daemon · data-shape=the same credential percent-encoded and base64-encoded in log lines
subject.note: A secret does not always reach a log line as itself. It reaches it percent-encoded when it travelled in a URL and base64-encoded when it travelled in a `Basic` credential, and a scrubber that knows only the literal reports a clean bundle over both. Both out-of-family lanes raised this independently and it is the one addition of theirs taken wholesale. JSON escaping is DELIBERATELY NOT a third variant, and that is where this departs from both reviews. They are right that a token containing a quote appears in the SERIALISED document as `\"` and would survive a needle search over the finished bytes. The scrub does not search the finished bytes: it walks the value tree before serialisation, where every string is still unescaped. Scrubbing earlier removes the whole class rather than enumerating its members.

subject.cell: execution-plane=daemon · data-shape=an untokened GET against a router holding a planted secret
subject.note: The preview is a GET and GET is UNGATED in this router — `ControlHandler.gate` reads the token only for POST/DELETE/PATCH, matching the reference, recorded there as a ported defect rather than quietly fixed. So the preview is written to one rule: it discloses nothing `GET /servers` does not already disclose. Category names, counts, key names, and the redaction plan. The assertion that makes this a real constraint rather than a restatement of `no secret leaked` is the canary one: the preview must NOT contain the public log canary either. A preview carrying no secret is satisfied by a preview that carries the whole log with the secret scrubbed out; a preview carrying no log LINE is not.

subject.cell: execution-plane=daemon · data-shape=the bundle path asked three ways: untokened POST, GET, tokened POST
subject.note: The verb IS the gate, and it is not describing a mutation. The bundle changes nothing. It is a POST because stage 2 of `ControlHandler.handle` gates the token on POST/DELETE/PATCH only, so the verb is the only thing deciding whether this router hands its whole diagnostic corpus — log lines included — to any unauthenticated caller that can open the loopback port, which per `ControlToken` includes a web page the user merely visits. All three answers are pinned — 401 untokened, 405 on GET, 200 on a tokened POST — so a later tidy-up that makes the verb 'correct' goes red rather than silently opening the route. The 200 is asserted beside the other two so they read as refusals rather than as an absent route.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - modality=process diagnostics - data-shape=one injected fault per launch
subject.note: Each of the shell's three top-level unhandled-exception handlers made to fire on purpose, and the line it wrote read back out of shell-startup.log by a process that did not write it, after the process that did had exited. THIS CASE EXISTS BECAUSE REGISTRATION IS NOT FIRING. DEF-079 was raised on sixteen launches that wrote no `unhandled:` line including eight that terminated at 0xC000027B, and it stayed open through the fix - two more handlers registered - because none of the three had been observed catching anything. App.xaml.cs takes `--fault <ui|appdomain|task|dispatcher>`, compiled out outside DEBUG and inert unless passed; win-shell-unhandled-witness.ps1 launches the shell once per kind. FOUR ARMS. BASELINE is a launch with NO --fault and requires its region of the log to hold `launched` and no `unhandled:` line, which is what makes the three EFFECT lines the injection's rather than startup's; and every arm reads only the bytes appended after its own launch, so a line an earlier run left behind cannot satisfy one. The three EFFECT arms then require, each after its own fault, `unhandled: [xaml]` for a throw on the UI thread inside XAML's dispatch of OnLaunched, `unhandled: [appdomain terminating=True]` for a throw on a non-UI foreground thread, and `unhandled: [unobserved-task]` for a faulted task nobody awaits after a collection and WaitForPendingFinalizers. All four held. WHAT THIS CASE DOES NOT SETTLE, and what has since moved. The DispatcherQueue route ran here as an UNGRADED probe while DEF-085 was open. DEF-085 is fixed, the probe is a graded fifth arm of the same script, and it is carried by CASE-0386 rather than by this case: what this one grades is still the three top-level handlers, and folding a guard this repository owns into a case about framework handlers would make one verdict answer two questions. Whether any of these three would have caught the 0xC000027B Skills crash was unmeasured when this case was written; it is measured now, and the answer is no - CASE-0387 and DEF-086 carry it. And the injection is compiled out outside DEBUG, so this grades the Debug binary only. The shell's own `handlers:` line saying which handlers it attached is carried in runs[] as writerSelfReport and is graded by nothing. ACTUATES VOCABULARY, corrected at merge: `actuates` is read by planning/test-campaign/bin/control-census.py as a control the surface DECLARES, which is what gives the actuation census its denominator. This case originally listed the command the lane ran instead - App.UnhandledException, AppDomain.CurrentDomain.UnhandledException and TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException (handlers, not controls, and this case names no surface) - and that is DEF-080, two meanings sharing one field. The command is here in the note where it can be read; the field now carries nothing, because the case drives no declared control.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - modality=process diagnostics - data-shape=one injected fault per launch
subject.note: DEF-085's guard: a throw inside a DispatcherQueue callback made to happen on purpose, and the line the guard wrote read back out of shell-startup.log by a process that did not write it, after the process that did had exited. WHY IT IS A CASE OF ITS OWN. CASE-0342 grades the shell's three top-level unhandled-exception handlers, which are the framework's. This route reaches none of them - a callback posted to a DispatcherQueue runs below XAML's own dispatch - so what catches it is code this repository owns: DispatcherGuard, applied at every posting site through GuardedDispatch.TryEnqueueGuarded. It ran in the same script as an UNGRADED PROBE while DEF-085 was open, because there was nothing yet to grade. THE ARM. win-shell-unhandled-witness.ps1 launches the shell with `--fault dispatcher` and requires `unhandled: [dispatcher` in the region of the log appended after that launch - so no earlier run's line can satisfy it - on a run whose BASELINE arm proved an ordinary launch writes no `unhandled:` line at all. Held: `unhandled: [dispatcher site=App.InjectFault] System.InvalidOperationException: DEF-085 fault injection: unhandled in a DispatcherQueue callback`. A SECOND EFFECT is recorded beside it and graded by nothing here: the guarded run leaves NO WER Application Error, where the unguarded one fails fast at 0xC000027B - see CASE-0387. WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE. GuardedDispatch is a convention and not a wall: nothing in the compiler stops a future caller from writing DispatcherQueue.TryEnqueue directly, and this arm would not notice a new unguarded site. The neighbouring `async void` XAML event-handler route is not covered here either. And the injection is compiled out outside DEBUG, so this grades the Debug binary only. ACTUATES: empty, because this case drives no control the surface declares - the command it ran is `--fault dispatcher` and it is in this note, which is where DEF-080 says it belongs. THE DEBUG-ONLY GRADING WAS A DECISION, not an oversight, and it is recorded here because DEF-079 left it open. The injection stays compiled out outside DEBUG: turning it on in Release would ship a code path whose whole purpose is to terminate the process, gated by nothing but a command-line flag, which is a worse risk than the observation is worth. What is Debug-only is the INJECTION and not the remedy - DispatcherGuard and GuardedDispatch compile into Release unchanged, and so do the three top-level handlers - so what goes unobserved in a Release build is whether the fault can be raised there, not whether the guard exists. The cheaper way to close it, if somebody wants it closed, is a third build configuration that defines the injection symbol without being the shipping one; that needs a new configuration and a lane re-run and was out of this item's scope.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - modality=operating-system crash record - data-shape=one deliberate fail-fast
subject.note: A REAL STATUS_STOWED_EXCEPTION, raised on demand, and what the XAML handler did about it - DEF-086. That row said this repository had no way to raise one: the original Skills crash was removed by DEF-077 and DEF-078, and a cross-ABI fault was not something product code could ask for. It turned out the lane already raised one without recognising it. An UNGUARDED throw from a DispatcherQueue callback - `--fault dispatcher --fault-unregister dispatcher`, which is DEF-085 as found - terminates MCPRouter.Shell.exe with WER Application Error 1000, exception code 0xc000027b, faulting module CoreMessagingXP.dll, fault offset 0x0000000000093b76. WHAT IT MEASURES: on that same run the region of shell-startup.log ends at `fault: injecting dispatcher` with nothing appended, so Microsoft.UI.Xaml.Application.UnhandledException does not see this class. DEF-079's mechanism field guessed exactly that and recorded it as unestablished; it is established now. THE RECORDER IS NOT THE WRITER, twice over: WER is written by the operating system after the process is gone, and it is read here through Get-WinEvent over the Windows Application log, which is a different API from the file the shell appends to. THE CONTROL: the guarded run of the same fault leaves no Application Error at all, so the record is the injection's rather than something this machine produces anyway. WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE, and this is the narrower thing rather than the wider claim: what matches the Skills crash of 2026-09-02 is the exception code, the faulting module and the fault offset - identical to the Application Error entries this machine still holds from 18:57:35 and 19:03:30 that day - and NOT a stack. This case says this host raises the same stowed-exception fail-fast and that the XAML handler does not catch it. It does not say the original throw took the identical path; DEF-077 named that throw and fixed it.

subject.detail: Two instances of one mistake, found together. **The camera adapter** was constructed in `MCPRouterIOSApp.body`; `LiveCameraAuthorization` is a fieldless struct so a fresh one per render cost nothing and hid it, and the moment the lane asked for `FixtureCameraAuthorization` — an actor — the identity changed under the flow on every body pass. Stored once as a `let` beside `storage`, which was already stored for the same reason. **The pairing model** was the real defect. `PhoneSettingsScreen` built `PairingFlowModel(pairing:camera:store:)` inline inside its `navigationDestination` closure, and `PairingFlowView` takes it as `@Bindable` — which observes an object someone else owns rather than owning one. So every re-render of the Settings screen replaced the model, and `step`'s initial value is `.scan`, so each replacement discarded whatever `start()` had decided and put the scanner back. Now held in `@State` on the screen and created in `onPair`, before `isPairing` is set. This is a product defect and not a harness artefact: on a phone whose camera has not been asked for yet, the pre-prompt that explains what the camera is for can be replaced by the scanner it was meant to precede, and that scanner has no permission to show anything. It was invisible for as long as it existed because the simulator reports camera access as `.authorized`, which makes `start()` set `.scan` — the same value the reset produced. Two wrongs agreeing is why no host test could see it: the fault is in view composition, and only the on-glass lane exercises that. Left open as a standing note: `Step`'s default of `.scan` is a second hazard of the same shape, since a slow `current()` shows the scanner and then swaps. Fixing that needs an undecided case and is a design call rather than a repair.
subject.title: the phone rebuilt two owned objects inside body, resetting the pairing flow

subject.text: Measured 20 Aug 2026. `make test` failed with 4 issues at a one-minute load average of ~700 and passed all 1473 tests in 179 suites at load 46, on the same source, minutes apart. The four were `ActivityReconnectTests` (`a reconnect over a feed that stays live releases its guard`), `DiscoverBoardTests` (`client.searchQueries.count` reading 1 where the baseline said 2), and `SettingsAndMenuBarTests` twice (`model.trackerState` still nil). An earlier run at the same load failed only the first, so the set was not stable either — which is what separated this from a product defect. A suite that reports a defect the product does not have is the failure this campaign has already paid for once, in DEF-029, where a dead instrument read as a dead product for ten consecutive runs. CLOSED by making each wait a condition rather than a deadline, at three sites: 1. `ShellTestSupport.waitUntil` — ceiling 5s → 30s. It returns the moment the condition holds, so a passing test pays nothing for the larger bound; the bound exists only so a condition that never arrives fails instead of hanging. Five seconds was inside the scheduling noise of a contended host, which is the whole finding. 2. `ActivityReconnectTests.completes` — 2s → 30s, same argument. The defect it bounds is a call that *never* returns, so it exhausts any budget and a generous one costs only the time a genuine hang takes to report. 3. `DiscoverBoardTests.searchIsDebounced` — a fixed sleep replaced by two waits, because the claim has two halves and one sleep proved neither on a slow host. First a bounded wait for the debounce to fire at all; then a full debounce window of quiet with the count still at one, which is what rules out one request per keystroke. The second is a real quiet period rather than a deadline, so load cannot shorten it into a false pass — the wait on its own is satisfied by the *first* request and would pass against exactly the defect this test exists to catch. Armed 20 Aug 2026, all three, each watched to fail with its own message: `waitUntil` at `.seconds(0)` reads `no poll ran at all`, `the poll died with the scene that started it` and `five keystrokes issued 0 requests`; `completes` at `.milliseconds(1)` reads `reconnect did not return while the feed stayed live`; and a `queryChanged()` inserted inside the quiet period reads `a later request arrived: five keystrokes issued 2 requests in total`. The original trigger is not reproducible on demand from here — the load came from another project's Rust test binary, two node processes and `lsdiagnose` — so the fix is proven by the arms rather than by reproducing the contention.
subject.title: four async package tests asserted on a deadline the machine could miss

subject.text: Measured 20 Aug 2026 on two different worktrees the same afternoon. A fresh `git worktree` has no `node_modules` and no `dist`; `parity-selftest` is the last target `make all` runs, and its own environment check therefore fires only after lint, both builds, 1483 package tests, the iOS lane and the on-glass lane have all passed. Both runs came back `exit=2` on a tree where nothing was wrong with the code — roughly forty minutes each, twice. It is a lane defect rather than a product one, and the shape is familiar: the gate was honest (it said `the MCP SDK is not installed. Run npm install.` rather than skipping) and it was honest at the wrong moment. A check that can only fail on the environment belongs where the environment is checked. CLOSED by moving both checks into the `tools` target, which `all` runs first: `node_modules` must exist, and `dist/index.js` must exist because without it `parity-lane-selftest` SKIPS, and a skip is not a pass. Each names the command that fixes it. Armed 20 Aug 2026 in a bare directory holding nothing but the Makefile: with no `node_modules` it exits 1 naming `npm install && npm run build`, and with `node_modules` present but no `dist` it exits 1 naming `npm run build` and saying why a skip is not a pass. Costs a millisecond on a tree that has both.

subject.text: CleanupBoardRow carries three treatments for a skill row — the `Read first…` substitution when SkillChecks.originUnchanged fails, the skill-kind `Remove…` drawn disabled because the router removes servers and never files on disk, and the candidacy reason — and none of them had a rendered path in any configuration of the product. A skill is proposed for cleanup only when every readable client lacks it, and all six skills in SkillFixtures.populated are installed somewhere, so the Debug Cleanup board drew three servers and zero skills. Release reaches the branch only if a real user happens to hold an orphaned skill. CASE-0136 asserted the branch exists by reading CleanupBoardRow and said in its own note why it stopped there; what nobody could say was that a build had ever drawn it. Fixed in-campaign by adding a Debug-only `cleanupSkills` scenario and two SkillFixtures.uninstalled rows, kept separate from `populated` because SURF-004's on-glass predicate asserts the count populated publishes. No view code was touched and no assertion was weakened. Now photographed by CASE-0138/CASE-0139 and guarded in the harness by CASE-0144.

subject.text: Found while building R22's redactor, filed rather than fixed. `Describe.row` emits `command` and `args` RAW, and `ControlHandler.gate` reads the token only for POST/DELETE/PATCH, so the complete command line of every stdio upstream is readable by anything that can open the loopback port. The same function is careful in the adjacent case — it emits `envKeys` and `headerKeys` and never a value, with B10's reasoning attached — so argv is the one credential-carrying position on that route that is published whole. It matters because argv IS a credential channel: `--token=`, `--api-key=` and a connection string with an inline password are ordinary MCP server invocations, and R22 scrubs args for exactly that reason. The exposure predates R22 and is not made worse by it: the bundle's args go through the value scrub, and this route's do not. NOT FIXED HERE, and the reason is a parity decision rather than effort. `GET /servers` is reference-diffed — `control-servers-get` in planning/parity/surface.tsv, verdict `proven` — so redacting args moves a surface R4 compares byte for byte, and the ungated GET is itself a ported defect this repository records rather than silently repairs. Closing it means changing both routers or declaring a divergence, and that is the owner's call. 2026-10-19 — FIXED IN BOTH ROUTERS by merge 74d15306 (Merge ai/argv-redact), whose subject records that GET /servers stops publishing secret-bearing argv. Unit evidence: ArgvRedactionTests (app/Tests/RouterCoreTests/ArgvRedactionTests.swift) and test/argv-redact.test.ts, with parity vectors in argv-redact.json. Verified 2026-10-19: the `ArgvRedactionTests` suite passed under `swift test`, and `node --test` on test/argv-redact.test.ts passed. Status is fixed · in-test. No campaign re-run is recorded against this row.
subject.title: GET /servers discloses every stdio upstream's full argv to an unauthenticated local caller

subject.detail: Measured 2026-08-27 by G16 while enumerating SURF-026, and independently by G15. M15 made Settings a Scene and removed the case from `Destination`, and capture-mac-glass.sh still ran `axkit select Settings`. That select fails — `axkit: no sidebar row starting 'Settings'` — the app stays on whichever board the loop visited last, and the shutter filed THAT board's pixels under SURF-011: byte-identical to the Cleanup board on one loop ordering and to the Insights board on another. THE CAMPAIGN'S OWN INSTRUMENTS CAUGHT IT FROM TWO DIRECTIONS, which is the part worth keeping. glass-assert.py's raster uniqueness check went red because two cases shared a sha256; `--discriminate` reported the neighbouring board's predicate wrongly accepting SURF-011's dump, because that dump IS the neighbouring board; and the capture manifest's readback recorded the picture's target as the neighbour's route under subject SURF-011, contradicting its own filename. FIXED HERE, NARROWLY: the capture script now refuses to photograph a select that did not take, and says which board the window is actually showing. That is the script's own standing rule rather than a new one — it already declines to substitute a picture for the pairing sheet and the status item, and its header records the run that filed the Inbox board as SURF-010. The title and the dump are still written from what the app is really showing, so the failure stays visible downstream; what is withheld is the photograph, because a misattributed picture is the one artefact nothing downstream can correct. STILL OPEN, and deliberately not fixed here: 1. SURF-011 has no route to the Settings SCENE. It needs Cmd-comma or the app menu, not a sidebar select that cannot succeed. CASE-0016 and CASE-0111 fail until it does. 2. THE MENU MAP IS PRE-M22. Committed SURF-001.menu.txt binds Cmd-4 to `Discover`; the running app binds Cmd-4 to `Harnesses`, exactly as Destination.selectionDigit declares (activity 1, servers 2, skills 3, harnesses 4, discover 5, inbox 6, evals 7, cleanup 8, insights 9). glass-assert.py's SURF-001 `menu` dict is the old map, so CASE-0001 asserts five bindings this build does not have. Correcting it is editing an assertion to restore a green, which this campaign forbids — it is owed as its own item, from Destination.selectionDigit rather than by hand. WHY IT IS THE SAME FINDING AS G14'S, ONE LAYER DOWN. G14 found the surface LIST had stopped growing while the product did. This is the EVIDENCE not having been re-taken since the build moved: the committed glass artefacts were last written on 20 Aug by cef3729, before M22 added two destinations and renumbered four accelerators. In both cases a completeness gate reported clean because what it measured was a stale artefact rather than the product. CLOSED ON THE EVIDENCE SIDE, 2026-08-27 (G21/G29). The frame this defect produced was still published: `inventory.json` gave SURF-011 the shot `evidence/shots/SURF-011.build.png`, and at `519aebc` those bytes were the Insights board. `capture-lineage.py --gate` reported it UNTIED because the capture step's own row said `target: app://mac/insights` while the filename said SURF-011 -- the manifest was right and the wall was wrong. Two moves, both provable from git. The Insights frame is renamed `evidence/shots/DEF-059.insights-filed-as-SURF-011.png`, keeping every capture-time field, so the defect keeps its exhibit and no filename match can offer it to SURF-011 again. The Settings capture it overwrote is restored to `SURF-011.build.png` from `cef3729`, TOGETHER WITH ITS MANIFEST ROW from the same commit -- the last commit where those bytes and that row agreed (sha 3b5a26ef, `target: app://mac/settings`, readback `Settings`, 2026-08-20T11:32:58Z). Restoring the pair from one commit is a recovery of a capture-time record; restamping the row against the new bytes would have been the manifest-after-the-fact defect. What is NOT closed is the cause: `axkit select Settings` still fails, so the campaign still has no Settings capture newer than 2026-08-20 and the glass script still declines to take one. THE CAUSE NOW HAS A READER, 2026-09-02 (wa5). `axkit select Settings` still fails, and the campaign still has no Settings capture newer than 2026-08-20 -- unchanged. What has changed is that the age is no longer invisible: `bin/glass-build-gate.py` reports `evidence/shots/SURF-011.build.png` and `evidence/ax/SURF-011.*` as STALE against the build this tree would produce, so the lane cannot be green over them again without somebody re-taking them. `bin/capture-mac-glass.sh`'s refusal to photograph a select that did not take is the other half and is unchanged. Both halves of the remaining work -- a route to the Settings SCENE, and the re-capture -- are macOS work and are not attempted here. CLOSED 2026-10-19 on glass. capture-mac-glass.sh opens Settings with ⌘, (backgrounded), selects the Router pane in the Settings window's own source list, photographs that window as SURF-011 (target app://mac/settings), dumps the Security pane as a second dump of the same surface, and closes the window. glass-assert at the current build: checked=435 failures=0; --decoy SURF-011 reddens 6.
subject.title: `Settings` is no longer a sidebar row, so the glass capture filed a neighbouring board's pixels under SURF-011 — and the committed glass evidence predates M22

subject.detail: Measured 2026-08-27 by G15, while enumerating SURF-025. The committed glass evidence under planning/test-campaign/evidence/ax was last written by commit cef3729 on 20 Aug. M22 then added two destinations and RENUMBERED four accelerators, and nothing re-took the pictures. Running bin/capture-mac-glass.sh against the current build turns four previously-passing cases red, and in every one of them the PRODUCT is right and the recorded evidence is stale: 1. THE MENU MAP. Committed SURF-001.menu.txt binds Cmd-4 to `Discover`; the running app binds Cmd-4 to `Harnesses`, exactly as Destination.swift's selectionDigit declares (activity 1, servers 2, skills 3, harnesses 4, discover 5, inbox 6, evals 7, cleanup 8, insights 9). glass-assert.py's SURF-001 `menu` dict is the pre-M22 map, so CASE-0001 asserts five bindings the shipped build does not have. 2. SETTINGS IS NOT A SIDEBAR ROW. M15 made Settings a Scene and removed the case from Destination, and capture-mac-glass.sh still does `axkit select Settings`. That select now fails — `axkit: no sidebar row starting 'Settings'` — the app stays on Cleanup, and the script photographs the CLEANUP board and files it as SURF-011. CASE-0016 and CASE-0111 fail against it. THE CAMPAIGN'S OWN INSTRUMENTS CAUGHT BOTH, WHICH IS THE ONE GOOD PART. The capture manifest's readback records that picture as target `app://mac/cleanup` under subject SURF-011, contradicting its own filename — the exact mechanism the script was rebuilt around. Independently, glass-assert.py --discriminate reports LEAK SURF-007 wrongly accepted 1 of 8 foreign board dumps: SURF-011 — because SURF-011's dump IS the Cleanup board. Two instruments, one cause. WHY THIS IS THE SAME FINDING AS G14'S, ONE LAYER DOWN. G14 found the surface LIST had not grown since it was written. This is the EVIDENCE not having been re-taken since the build moved. In both cases a completeness gate reported clean because the thing it measured was a stale artefact rather than the product. NOT FIXED HERE, DELIBERATELY. G15's remit is the Harnesses enumeration, and correcting glass-assert.py's menu map or the Settings navigation would be editing an assertion to restore a green — even though the product is right, that is the move this campaign forbids, and the stale assertion is the instrument that found this. The four cases are set to `fail` with this id in their notes. Owed: re-map SURF-001's menu dict from Destination.selectionDigit, and give SURF-011 a route to the Settings SCENE (Cmd-comma or the app menu) instead of a sidebar select that cannot succeed. INSTRUMENTED 2026-09-02 (wa5), NOT CLOSED. The cause this row names -- a committed capture carrying no tie to the build it came from -- is now measurable. `planning/test-campaign/bin/glass-build-gate.py` binds every artifact the macos-glass lane cites to the git blob identity of the Mac app's build inputs (the set `scripts/acceptance/build-freshness.sh` compiles from) and exits 2 when that identity is not the one the lane is being read against. It is RED on this tree over all 56 artifacts, in 7 capture groups spanning 20-29 Aug: `evidence/runs/glass-build-gate.log`. The stamps it reads are marked `reconstructed-from-git` and are deliberately the weaker claim -- git can prove which commit last wrote each artifact, so the record establishes the build the evidence CANNOT BE NEWER THAN rather than the build it was taken from. `bin/capture-mac-glass.sh` now calls `glass-build-gate.py --emit` in the run that takes the pictures, stamping from the bundle's own CFBundleShortVersionString/CFBundleVersion and the `.mcprouter-build-stamp` the Makefile writes after `xcodebuild` exits 0, so a re-capture replaces each reconstructed row with a capture-time one. Watched both ways: `evidence/runs/glass-build-gate.selftest.log`, four arms, green over a current capture and red over a stale one, an uncovered one and an undatable row. Case CASE-0342. WHAT IS NOT SETTLED. The re-capture itself, which is the whole of what this defect asks for. It needs a macOS host with Xcode and a display server; the work above was done on Windows, where there is no Swift toolchain, no xcodebuild and no way to open the app's window. The four cases stay `fail` with `owed` recording the re-capture and its owner. The second half of the row -- SURF-001's menu map, to be re-read from `Destination.selectionDigit` rather than by hand -- is equally macOS work and equally untouched. Nothing here edits an assertion, a stamp or a recorded identity to restore a green.
