subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=package not installed
subject.note: A real MSIX, built, deployed and removed, with a recorder at each step that is not the thing that wrote it. MakeAppx packs and .NET's ZipArchive reads the OPC container back - so the identity assertion is made against the PACKED ARTIFACT rather than against the file on disk that was handed to the packer. `winget validate` is the winget client applying a schema this repository does not own. Add-AppxPackage deploys and Get-AppxPackage reports: Fledgeling.MCPRouter_0.1.0.0_x64__facmrsw33693e. THE INSTALL ARM IS WHAT TURNS A FILE INTO A PACKAGE. A manifest can pack cleanly, validate cleanly, and be refused at deployment for a capability, an architecture or a signature - and every static check in the world passes right up to that point. 'CLEAN UNINSTALL RULES' IS THE HALF WORTH READING TWICE. UninstallGuidance promises that uninstalling preserves %USERPROFILE%\.claude\mcp-router. That is a promise about what SURVIVES, and a promise about survival cannot be checked by any amount of reading - only by an uninstall that actually ran. The lane plants a marker, installs, removes, and requires both that the deployment stack reports the package gone and that the marker is still there. WHAT THE LANE PUTS BACK: a self-signed certificate is added to LocalMachine\TrustedPeople so an unsigned developer package can deploy at all, and removed in a finally block however the run ends. Verified afterwards: zero Fledgeling.* packages, zero witness certificates. A lane that left a trusted publisher behind would have changed what this machine will install, silently and for every future run. NOT SETTLED: that anyone can obtain the package. Nothing publishes it, the winget InstallerUrl is a deliberate example.invalid placeholder, and this lane asserts the placeholder is PRESENT so the manifest cannot be mistaken for a shipping one. DEF-083 carries the publishing step, which needs a signing certificate and a pull request into a third-party repository.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=no task registered
subject.note: The Windows task scheduler holding a task the product registered, read by an API that did not write it. The writer is MCPRouter.Shell.Live's LogonTaskSupervisor driving schtasks.exe with the Task Scheduler XML it builds; the recorder is Get-ScheduledTask, the ScheduledTasks module over the scheduler's WMI provider - a different API, a different process and a different vocabulary for the same facts. The XML says RunLevel LeastPrivilege and the recorder answers RunLevel Limited, and nothing in this repository translates between them. The scheduler also normalised the interval this run asked for, PT60S, into PT1M, which is the plainest available evidence that the read did not come back through anything this code wrote. EIGHT ARMS, AND TWO ARE ABOUT THE INSTRUMENT. BASELINE requires the recorder to report the task ABSENT before registration - without it, a task left behind by an interrupted run makes every other arm pass over a run that registered nothing. SILENCE requires it to report absence again after removal, which is what separates a reader from an echo: a recorder that always answered yes would satisfy the six product arms by construction. The other six read the three claims LifecyclePresentation prints to the operator - triggered at logon, un-elevated, restarting on failure - plus the executable and port this run asked for, plus presence and removal. WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE, and the reason it is one case rather than the whole of REQ-035: nothing here logs the user out, so the trigger has never been watched to fire, and nothing here starts or kills a daemon, so the restart has never been watched to happen. DEF-081 carries those two. This case settles that the registration the product performs produces, in the Windows task scheduler, a task carrying the properties the product's own UI describes - which before 2026-09-02 was unmeasured entirely, and which DEF-074 recorded as a supervision model nothing performed.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=a supervised process that dies
subject.note: The half of WIN23's supervision promise that had never been watched: a daemon the Windows task scheduler starts, loses, and starts again. DEF-081 filed it as unmeasurable and named the blocker as a missing Windows daemon binary; the blocker was real and is gone - app/windows/MCPRouter.Witness.Daemon is a harness process that starts, records its own start and waits to be killed, so there is something for the scheduler to supervise. WHAT THE MEASUREMENT FOUND IS NOT WHAT THE ROW EXPECTED. The registration the product wrote carried RestartOnFailure with a 60-second interval and a count of 3, and it did not restart the daemon at all. Killed, watched 150 seconds, on the unified scheduling engine and the legacy one, for a run started by a trigger and one started on demand: four registrations, no restart. The same block DID restart, three times at exactly 60 seconds, a task whose Command named a file that does not exist - so the instrument can see a restart, and RestartOnFailure governs a task that fails to LAUNCH rather than one whose action launched and later died. DEF-320 carries that, and the product now writes a Repetition on the trigger alongside MultipleInstancesPolicy IgnoreNew. THE RECORDERS ARE TWO AND NEITHER WROTE ANYTHING: Get-ScheduledTaskInfo for the scheduler's own account of its runs, and Get-CimInstance Win32_Process for the process identity, which is what makes 'it came back' a different process id rather than a report from the thing that came back. The daemon's own run log is carried and graded by nothing. EIGHT ARMS, THREE OF THEM ABOUT THE INSTRUMENT: BASELINE requires both tasks absent and no daemon running, so nothing below is inherited from an interrupted run; CLAIM.repetition and CLAIM.ignorenew read the product's own unmodified logon registration back through the WMI provider; SILENCE requires both recorders to say no once the tasks are gone. ONE SUBSTITUTION, SAID OUT LOUD: a trigger repetition does not apply to an on-demand start - measured, twice - so the live task carries a TimeTrigger where the product writes a LogonTrigger, because this lane must not log the machine out. Every Setting, the repetition interval, the principal, the action and the instances policy are the product's own document. That the trigger fires AT LOGON is still unwitnessed and DEF-081 keeps it.

subject.evidence: scripts/windows/win23-logon-task-witness.ps1 measures the REGISTRATION and says so in its own notMeasured[]: it does not log the user out and it does not start or kill a daemon. So the two behaviours the operator is actually promised - that the daemon comes up at logon, and that a crashed one comes back - rest on the Windows task scheduler honouring a LogonTrigger and a RestartOnFailure block that this repository has confirmed are present and has never confirmed are honoured. UPDATED 2026-09-03: planning/evidence/WIN23/run/restart-witness.json (all 8 arms held) and restart-witness-armed.json (exactly LIVE.restarted broke).

Every sidebar row is selected in turn and the effect is read in the RESTORATION STORE, which is a different channel from the one that struck: `ShellModel.selection`'s `didSet` calls `store.save(destination:)`, so a real selection leaves a value in a scratch `UserDefaults` suite that nothing in the test wrote, and that a relaunch reads. `model.selection == .servers` after `model.select(.servers)` was deliberately NOT used — it reads the property the call just wrote, which is the actuation side of the vacuous assertion (`references/inert-ui.md`, `detector-defects.md` §11). Each row is approached from a DIFFERENT destination, because `didSet` guards on `oldValue != selection` and a loop starting where the model boots would have the first row write nothing at all. The destination-collapse relation is asserted as a count rather than as seven separate greens: seven presses, seven DISTINCT persisted values, so a shell whose rows all led to one place fails on the cardinality. A second model built on the same store comes up where the last row left it, which is the read-back a relaunch actually performs. `Settings` is the eighth control and is not a destination: M15 moved it to a scene of its own, so the effect read is the installed opener firing exactly once AND the console's persisted destination not moving. Both halves, because an implementation that opened the scene and also selected a board would pass the first alone. LIMIT, stated rather than left implicit: a persisted destination proves the selection took. It does not prove a different board was DRAWN — SwiftUI's view tree is opaque to a SwiftPM test and `ContentZone`'s switch is unreachable from here. That half is CASE-0001's, on glass, and it is FAILING (DEF-058, DEF-059), so it counts nothing. This is the in-process half and says which half it is.

SURF-004 reaches 2 of 21 and the remaining four state-changing controls are recorded in `inventory.json` under `controlsUnactuatable` rather than left in the denominator unexplained: the build draws none of them. That is DEF-062, and it is the finding this case produced — `references/inert-ui.md`'s own stated limit is that no amount of testing the build reveals what the build lacks, and giving the surface a denominator is what made the four visible.

N8. The inertness guard on the untrusted-input boundary, made capable of failing. M19 shipped `MarkdownSecurityTests.htmlIsInert` with four spellings that named `javascript:`, no scheme, or nothing, and two assertions -- no link, no `imageURL` -- that `MarkdownInline.sanitized` makes true of every input it touches. It could not go red. M30 wired `ControlAPICapabilityDocumentSource` into the shipped UI, so router-served third-party text now reaches this renderer in a Release build, and the guard on it measured nothing. MEASURED, not assumed: the platform parser does keep inline HTML inert -- under `MarkdownInline`'s own options it hands each tag back as characters and marks it `.inlineHTML`, an intent naming no destination, and it does so under all four combinations of `allowsExtendedAttributes` and `interpretedSyntax`. Swift 6.2, macOS 26.6.2 (25G83), Debug, `swift test`. So this was an evidence defect and not a live vulnerability, and the fix is the assertion rather than new sanitisation. Two `https` spellings were added, because `https` is the one scheme the allowlist keeps and therefore the only one that can carry an interpreted `<a>` through to the assertion; a presence control runs the same reader over the markdown twin of the same destination first; and two clauses were added that the old body did not have -- handed back verbatim, and no attribute beyond the `.inlineHTML` marker. That last clause also corrects the test's own claim: the parser DOES attach one attribute to inline HTML and `sanitized` carries it, so the old name -- `inline HTML acquires no attribute of any kind` -- was false as written as well as unfailable, which is why nobody found out.

This case opens the overflow through ExpandCollapsePattern.Expand and reads both commands back with their names and ControlType.Button, between a BASELINE and a SILENCE that both find them absent from the control view AND the raw view. The writer is not the reader: overflow-actuate.ps1 expands in its own process and writes only the ExpandCollapseState it saw, while every element reading comes from uia-dump.ps1 started separately. TWO FINDINGS FROM THE FIRST RUN, neither planted, both corrected in the manifest rather than in the assertion. (1) probe-expectation.json predicted that opening the overflow would cost the never-activated guarantee, and IT WAS RIGHT: the probe held the foreground at none of the three baseline samples and at all six effect and silence samples, so Expand activates the window and Collapse does not hand the foreground back. That cost is now DECLARED as `overflow.activationCost` and compared both ways, so the day WinUI stops activating, this arm reddens rather than quietly acquiring a guarantee nobody re-checked. Baseline stays a hard assertion. (2) each command resolves to TWO tree paths with the overflow open, because WinUI publishes the OverflowPopup subtree once through a Microsoft.UI.Content.PopupWindowSiteBridge child and once in place beneath the ApplicationBar. Both copies agree on name, controlType, className, isEnabled, isOffscreen, accessKey, patterns and bounding rectangle, so it is one control on two routes; the assertion now permits several matches only while they agree on everything a caller would act on, and plant (H) watches that a genuinely different control under one id still fails. WHAT THIS DOES NOT BUY. It is not at-rest coverage and does not close DESIGN.md section 11 rule 9 for these two commands. The product fix is a surface that realises them without an actuation, and that is DEF-340. Neither command is INVOKED, so both stay outside the actuation census with a stated reason on SURF-029; this arm's subject is realisation and vocabulary, not effect. subject.note: The verb IS the gate, and it is not describing a mutation. The bundle changes nothing. It is a POST because stage 2 of `ControlHandler.handle` gates the token on POST/DELETE/PATCH only, so the verb is the only thing deciding whether this router hands its whole diagnostic corpus — log lines included — to any unauthenticated caller that can open the loopback port, which per `ControlToken` includes a web page the user merely visits. All three answers are pinned — 401 untokened, 405 on GET, 200 on a tokened POST — so a later tidy-up that makes the verb 'correct' goes red rather than silently opening the route. Written from the ambient section of scripts/windows/uia/shell-lane.ps1, which runs out of process against the real shell binary in the interactive session and DRIVES THE ROUTER FROM OUTSIDE THE APPLICATION: the lane owns the router the shell is pointed at - its own node process, on its own port, over its own MCP_ROUTER_HOME - and these rows stop it, put a stand-in on that port and start it again while the shell is told nothing at all. What is read back is the pane footer, addressed by AutomationId, never by name. The lane recorded: the router was stopped from outside the application - this script killed the process and then confirmed, over the loopback port, that nothing answers http://127.0.0.1:62755/status - and the shell's pane moved to 'Cannot reach router' / 'The router daemon is not responding on 127.0.0.1:62755.'. It does not say 'Router ready' over a router that is not running, which is DEF-301 exactly. THE RECORDER IS NOT THE WRITER, and on this row it is not even the shell: UI Automation read of the shell pane, over a router state driven by starting and stopping processes outside the application. That is what makes this row a claim about the MACHINE rather than about the application's own report of itself, which is the whole of DEF-087. WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE: that the registration fires at a real logon, and that a daemon executable resolves on an operator's machine - the lane points the shipped resolution at a witness task name and a witness executable of its own so it cannot disturb the operator's real registration. Both limits stay on DEF-087's resolution rather than being folded into this green. THE CALL THIS LANE MADE, which is what `actuates` is NOT for: the row was driven through System.Windows.Automation's TogglePattern.Toggle() from shell-lane.ps1. `actuates` carries the control the surface declares - DEF-080.

subject.text: PARTLY CLOSED 20 Aug 2026, and the part that is not closed is named rather than left as a silent gap. The vocabulary differential compared accessible names of AXButton/AXCheckBox/AXPopUpButton/AXTextField against their DOM counterparts board by board, with the shell and the fixture rows subtracted, and reported examined=8 boards, in-design-not-build=20, in-build-not-design=16. Cleanup's design specifies Inspect, Read first… and Remove on each row and the running board published none of them. FIXED: `CleanupBoardRow` now draws a trailing action column — `prototype.html:950` gives it `width:150px` — carrying `Inspect` and `Remove…`, wired by `CleanupBoard` to the selection and to the removal dialog. Removal opens the dialog rather than removing, because the one destructive act on this board is never one click. It is dimmed in place for a skill with `CheckCopy.skillRemoveDisabled` as both tooltip and accessibility hint, exactly as `CleanupInspector.actions` already does it — a reason only a mouse can reach is not a reason. The row's accessibility element moved from `children: .combine` to `.contain`, because combining flattens the buttons into the label and leaves nothing to press: the same failure this campaign already recorded for a time-limited undo inside a live region. FIXED 20 Aug 2026, and it was the half this row was held open for: (a) `Read first…`. `CleanupBoardModel.Candidate` now carries `provenance: String?`, read through `SkillChecks.originUnchanged` rather than off `skill.provenance` directly so this board and the Checks board cannot disagree about what counts as moved, and a server's call site passes `nil` because a server has no marketplace to have moved from. The row draws `Read first…` **in place of** Inspect and Remove rather than beside them — `prototype.html:961` is making the same argument this pane makes everywhere else, and a removal left on that row is one click from a fact nobody has read yet — plus the three other things the design keys on the same field: the fail-coloured leading tile standing in for `dot f`, the warn icon, and the provenance note substituted for the candidacy reason in the `why it is here` column. The tint is painted **behind** the selection fill rather than in front of it, which is a deliberate divergence: the mock sets it as an inline style, which in CSS beats the selected class, so a selected flagged row there reads as unselected. The sheet behind the button states the three fields `SkillProvenance` carries and none of the four the prototype invents — an owner at install, a force-pushed branch, a hash no longer in history, and an eval score — one of which is not computable at all, and it says on screen that its date is the router's own first sighting rather than an install date. Its dismiss reads `Leave it` because there is nothing to cancel, and removal is dimmed in place with `CheckCopy.skillRemoveDisabled` rather than offered, because the control API is read-only for skills and the prototype's `Remove it` would have been a control that does nothing. Guarded by CASE-0135, CASE-0136 and CASE-0137, nine assertions across five tests, all armed — nine mutation arms, each red for its own stated reason. STILL NOT FIXED: (b) the reason column still truncates where the design shows the whole sentence; (c) Checks' `Edit cases` and `Run again`, a different board; (d) Settings' `Pair another device` and `Unpair`, which is DEF-001 reaching this instrument through the design rather than through a failing assertion. Guarded by `CleanupRowActionsTests`, four assertions, all armed 20 Aug 2026: blanking the Inspect label, switching `.contain` back to `.combine`, dropping the board's `inspect:` wiring, and performing a real removal to prove the write-guard predicate is live rather than vacuously true. Measured on the fixed build before it was reported: adding a 156pt action column to every row does **not** push this board into DEF-015's overflow. `AXSplitGroup` reads 980pt inside a 980pt window on Cleanup, unchanged, while Checks, Skills and Discover still read 988, 1044 and 1119 — the same three as before. Worth measuring rather than reasoning about: the row's fixed widths sum close enough to the pane that arithmetic predicted a 7pt overflow and the running app disagreed.
subject.title: Cleanup's per-row actions are specified by the design and drawn by nothing

subject.text: CAUSE FOUND AND FIXED 20 Aug 2026; this record replaces one that said the cause was unknown and named machine saturation as a candidate. The candidate was wrong. The process-wide accessibility engine was OFF, so SwiftUI's `_UIHostingView` built its accessibility container and vended an EMPTY element array — `accessibilityElements == []`, not nil — and every label assertion in the target read empty and reported its own honest verdict, `nothing was measured, so this proved nothing`. That is indistinguishable, from inside the suite, from a product that renders no copy. A probe settled it: calling `_AXSSetAutomationEnabled(true)` took the same hosted view's published element count from 0 to 1. THE ENGINE HAD BEEN ON BY ACCIDENT — something else on this machine had switched it on — which is why this suite was green for months while depending on ambient host state no file in this repo controls, and why it went red with no change to the branch. THREE CHANGES ARE THE FIX, and the third was found only because the first two were not enough. (1) `PhoneSurfaceTests` resolves `_AXSSetAutomationEnabled` out of `/usr/lib/libAccessibility.dylib` (falling back to `AccessibilityUtilities.framework`) via dlopen/dlsym and calls it once per process, before the first `host()`. (2) The walker reads `accessibilityElements` first, because SwiftUI publishes through the array and leaves `accessibilityElementCount()` at 0 — measured on iOS 26.5, where one hosted `Text` reported `accessibilityElements.count == 1` and `accessibilityElementCount() == 0` in the same breath, so reading only the indexed API walked past every element SwiftUI had. Those two took `make test-ios` from 52 failures to 0 — and then `make all`, run immediately afterwards on the same device, came back with 39. (3) THE STATE IS DEVICE-SCOPED AND THE CALL LANDS ON THE NEXT PROCESS, NOT THIS ONE. On a device left in the disabled state, the run that re-enables it fails a DETERMINISTIC set of 15 test cases — identical set, measured three times, verified with `comm` in both directions — and the run after it, with no change to anything, is clean. The 15 are exactly the cases that host a `ScrollView`; the tests that pass alongside them are geometry, counts and negative assertions, all of which an empty tree satisfies, so the green half of that run was vacuous too. `test-ios` therefore runs a throwaway single-test process before the graded one and discards its exit code. MEASURED END TO END: three consecutive runs with the call mutated to `(false)` drive `MCPRouter-Unit` into the disabled state (54 failures each, the whole suite red, which is correct for a dead engine); the very next `make test-ios`, with the warm-up in the recipe, is 36 tests and 0 failures in 1.4s. THE INSTRUMENT CHECK IS ITSELF INSTRUMENTED. `testTheAccessibilityEngineCanBeSwitchedOn` blocks on a probe that hosts `ScrollView { Text }` and reads it back through the same walk every other assertion uses, with a 20s deadline. Two narrower probes were built first and both were wrong in opposite directions, which is why the shape is stated rather than assumed: a bare `Text` read either way reports the engine live at t=0 of a run in which 15 cases went on to read empty, and a `ScrollView` read through the accessibility-container path alone reports the engine dead on a device where all 35 other tests pass. A probe that answers differently from the thing it stands for answers a different question. On a dead engine the deadline fires and the case fails with `no hosted Text published a label within 20s`, measured. ARMED THREE WAYS. (a) Renaming the symbol to `_AXSSetAutomationEnabledXXX` on a device whose engine is already live fails exactly one test — the instrument check — and leaves the other 35 green, which is correct for that arm and proves only the resolution assertion. (b) With the call mutated to `(false)`, the first run on `MCPRouter-Arm`, a device created for the arm, recorded 53 failures across 36 tests: that is what proves the other 35 depend on the engine. (c) The first run ever taken on `MCPRouter-Arm2`, a device whose engine had never been live, is 36 tests and 0 failures, so a fresh device needs no warm-up and only an explicitly disabled one does. Both arm devices were deleted afterwards; `make test-ios IOS_UNIT_DEVICE=<name>` recreates either. TWO HARDENING CHANGES from the investigation are kept and neither is the fix: `test-ios` creates and owns `MCPRouter-Unit` instead of sorting booted devices first — the exact picker DEF-020 condemned, still live in this recipe — and the walk retains every element it visits so `ObjectIdentifier` is unique among live objects as its use assumes. A third, waiting on a product surface's tree over a two-second deadline, was written, measured to change nothing, and removed: it cost 130 seconds a run and bought no measurement. The wait that IS kept differs from it in the one way that matters — it waits on a probe whose answer is known, so a timeout is a fact about the instrument rather than about the view. THE DEPENDENCY IS ON A PRIVATE SYMBOL, in the test target only, never linked into the app; the instrument check fails loudly if a future runtime renames it, so this target goes red rather than quietly empty. Carried as CASE-0126.
subject.title: the iOS unit lane read an empty accessibility tree because the engine was off

subject.source: app/Sources/MCPRouterKit/Control/Scenario.swift; evidence/runs/make-test-3.log (clean build, 1512 tests in 188 suites); app/Scripts/enum-layout-stamp.py; Makefile target enum-layout-stamp; evidence/runs/make-test-4.log
subject.text: Adding a 14th case to `Scenario` made `make test` fail with 31 issues, two of which cannot be true of the source: `Expectation failed: (… → .live) == (.live → .fixture(…cleanupSkills))` in ShellClientFactoryTests and TriageSourceGuardTests, both asserting a Release-posture guard that returns .live unconditionally. `git stash` of the two changed source files → 19 tests pass; unstash → the same failures return, which reads as a real regression. It is not. `Choice.live` is encoded in the spare inhabitants of `Scenario`'s tag, so a new Scenario case shifts that encoding, and stale MCPRouterUI object files compiled against the old layout compare a value that no longer means what they think. `rm -rf app/.build` then rebuild: 5/5 pass, then 1512/1512. The hazard for this campaign is the mirror case — a stale build can as easily produce a green — so any test evidence taken across an enum change is taken from a clean build. MITIGATED 2026-08-20: `app/Scripts/enum-layout-stamp.py` hashes the ordered case list of every enum in the package (212 of them) and removes `app/.build` when that hash moves; `make test` now depends on it. The stamp is the case lists rather than the source, so it holds still for an ordinary edit and for a `switch` over the enum — the false positive a naive grep for `^\s*case` would hit — and moves for an added or renamed case. Armed on all four: comment SAME, switch statement SAME, added Scenario case MOVED, renamed Scenario case MOVED, restore back to baseline. The SwiftPM behaviour itself is unchanged and still upstream; what is fixed is this repo's exposure to it.

subject.detail: `vacuity-check.py`'s blind pass reports `examined=1820 mutating=3 re-read-after=0 blind=3` over this test tree. All three read after the mutation: `restartIsIssuedBeforeTheStagingWrite` reads `WatchWorld.serverNames`, the log, `kicks.issued` and `WatchState.load`; `restartIsOwedBeforeTheWriteLands` reads `WatchState.load` inside the lock and `WatchWorld.serverNames` on both sides of the rename; `restartRechecksTheCamera` reads `model.entry.characters`. The heuristic looks for a read AFTER the last occurrence of a mutating verb, and in this product the verb `restart` is also the name of the thing being observed — `restartPending`, `restarted scratch-label` — so the last `restart` in the file sits inside the final assertion and nothing is textually after it. Recorded rather than acted on: the tests are correct as written, and rewording an assertion to satisfy a text heuristic would make the suite worse. The pass is still worth running; 3 of 1820 is a reviewable rate, and it is the check that would have caught 26 of 32 on the campaign it was built from. CAUSE CORRECTED 21 Aug 2026; the diagnosis recorded above was wrong. It said the mutator's name is the observable's name (`restart` inside `restartPending`). Measured against 0.9.2's actual patterns, that cannot happen: the mutator scan at vacuity-check.py:180 requires `(?<![A-Za-z0-9_])` + verb + `\w*\s*\(`, so `state.restartPending == false` never matches for want of the call parenthesis. The real cause is that the seven default readers are all snake_case -- list_, get_, read_, fetch_, sample_, count_, load_ -- and the nine default mutators mostly are too (stop_all, stop_runner, clear_, cancel_). This is a camelCase Swift codebase, so NEITHER side could fire. The pass examined 1657 test bodies and found 3 mutating, 0 re-reading and 3 blind: `blind=3` reads as almost nothing wrong, and meant almost nothing looked at. The denominator was printed and nobody read 3-of-1657 as the alarm it was. Fixed by declaring the project's own vocabulary, which 0.9.2 added for exactly this: campaign.json now carries `blindVocabulary` with 14 camelCase mutators and 13 readers, and the pass reports examined=1657 mutating=320 re-read-after=232 blind=88, with the vocabulary it used printed above the findings. Two of the three original findings resolved on their real reads (`WatchState.load(`, `WatchWorld.read(`). The third, restartRechecksTheCamera, stays flagged and correctly so for a verb heuristic: its only reads are property comparisons -- `model.step`, `model.entry.characters` -- which carry no verb at all. That is the ceiling of this instrument rather than a defect in the test, and it is why the 88 is a worklist and not a verdict: the vocabulary is hand-declared and unvalidated. Of the 21 findings the tool prints, 15 carry a @Test attribute and 5 are fixture helpers in dedicated client files that 0.9.2's per-file helper heuristic does not exclude, because it keys on a function being called more than once in its OWN file and these are called from their importers.
subject.title: the blind-test pass flags three tests that do read after mutating, because the mutator's name is the observable's name

subject.detail: DETECTOR DEFECT, recorded so its numbers are not published as product findings. `vacuity-check.py`'s `blind` pass asks whether any READER appears after the last MUTATING call in a test body, both matched by name prefix. Run with the shipped defaults it reports `examined=1820 mutating=3 blind=3` — and all three are false: DEFAULT_READERS is snake_case (`load_`, `get_`, `read_`, `list_`) while this is a camelCase Swift codebase, so NO Swift reader can ever match, and the three `mutating` hits matched the token `restart` in their own function names. Both flagged WatchRestartTests cases read extensively after the mutation. Run with a hand-derived camelCase verb list it reports `examined=1834 mutating=258 re-read-after=158 blind=100`. Two of the flagged real tests were read in full and BOTH re-read: `undoRestoresTheItem` calls `queue.all()` three times after `model.remove(...)`, and `resetReindexesAnIndexFailure` reads `client.calls` after `board.reset(...)`. Neither `all` nor `calls` was in the list. Of the 20 findings the script prints, only 6 are `@Test` functions at all; the other 14 are test doubles and helpers, because the population is every `func` in any file with `test` in its path. CONCLUSION: on this codebase the pass measures the verb list rather than the suite, and no verb list derived by hand is evidence of anything. It is recorded, not published, and the campaign claims no blind-mutation number. The pass's other two arms — `unclassed` and `uncensused` — are exact and are kept. ADDRESSED UPSTREAM in 0.9.2, confirmed by running it 21 Aug 2026. Commit 28ecd67 (`the blind-mutation check was measuring itself`) fixes four detector defects that each RAISED the blind count, and the pass now prints the vocabulary it used above its findings -- `vocabulary: defaults + campaign.blindVocabulary — 22 mutator(s), 20 reader(s)` followed by the reader list -- which was this defect's complaint: a number published without saying what configuration produced it. The denominator also moved, 1841 to 1657, because fixture helpers are no longer counted as tests. Left open rather than closed: the residual named on DEF-040 sits in the same pass. SUPERSEDED 21 Aug 2026 by DEF-055. The specific claim here — snake_case DEFAULT_READERS against a camelCase Swift codebase, giving examined=1820 mutating=3 blind=3 with all three false — was resolved by declaring campaign.json's blindVocabulary, which 0.9.2 reads. The general claim, that no hand-derived verb list is evidence of anything, is not resolved; it is now MEASURED rather than asserted. DEF-055 carries that measurement (7 of 7 sampled findings false, four named mechanisms, a two-way arm) and is the entry to read. Recorded as superseded rather than closed: the finding was real and its successor is open.
subject.title: test-campaign 0.9.1's blind-mutation pass is dominated by its own verb configuration on this codebase, in both directions

subject.note: `#expect(result.tools != nil, ...)` at ShellTests.swift:133. `ReindexResult.tools` is a non-optional `Int` (MCPRouterKit/Control/Models.swift:263), so the comparison could not fail. The Swift compiler emitted `comparing non-optional value of type 'Int' to 'nil' always returns true` on every build of the test target; it was the only such warning in the suite. The intent was stated in the comment directly above it -- `.success` is distinguished from `.populated` by `a reindex that comes back with no error and a tool count` -- so the assertion was one character from doing its job. Repaired to `result.tools == 14`, the value FixtureControlAPIClient+Writes.swift:33 overrides for `.success`, which discriminates against the base `reindex-failure.json` fixture it starts from (`{"tools":0,"error":"fetch failed"}`). Armed in evidence/arming/CASE-0152.arming.log: with the override changed to 0 the assertion goes red (`(result.tools -> 0) == 14`), and the log records that the pre-repair form would have stayed green under the same mutation.
subject.text: A ShellTests assertion on the `.success` reindex scenario compared a non-optional Int to nil, so it was always true and read nothing.

subject.detail: Measured 2026-08-21. `.gitmodules` vendors `.claude/plugins/fledgeling-plugins` at `main`, and `planning/features-to-triage/LEDGER.md`'s allocation notes state the reason: 'a runner reads mockup-fidelity, mac-craft, design-craft and ux-craft at a repo-relative path rather than depending on the machine.' For test-campaign that is not what happens. The submodule (HEAD baaf79a, branch main, clean) carries `plugins/test-campaign` at version 0.5.0, whose `skills/test-campaign/scripts` holds five files: attach-shots.py, campaign.py, evidence-page.py, strict-check.py, witness-worklist.py. It has no `vacuity-check.py` and no `capture-lineage.py`; `grep effect-witness strict-check.py` returns nothing and `grep -c blindVocabulary vacuity-check.py` cannot run because the file is absent. Every gate this campaign reports ran from `~/.claude/plugins/cache/fledgeling-plugins/test-campaign/0.9.2/`, on the machine. The vacuity census, the effect-witness rung, the blind-mutation pass, the capture-lineage ratchet and the strict score of 65 all come from code the submodule does not contain, four minor versions ahead of it. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE PIPELINE, and it is the reason this is filed rather than noted: DEF-051, DEF-052, DEF-054, DEF-055 and DEF-056 are defects in 0.9.2's scripts. None of that code is in this repo at any path, so no ship-feature runner working in an mcp-router worktree can fix them. They are upstream work in github.com/fledgeling-co/fledgeling-plugins, and closing them requires a change pushed to that repo plus a submodule bump here — a different repo and an outward-facing action. Separately, a fresh clone that follows the documented `git submodule update --init --recursive` gets 0.5.0 and would reproduce none of this campaign's numbers. Not fixed here: which version the submodule should track, and whether the campaign should run from it rather than the cache, is the owner's call.
subject.title: the vendored fledgeling-plugins submodule is test-campaign 0.5.0 while every gate in this campaign ran from the machine's 0.9.2 cache

subject.evidence: TWO COMMENTS IN THIS REPOSITORY ALREADY NAME THIS AND NEITHER REMOVED IT. sweep-control-gate.py's own note on CONTROL_TIMEOUT says 'a timeout there answered nothing about whether the control is rotted'. scripts/windows/verify.ps1, declaring SWEEP_CONTROL_TIMEOUT=600, says the 120s default 'produced two findings reading its declared control does not pass, which is the gate reporting the host's shell as a rotted control - a false finding, and the direction that gets a gate switched off'. Both diagnose it exactly. The remedy taken was to raise the budget, which removes the symptom on this host and leaves the conflation in place: `run_control` returned False on TimeoutExpired, indistinguishable from a control that ran and exited non-zero. HOW IT SURFACED, AND IT WAS NOT A RED IN THE LANE. The gate was invoked bare during Wave C integration - outside verify.ps1, so without the 600s declaration - and reported six to eight controls as not passing. That red was the invocation's, not the tree's. What the investigation did establish is a measurement: planning/hooks/prove-pre-commit.sh exits 0 with 8 assertions over 6 directions in 258s on LUKESFF, so under the 120s default a control that fully holds is reported as one that does not.

subject.detail: DETECTOR DEFECT in test-campaign 0.9.2, found 21 Aug 2026. attach-shots.py iterates every image under evidence/shots and assigns `hit['shot'] = rel` on each match, last write wins, with no preference for a build capture over a design render. This campaign keeps six directories under evidence/shots (16 root, 8 design-size, 16 fidelity, 9 ios, 17 mock, 11 mock-hidpi), so for SURF-001 the candidates in iteration order are SURF-001.build.png, SURF-001.shell.png, mock/SURF-001.png, mock-hidpi/SURF-001.full.png -- and the last one wins. MEASURED for SURF-001, SURF-002 and SURF-006: `--apply` would repoint each surface's `shot` from its build capture to `evidence/shots/mock-hidpi/SURF-00N.full.png`, which is the render of the DESIGN, not the build. That is the skill's own headline failure mode -- publishing a picture of one thing under the name of another -- arriving in a sibling of the plane built to prevent it, and it would do so while every other gate stayed green, because capture-lineage.py gates the 16 captures cited by CASES and the surface wall is a different population. The report compounds it: the UNCORROBORATED block prints surface ids (SURF-001 ... SURF-011) rather than the file each verdict is about, so a reader sees eleven surfaces apparently lacking provenance when in fact each surface's ACTUAL `shot` field points at a corroborated build capture and the complaint is about a mock render nobody intended to attach. Distinguishing the two costs a re-derivation of the matcher by hand. Recorded rather than patched, precedent DEF-048, DEF-051, DEF-052 and DEF-053. The campaign's standing refusal to run `--apply` here predates this and was based on the DEF-006 mis-wire; it now has a measured mechanism behind it. Separately closed while investigating: this campaign's design-size captures carried their provenance in a second manifest, evidence/shots/design-size/captures.json, in a different schema ({captures:[...]} against the root's bare list) that no gate reads. Its 8 entries were merged into the root manifest with `target` derived from the root's declared target for the same subject and corroborated by each capture's own windowTitleReadback -- Servers, Activity, Skills, Discover, Inbox, Checks, Cleanup, Settings, every one matching -- recorded at capture time, and each carries `targetDerivedFrom` saying so. That was the campaign's own inconsistency and is fixed here; it was not the cause of the 11. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-27 (G21) after `evidence/shots/captures.json` was made a derived file. The uncorroborated count is 12 and stays 12: SURF-001..011 and SURF-022. Eleven of them are this defect -- `mock-hidpi/` sorts last, so it is the row that decides each surface's `shotProvenance`. The mock rows in the manifest deliberately carry NO `target`; the address the channel was pointed at is recorded in full as `renderedFrom`, with an `attachHazard` field naming this defect. Measured both ways on this tree: writing that address as `target` instead drops the uncorroborated count from 12 to 1 and DISARMS `--apply`'s refusal, because `attach-shots.py` only checks the field is present and never compares it to the subject's route -- which is item 5 of X8's work order. So the report going quiet would have been this defect getting worse while looking fixed. The twelfth, SURF-022, is not this defect: see DEF-061.
subject.title: attach-shots --apply would attach the design mock render as the build's surface shot for 11 surfaces, and its report names the surface rather than the file

subject.evidence: observed
subject.note: Added by G17. `filesystem-read` is a new value in this campaign's effect vocabulary — the five that existed were none, inbound-socket, outbound-socket, subprocess and filesystem-write, and none of them describes a route that reads a directory it was told about. The requirement itself is not new work: M19 and M30 both shipped against it and the campaign had no row for it, so the feature had no denominator and no case could have failed on it. Reach limit, stated rather than buried: the route serves only servers declaring a package directory and 0 of the 21 upstreams on this machine declare one (M30, planning/evidence/M30-reach.txt), so every case citing this requirement is measured against a CONSTRUCTED server. RECONCILED 2026-08-27. This row was allocated REQ-026 by G17 and G19 at the same time, off the same `main`. G19's REQ-026 keeps the number and states the WIRE contract: what GET /servers/:name/document serves and the exact refusal each rule names. This row keeps the half G19's does not carry -- that those documents are DRAWN in the Mac capability document panel, that a figure resolves from inside the package and nothing else is fetched, and that each refusal identifies itself on screen. Its cases are the swiftui lane's (CASE-0185..0190, CASE-0194) and they need a requirement to trace to; folding them into a router-daemon requirement would put a panel assertion inside a route's contract. G17's one WIRE case, CASE-0184, traces to REQ-026 instead, because that is the requirement its assertion is of. The two rows overlap on 'read out of the declared package directory' deliberately: neither text was rewritten, so the overlap is visible rather than resolved by editing delivered work. The `filesystem-read` effect class is left exactly as G17 declared it and is NOT in campaign.py's closed EFFECT_CLASSES -- `check` has flagged that since G17 landed and still does; G19's REQ-026 note records the same gap from the other side, having declined to name a class the vocabulary does not hold. Reconciling the vocabulary is the campaign owner's, not this renumber's. VOCABULARY RECONCILED 2026-08-29 by K4, which is the campaign-owner decision the paragraph above defers. `filesystem-read` is NOT added to the census vocabulary and this row no longer declares it as its `effect`. The list is the instrument's and it is closed: 24 copies of `campaign.py` and `vacuity-check.py` visible to this repository -- the `vendor/` pin and eleven cache versions from 0.9.3 to 0.16.0 -- carry the same nine-member tuple, `vendor/README.md` forbids editing the vendored copy ('a script that behaves one way in this repository and another way everywhere else stops being evidence of anything'), and upstream is a different repository. So the branch taken is the acceptance sketch's first: declare a class the census knows. THE CLASS IS `none`, AND `none` HERE MEANS `no representable class`, NOT `no external interaction`. The router does read the filesystem and the row still says so, in `effectUnrepresentable`, which `planning/test-campaign/bin/effect-class-census.py` reads and holds to a HARDER obligation than an ordinary row rather than a softer one: the named class must be outside the instrument's set, `effect` must be exactly `none` so the narrowing is stated rather than implied, and `provider` must RESOLVE against `campaign.json`'s `sourceRoot` through vacuity-check's own `resolve_provider`. Measured 2026-08-29 at `83e5380`: it resolves by path on `RouterCore/Control/ControlDocument.swift`, so deleting the read site reddens this row even though it has left the external-effect census. WHY NOT `inbound-socket`, which is the option a second reader picked. The route is served on the loopback listener and the class is defensible, but declaring it would trade one blocker for another and neither reader had the fact: `campaign.py`'s `unbacked_effects` (campaign.py:1078) blocks a requirement that names an external effect, is recorded `observed`, and has no passing case at the `effect-witness` rung. REQ-027's seven cases are structural, structural-visual, raster-visual and metamorphic; none is a witness, and the eight witnesses this campaign holds belong to other requirements. Choosing `inbound-socket` therefore means BUILDING a witness with a recorder, a non-zero count and a sabotage arm -- real engineering, and its subject would be the accept that CASE-0183 already witnesses for REQ-026. Recorded as the alternative it beat, with the axis it is better on: `inbound-socket` keeps the row inside the instrument's own external-effect denominator, where `none` moves that obligation into a repository-owned gate. WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE. The gate proves a provider exists in production source. That is the census floor, not a witness, and no case here observes a read at the boundary. The reach limit recorded above is unchanged.
subject.text: A capability's own read me, changelog and capability list are read out of the package directory its server declares and drawn in the document panel; images resolve from inside that package and nothing else is fetched, and every refusal names which one it is.

subject.note: FLOW-006.02. The panel drew a document THE ROUTER SERVED, not M19's fixture: the titlebar names g17-capability, the package's own H1 and prose are on screen, all three tab controls are drawn, and 'trawl' — the fixture capability every previous dump and capture of this panel was a picture of, M23's included — appears nowhere in the tree. Checks G17-P1, G17-P2, G17-P3. Picture: evidence/g17-document/readme.served.png. The server is CONSTRUCTED by the harness and labelled so in three places — the harness header, the package's own read me, and every row of evidence/g17-document/captures.json. 0 of the 21 upstreams on this machine declare a package directory (M30, planning/evidence/M30-reach.txt), so there is no real one to point at. The router, the route, the transport, the parser, the image resolver and the panel are all the product's. --- RUNG CORRECTED by J3, from `raster-visual`. Its three checks are G17-P1, G17-P2 and G17-P3, and all three read `readme.served.dump.json` — a titlebar's text, a heading and a sentence, the three tab labels, and the absence of the string `trawl` from the tree. Not one of them opens the PNG. The claim is true and it is structural, and it was carrying the strongest rung's badge on a frame it never read. The picture stays cited because it is the frame this dump was taken in the same render as, and it stays on the wall as FLOW-006.02's step shot.

FLOW-006.02, and the claim nothing had ever made: an image inside a served document DRAWS. M19's resolver returns bytes precisely so the app never opens a file, and until now the strongest available statement was that four image cards were laid out — `MarkdownBlockView` draws a figure and a refusal placeholder inside the same measured `card`, so the two are one record. This case does not fix that by adding a node: a node would say two views differ, and what needed saying is that bytes arrived and were painted. The pixels answer it. 65.7% of the figure card's own frame in readme.served.png is the constructed band's authored colour, read at the scale derived from the dump's size rather than assumed to be 2, with a 25% floor and a tolerance on the colour because the backing store resolves in the display's space (authored #2F9C9C reads back near #519A9B). Check G17-P4. --- ARTIFACT CORRECTED by J3. This case reads pixels — G17-P4 counts the band's colour over the figure card's own frame — so the rung is right and the picture was not: it cited the whole 1536x1640 frame, byte for byte the same file CASE-0185 and CASE-0187 cited, and that file does not show which card was measured. It now cites the crop of the card itself, written by the check at the moment it counted those pixels, with the parent frame and its sha256 recorded in `capture.derivedFrom` and in verdicts.json.

The 'outside the package' refusal, rendered and distinguishable. A reference climbing out of the package is refused by the router as escapesPackage, and the panel draws its own sentence — 'Not shown — this image points outside the package it came with.' — read back off the `figure-refusal` node G17 added, in a card carrying 0.00% figure colour. Both halves matter: the node says WHICH refusal landed, which no dump could say before, and the pixels say the card really is a placeholder rather than a picture nobody checked. The node costs the readme fidelity census nothing, because it is drawn only when a reference is refused and the M19 fixture's one image resolves. Check G17-P5. --- ARTIFACT CORRECTED by J3, on the same finding as CASE-0186 and from the other side of it. G17-P5 reads the `figure-refusal` node's own frame and requires under 1% figure colour, so the pixels are real and the picture was the whole frame the other two cases also cited. It now cites the crop of the refusal card — 708x28 of drawn sentence and no picture, which is exactly what the check asserts.

Refusal 1 of 3 — nothing served. A server declaring no cwd is refused noPackageDirectory on the wire, and the panel draws the designed state: 'g17-no-package has no package to read', and no figure. This is the state EVERY ONE of the 21 upstreams on this machine is in today, so the frame is a picture of the product as configured rather than of an edge case. Checks G17-W4, G17-R1. Picture: evidence/g17-document/refusal.nopackage.png. --- RUNG CORRECTED by J3, from `raster-visual`. Its checks are G17-W4 — `reason == "noPackageDirectory"` read off the router's own response — and G17-R1, which reads the state title out of `refusal.nopackage.dump.json` and asserts no `figure` node. The wire read is a real outcome and this case is the only home of it; the drawn half is structural. Neither opens `refusal.nopackage.png`, which stays cited as the frame the dump came from and is claimed as evidence of nothing.

Refusal 2 of 3 — too large. A read me of 600,012 bytes is over the 524,288-byte transport cap for one document; the route refuses `documentTooLarge` naming the file and the limit, and the panel draws 'README.md is too large to show here' with the 512 KB cap in its advice. Note the wire spelling: `documentTooLarge`, not `tooLarge` — the latter is the IMAGE refusal one level in, and a check written against the Swift enum's case name rather than against the wire would have passed on a router that refused nothing. Checks G17-W5, G17-R2. This frame is also DEF-060: it never names the capability it refuses. --- RUNG CORRECTED by J3, from `raster-visual`. Its checks are G17-W5 — `reason`, `file` and `limit` read off the router's own response — and G17-R2, which reads the state title and the `512 KB` string out of `refusal.toolarge.dump.json`. The wire read is a real outcome and this case is its only home; the drawn half is structural. Neither opens `refusal.toolarge.png`, which stays cited as the frame the dump came from.

STRUCTURAL AND PERMANENTLY SO, and the reason is not a missing instrument. Its subject is the correspondence between the capture manifest and the artifacts on disk — a property of the EVIDENCE RECORD rather than of the product, so there is no product state a change could move and no rung on the ladder it could climb to. It is counted against the strict total rather than dropped from it, because a campaign that hid its own record-keeping checks from the denominator would be scoring itself on a smaller suite than it runs. Capture lineage over this flow's own wall of pictures. Each of the five rows in evidence/g17-document/captures.json names the campaign surface and the flow step it is of, carries the sha256 of the file on disk, and — for four of the five — names a string the PANEL draws which the assertion pass then reads back out of that frame's own dump. So a picture is tied to the package it is of independently of its filename. The fifth, refusal.toolarge, cannot do this and is NAMED rather than counted as corroborated: G17-L2 fails if that set is ever anything other than exactly it. DEF-060. Checks G17-L1, G17-L2.

FLOW-006.03. Raised from `structural-visual` on two checks that ask what the old one could not. G17-P6 asked whether a heading carrying the tab's own name is in the dump, which is true of a panel that draws a heading — so this case sat one rung below an effect and its own note said it moved no count. G17-P6W ties the drawn body to the wire: the words of six letters or more that `wire-served.json` carries ONLY in the changelog are COMPUTED from the response rather than written into the check, and all 4 of them are in the panel's own body while none of the 20 unique to the read me is. G17-P6R reads the same step in pixels — 22.7% of the body region's 1,572,864 pixels differ from the read me frame's, against a 1% floor, where a tab that repainted nothing reads 0.0%. Each crop is taken from its own frame's dump at its own scale, so the titlebar and the tab bar cannot supply the difference. Both denominators are checked before the result: a wire response whose three documents shared every word gives both word lists empty, and a clean answer from an empty search is the reading this harness exists against. Rated `metamorphic` rather than `raster-visual` for two reasons — the claim is a RELATION (vary the tab, require the drawn body to track the document the router served) rather than a comparison against a reference image, and these frames come off the hosting view's own backing store rather than off a display server, which is what `raster-visual` names. Checks G17-P6, G17-P6W, G17-P6R. Picture: evidence/g17-document/changelog.served.png.

The flow's whole shape in one relation: one package, three tabs, three different documents. The three frames' drawn text is pairwise distinct and all three titlebars name the same package — so the tab is what changed and the subject is not. Check G17-P8.

The three refusals are pairwise distinguishable in the words the panel actually drew: 'g17-no-package has no package to read' / 'README.md is too large to show here' / 'Not shown — this image points outside the package it came with.' Three distinct strings, each read out of the frame that drew it rather than out of the enum that declares it. Two are whole-panel states and the third is a placeholder inside a document, which is the honest shape: the route has no document-level refusal for a reference escaping the package. Check G17-R3.

J2. Every sidebar row is selected in turn and the effect is read in the RESTORATION STORE, which is a different channel from the one that struck: `ShellModel.selection`'s `didSet` calls `store.save(destination:)`, so a real selection leaves a value in a scratch `UserDefaults` suite that nothing in the test wrote, and that a relaunch reads. `model.selection == .servers` after `model.select(.servers)` was deliberately NOT used — it reads the property the call just wrote, which is the actuation side of the vacuous assertion (`references/inert-ui.md`, `detector-defects.md` §11). Each row is approached from a DIFFERENT destination, because `didSet` guards on `oldValue != selection` and a loop starting where the model boots would have the first row write nothing at all. The destination-collapse relation is asserted as a count rather than as seven separate greens: seven presses, seven DISTINCT persisted values, so a shell whose rows all led to one place fails on the cardinality. A second model built on the same store comes up where the last row left it, which is the read-back a relaunch actually performs. `Settings` is the eighth control and is not a destination: M15 moved it to a scene of its own, so the effect read is the installed opener firing exactly once AND the console's persisted destination not moving. Both halves, because an implementation that opened the scene and also selected a board would pass the first alone. LIMIT, stated rather than left implicit: a persisted destination proves the selection took. It does not prove a different board was DRAWN — SwiftUI's view tree is opaque to a SwiftPM test and `ContentZone`'s switch is unreachable from here. That half is CASE-0001's, on glass, and it is FAILING (DEF-058, DEF-059), so it counts nothing. This is the in-process half and says which half it is.

J2. `Held` and `All` are the two filter chips SURF-004 declares, driven off one loaded reading of the fixture. `Held` is asserted in both directions against `Skill.held?.wantsMore` — every row it draws has an update held, and every row it hid does not — and `All` is asserted as the RESTORATION, which is the assertion that fails if a segment latches. SURF-004 reaches 2 of 21 and the remaining four state-changing controls are recorded in `inventory.json` under `controlsUnactuatable` rather than left in the denominator unexplained: the build draws none of them. That is DEF-062, and it is the finding this case produced — `references/inert-ui.md`'s own stated limit is that no amount of testing the build reveals what the build lacks, and giving the surface a denominator is what made the four visible.

J2. `Remove` is driven with the history checkbox both ways and the effect is read as the operation the client recorded — `remove(keepHistory)` then `remove`. The sheet closing and the selection dropping are the app's own report that it worked and are deliberately not the observable: `references/inert-ui.md` §3 is exactly a handler that changes a banner and does nothing else.

N8. The inertness guard on the untrusted-input boundary, made capable of failing. M19 shipped `MarkdownSecurityTests.htmlIsInert` with four spellings that named `javascript:`, no scheme, or nothing, and two assertions -- no link, no `imageURL` -- that `MarkdownInline.sanitized` makes true of every input it touches. It could not go red. M30 wired `ControlAPICapabilityDocumentSource` into the shipped UI, so router-served third-party text now reaches this renderer in a Release build, and the guard on it measured nothing. MEASURED, not assumed: the platform parser does keep inline HTML inert -- under `MarkdownInline`'s own options it hands each tag back as characters and marks it `.inlineHTML`, an intent naming no destination, and it does so under all four combinations of `allowsExtendedAttributes` and `interpretedSyntax`. Swift 6.2, macOS 26.6.2 (25G83), Debug, `swift test`. So this was an evidence defect and not a live vulnerability, and the fix is the assertion rather than new sanitisation. Two `https` spellings were added, because `https` is the one scheme the allowlist keeps and therefore the only one that can carry an interpreted `<a>` through to the assertion; a presence control runs the same reader over the markdown twin of the same destination first; and two clauses were added that the old body did not have -- handed back verbatim, and no attribute beyond the `.inlineHTML` marker. That last clause also corrects the test's own claim: the parser DOES attach one attribute to inline HTML and `sanitized` carries it, so the old name -- `inline HTML acquires no attribute of any kind` -- was false as written as well as unfailable, which is why nobody found out.

cell.dataShape: a package publishing all three documents and one figure

subject.note: A served document returns its content, and the response carries NO filesystem path. Eleven assertions: 200; the read me carries the fixture's sentinel; changelog and capabilities both present; exactly one image travelled; its reference is the string the document spelled (`docs/figure.png`) rather than a resolved path; media `image/png`; the base64 decodes to the file's own bytes; nothing refused; the package root appears NOWHERE in the raw body; and no absolute path of any shape (/private/tmp, /Users, /tmp) appears in it either. The last two are M30's own assertion moved onto the wire — the app may not open a file, so a payload carrying a path is a payload that invites one. Run against BOTH implementations over a real socket: `dist/index.js serve` and the shipped `app/.build/debug/MCPRouterCLI serve`, each on 127.0.0.1:8981 with a scratch MCP_ROUTER_HOME. M30 already proves this route in process — `ControlDocumentRouteTests.swift` calls the handler and asserts on the string it returns — which is a different claim from this one: this lets the kernel carry the bytes and reads what a client actually receives, which is what the campaign asks of every other route on this lane. Observing only the TypeScript half would leave the SHIPPED router unobserved, so both are run and both pass. The server is CONSTRUCTED and labelled so: 0 of the 21 upstreams on this machine declares a package directory, so this route 404s noPackageDirectory for all of them and no real package here reaches this outcome.

subject.note: Nothing served — the three ways this route has nothing to give, each reachable and each NAMING ITS OWN RULE rather than a shared 404. `noPackageDirectory` (the server declares no cwd), `packageUnreadable` (it declares one that is not on disk) and `noDocuments` (the directory is there and publishes no README.md, CHANGELOG.md or CAPABILITIES.md). Nine assertions, three per refusal: the status is 404, the `reason` is the specific rule, and a human sentence rides along. The app maps each reason to different copy, so a shared code is a refusal the reader cannot act on. Run against BOTH implementations over a real socket: `dist/index.js serve` and the shipped `app/.build/debug/MCPRouterCLI serve`, each on 127.0.0.1:8981 with a scratch MCP_ROUTER_HOME. Too large, and it names WHICH cap it hit. A README.md of 524,289 bytes — the 512 KiB documentBytes cap plus one — returns 413 with `cap: documentBytes`, `limit: 524288`, `actual: 524289` and `file: README.md`. Seven assertions. There are three caps on this route that can produce a size refusal, so 'too large' without a cap name tells a reader nothing they can act on. The fixture is built one byte over the boundary rather than comfortably over it, and the runner REFUSES TO START (exit 2) if the caps declared in src/document.ts have drifted from the three the fixture is sized for — a fixture sized past a cap that has since moved is a fixture that passes by never reaching the boundary at all. subject.note: A reference attempting to ESCAPE THE PACKAGE is refused rather than served. Fifteen assertions over one response. The strongest of them is not a reason code: the fixture plants a secret file outside the package, and the case asserts that the secret's path appears NOWHERE in the raw body — if anything escaped, the bytes are in the response and no status code hides that. Then exactly one image travelled and it is the one inside the package (`docs/inside.png`), and nine references are refused with the reason each earns and no more than nine: `../outside/secret.png`, `../pkg-escape-evil/secret.png` (a SIBLING package whose path is a string prefix of this one), `link-out.png` (a real symlink out), `linkdir/secret.png` (a symlinked DIRECTORY), `../../../../etc/passwd` -> escapesPackage; `/etc/hosts.png` and `~/secret.png` -> absolutePath; `https://example.invalid/secret.png` -> remote; `%2e%2e/outside/secret.png` -> notInPackage. M30 armed this check with three planted divergences and a fresh-context verifier attacked it with 23 adversarial references for zero escapes. That evidence is real and it lives in M30's record, where it was proved ONCE. This case exists so the property is checked on a schedule instead. Run against BOTH implementations over a real socket: `dist/index.js serve` and the shipped `app/.build/debug/MCPRouterCLI serve`, each on 127.0.0.1:8981 with a scratch MCP_ROUTER_HOME. subject.note: An oversized image is refused ON ITS OWN TERMS and does NOT spend the shared budget. Ten assertions. The document names `oversize.png` (over the 2 MiB imageBytes cap) first, then a.png..d.png at exactly 2 MiB each — which together spend the 8 MiB imageBudgetBytes exactly — then tail.png. The discriminator is d.png: it travels only if the oversized figure spent nothing, because had it spent its own 2 MiB + 1 the budget would be gone before d.png was reached and d.png would come back budgetExhausted. tail.png is budgetExhausted either way and so proves nothing on its own, which is why the case does not rest on it. Also asserted: oversize.png is refused `tooLarge` naming the 2,097,152-byte per-image limit rather than `budgetExhausted`, and the budget was spent to exactly 8,388,608 bytes. Run against BOTH implementations over a real socket: `dist/index.js serve` and the shipped `app/.build/debug/MCPRouterCLI serve`, each on 127.0.0.1:8981 with a scratch MCP_ROUTER_HOME. subject.text: Measured by G17 on 2026-08-27. `CapabilityDocumentSheet`'s titlebar draws the capability's name from the DOCUMENT, so on any `unavailable` state it falls back to the generic word 'Documentation'. Three of the panel's refusals still identify themselves — `noPackageDirectory`, `packageUnreadable` and `notFound` all interpolate the capability into their headline — but `tooLarge`'s headline is '<file> is too large to show here', which names README.md and the 512 KB cap and never the server. So a photograph of that state is tied to the capability it refuses by its manifest row alone, which is the exact dependency the campaign's capture-lineage rule exists to remove. subject.note: The effect class is the socket, because that is the class this campaign's closed vocabulary can carry. The route's other effect is a filesystem READ inside the package, and EFFECT_CLASSES has no read class — filesystem-write is the only filesystem member and this route writes nothing. That effect is therefore proved at the outcome rung by CASE-0178 (the bytes on the wire are the file's own bytes) rather than by a witness, and the gap is recorded here rather than papered over by declaring a class the route does not perform.
subject.text: GET /servers/:name/document serves a package's own read me, changelog and capability list as bytes and never as a filesystem path, and every refusal names the rule it hit rather than a shared code: noPackageDirectory when the server declares no directory, packageUnreadable when the directory is not there, noDocuments when it publishes none of the three, documentTooLarge with the cap name, limit and actual size at 512 KiB, escapesPackage / absolutePath / remote for a reference that leaves the package, and budgetExhausted once the 8 MiB shared image budget is spent — an image over the 2 MiB per-image cap being refused on its own terms without spending that shared budget.

DETECTOR DEFECT in test-campaign, measured 2026-08-27 (G29) against the vendored 0.9.2 and the machine's 0.15.0, which carry a byte-identical `tie()`. SURF-028's route is `app://mac/servers/{server}/document` -- a family of addresses, one per server. `bin/g17-document-flow.sh` rendered its frames against three of them and recorded each target honestly. `tie()` normalises scheme, host, port, query and fragment away and then asks for string equality or a suffix match, so `mac/servers/g17-capability/document` against `mac/servers/{server}/document` fails all three tests and the gate reports UNTIED -- 'the recorded target does not resolve to the subject's route'. Nothing was pointed at the wrong thing. `references/capture-lineage.md` says resolution is 'deliberately loose on the parts a harness legitimately varies'; a `{server}` segment is exactly such a part, and it is the one case the looseness does not cover. THE FIX BELONGS UPSTREAM, and is not applied here. `vendor/README.md` pins the tree by checksum so the gates can be re-run from a clone, and a `tie()` that behaves one way in this repository and another way everywhere else stops being evidence -- the same reasoning that keeps X7 and X8 open. Referred out of family (gpt-5.6-sol, high effort, 2026-08-27) and it reached the same conclusion independently: patch upstream, cut a release, re-vendor and re-pin, rather than forking the pinned copy. The patch is one function: treat a route segment of the form `{name}`, `:name` or `*` as matching exactly one non-empty target segment, leaving literal segments, the source-file refusal and the normalisation untouched, and leaving the seeded swap red. WHAT THIS REPOSITORY DID INSTEAD, and why it is not a workaround. The three served frames are published by the FLOW-006 steps that rendered them, each carrying the concrete route its own capture recorded, and SURF-028 publishes none. That is the registry becoming more accurate rather than less: the surface is a template and has no single portrait, while a step is that surface at one address and can name it. Every frame is now filed at the address the channel was pointed at. The detector limit is unchanged and is what this row records.

The document response crossing a real kernel socket, seen by a party that is not the router. The six cases above read status codes and bodies back through urllib, which proves the route answered but takes the router's own word for how the bytes travelled; this takes the kernel's. `bin/witness-document-socket.sh` starts the SHIPPED router against a scratch home, then holds a socket open with a real `GET /servers/constructed-served/document` written into it while lsof(8) samples the socket table. Before: 1 LISTEN row on 8983 owned by the pid the shell launched, 0 on the decoy. During: 4 ESTABLISHED rows, 1 of them owned by the router pid — the ACCEPTED half, which is the half that proves the process took the connection rather than merely reserving the port; 0 on the decoy. The 589 bytes read straight off that socket begin `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` and contain the fixture's read me sentinel, so the connection lsof saw is the one that carried this route's document. After the process is killed: 0 LISTEN rows. The server is CONSTRUCTED and labelled so: 0 of the 21 upstreams on this machine declares a package directory, so this route 404s noPackageDirectory for all of them and no real package here reaches this outcome.

subject.note: Each of the shell's three top-level unhandled-exception handlers made to fire on purpose, and the line it wrote read back out of shell-startup.log by a process that did not write it, after the process that did had exited. THIS CASE EXISTS BECAUSE REGISTRATION IS NOT FIRING. DEF-079 was raised on sixteen launches that wrote no `unhandled:` line including eight that terminated at 0xC000027B, and it stayed open through the fix - two more handlers registered - because none of the three had been observed catching anything. App.xaml.cs takes `--fault <ui|appdomain|task|dispatcher>`, compiled out outside DEBUG and inert unless passed; win-shell-unhandled-witness.ps1 launches the shell once per kind. FOUR ARMS. BASELINE is a launch with NO --fault and requires its region of the log to hold `launched` and no `unhandled:` line, which is what makes the three EFFECT lines the injection's rather than startup's; and every arm reads only the bytes appended after its own launch, so a line an earlier run left behind cannot satisfy one. The three EFFECT arms then require, each after its own fault, `unhandled: [xaml]` for a throw on the UI thread inside XAML's dispatch of OnLaunched, `unhandled: [appdomain terminating=True]` for a throw on a non-UI foreground thread, and `unhandled: [unobserved-task]` for a faulted task nobody awaits after a collection and WaitForPendingFinalizers. All four held. WHAT THIS CASE DOES NOT SETTLE, and what has since moved. The DispatcherQueue route ran here as an UNGRADED probe while DEF-085 was open. DEF-085 is fixed, the probe is a graded fifth arm of the same script, and it is carried by CASE-0386 rather than by this case: what this one grades is still the three top-level handlers, and folding a guard this repository owns into a case about framework handlers would make one verdict answer two questions. Whether any of these three would have caught the 0xC000027B Skills crash was unmeasured when this case was written; it is measured now, and the answer is no - CASE-0387 and DEF-086 carry it. And the injection is compiled out outside DEBUG, so this grades the Debug binary only. The shell's own `handlers:` line saying which handlers it attached is carried in runs[] as writerSelfReport and is graded by nothing. ACTUATES VOCABULARY, corrected at merge: `actuates` is read by planning/test-campaign/bin/control-census.py as a control the surface DECLARES, which is what gives the actuation census its denominator. This case originally listed the command the lane ran instead - App.UnhandledException, AppDomain.CurrentDomain.UnhandledException and TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException (handlers, not controls, and this case names no surface) - and that is DEF-080, two meanings sharing one field. The command is here in the note where it can be read; the field now carries nothing, because the case drives no declared control.

THIS IS THE ROW THAT SEPARATES A BOUND CONTROL FROM AN INERT ONE. It toggles the switch through TogglePattern and then reads a DIFFERENT element - the board's state readout, which the view renders from the model - so a switch that moved and wrote through to nothing would leave that line unchanged and fail here. It went red for real on the first run, against a readout carrying a static AutomationProperties.Name that overrode its own text. WHAT THIS ROW DOES NOT SETTLE: anything outside the shell process. It is a read of the application's own accessibility tree, so a control that moved a model and reached no file and no scheduler passes it. The rows carrying a `recorder` are the ones that leave the process. THE CALL THIS LANE MADE, which is what `actuates` is NOT for: the row was driven through System.Windows.Automation's TogglePattern.Toggle() from shell-lane.ps1. `actuates` carries the control the surface declares - DEF-080.
