subject.text: The on-glass hierarchy reads `identifier: 'sparkles', label: 'Discover'` for the Discover tab. X2 set the label so VoiceOver announces the tab's name; the identifier still ships the SF Symbol's name, so any query written against identifiers addresses the icon rather than the destination — and three of the five icons are named for a word that appears nowhere in the interface (`inbox`, `tray`, `book`). MEASURED 20 Aug 2026 AND LEFT OPEN, because the obvious fix does not work. `.accessibilityIdentifier("tab-<raw>")` was applied in both places SwiftUI offers — inside the `.tabItem` closure on the `Label`, and on the view that carries `.tabItem` — and each was run on glass. Both CLEAR the tab button's identifier rather than set it: `app.tabBars.buttons` came back `["", "", "", "", ""]` on both attempts, against an expectation of `tab-discover, tab-triage, tab-queue, tab-library, tab-settings`. That is the same class of surprise as `.accessibilityHidden(true)` on the icon, which PhoneShell.swift already records as measured inert. Both attempts were reverted rather than shipped: an empty identifier is arguably less misleading than a wrong one, but it is a change with no passing assertion behind it, and this campaign does not ship those. The finding is recorded in `PhoneShell.swift` beside the label, so the next person does not spend the two glass runs again. Until a third route is found, query this tab bar by label — which is correct, and which is what `PhoneGlassTests.selectTab` already does.
subject.title: iOS tab buttons carry the icon name as their accessibility identifier, and it cannot be replaced

subject.detail: Three consecutive runs, same build, same booted iPhone 16 Pro, no product change between them: run 1 failed 3 of 5, runs 2 and 3 failed 4 of 5. The case that moved is `tapping 'X' did not produce a navigation bar titled 'X'` — green for all five tabs in run 1, red on the first tab in runs 2 and 3. The only edit between run 1 and run 2 was adding XCTAttachment captures to a different test, so the code under assertion did not change. A plausible mechanism is DEF-008: the tab button's accessibility identifier is the SF Symbol name while its label is the tab title, so `buttons["Discover"]` resolves on one attribute or the other depending on which the tree publishes first. Not diagnosed further here — this campaign records the instrument's reliability rather than repairing another branch's test. Consequence: the lane's outcome-rung claims are recorded inconclusive, because green twice is the campaign's own bar and this lane did not clear it. CLOSED 20 Aug 2026. Diagnosed from run 3's exported App UI hierarchy: at the failure the navigation bar's identifier was 'Settings' and the Settings tab carried Selected, so the opening tap had never landed. Run 1 passed because a freshly installed app launches on Discover, making its first selectTab a no-op; runs 2 and 3 restored to Settings and tapped a tab bar that existed but was not yet hittable. Existence is not hittability. `selectTab` now waits on a `hittable == true` predicate and retries the tap up to three times against the tab button's own `isSelected`, which is the tab bar's answer to 'which tab am I on'. Green twice since, across all three affected tests. DEF-008 was not the mechanism.
subject.title: the ios-glass lane's tab-navigation assertion does not reproduce

subject.detail: Two faults in the same step, both found by running the lane red. First, `set -e` killed the recipe at the failing xcodebuild, so the export never ran — the run whose pictures are worth most produced none, and diagnosing a failure meant re-running by hand against a bundle path scraped out of the log. The target now holds the status while the export completes and exits with it afterwards. Second, once the export did run, name-glass-attachments.py treated XCTest's own diagnostics as evidence: a red run attaches a Debug description per failed query, two of those were byte-identical because they describe the same query twice, and its shared-image check stopped the run half-renamed. The check is right and its population was wrong. PhoneGlassTests now prefixes every attachment it takes with GLASS-CAPTURE:, so the split is declared by the producer rather than inferred from filename shape, diagnostics are kept under diagnostics/, and nothing is renamed until every check has passed.
subject.title: a red glass run exported no captures, and the naming script policed the wrong population

subject.detail: `vacuity-check.py`'s blind pass reports `examined=1820 mutating=3 re-read-after=0 blind=3` over this test tree. All three read after the mutation: `restartIsIssuedBeforeTheStagingWrite` reads `WatchWorld.serverNames`, the log, `kicks.issued` and `WatchState.load`; `restartIsOwedBeforeTheWriteLands` reads `WatchState.load` inside the lock and `WatchWorld.serverNames` on both sides of the rename; `restartRechecksTheCamera` reads `model.entry.characters`. The heuristic looks for a read AFTER the last occurrence of a mutating verb, and in this product the verb `restart` is also the name of the thing being observed — `restartPending`, `restarted scratch-label` — so the last `restart` in the file sits inside the final assertion and nothing is textually after it. Recorded rather than acted on: the tests are correct as written, and rewording an assertion to satisfy a text heuristic would make the suite worse. The pass is still worth running; 3 of 1820 is a reviewable rate, and it is the check that would have caught 26 of 32 on the campaign it was built from. CAUSE CORRECTED 21 Aug 2026; the diagnosis recorded above was wrong. It said the mutator's name is the observable's name (`restart` inside `restartPending`). Measured against 0.9.2's actual patterns, that cannot happen: the mutator scan at vacuity-check.py:180 requires `(?<![A-Za-z0-9_])` + verb + `\w*\s*\(`, so `state.restartPending == false` never matches for want of the call parenthesis. The real cause is that the seven default readers are all snake_case -- list_, get_, read_, fetch_, sample_, count_, load_ -- and the nine default mutators mostly are too (stop_all, stop_runner, clear_, cancel_). This is a camelCase Swift codebase, so NEITHER side could fire. The pass examined 1657 test bodies and found 3 mutating, 0 re-reading and 3 blind: `blind=3` reads as almost nothing wrong, and meant almost nothing looked at. The denominator was printed and nobody read 3-of-1657 as the alarm it was. Fixed by declaring the project's own vocabulary, which 0.9.2 added for exactly this: campaign.json now carries `blindVocabulary` with 14 camelCase mutators and 13 readers, and the pass reports examined=1657 mutating=320 re-read-after=232 blind=88, with the vocabulary it used printed above the findings. Two of the three original findings resolved on their real reads (`WatchState.load(`, `WatchWorld.read(`). The third, restartRechecksTheCamera, stays flagged and correctly so for a verb heuristic: its only reads are property comparisons -- `model.step`, `model.entry.characters` -- which carry no verb at all. That is the ceiling of this instrument rather than a defect in the test, and it is why the 88 is a worklist and not a verdict: the vocabulary is hand-declared and unvalidated. Of the 21 findings the tool prints, 15 carry a @Test attribute and 5 are fixture helpers in dedicated client files that 0.9.2's per-file helper heuristic does not exclude, because it keys on a function being called more than once in its OWN file and these are called from their importers.
subject.title: the blind-test pass flags three tests that do read after mutating, because the mutator's name is the observable's name

subject.detail: STILL PRESENT in 0.9.2, re-measured 21 Aug 2026 and the gap widened by one. witness-worklist.py reports `pairs=20 judgeable=17 WITHOUT a reference=3` and a comparable fraction of 85%, while capture-lineage.py --gate on the same registry reports `published captures: 16` and `JUDGED 16 of 16 judgeable (100%)`. Two gates in one skill version disagree about the judgeable denominator, 17 against 16, and neither names the other's population. CAUSE PINNED 21 Aug 2026. The disagreeing member is SURF-009, the Mac menu-bar popover, and it is the only one: witness-worklist's judgeable set and capture-lineage's judged set are identical apart from it. SURF-009 has a rendered design of record on disk (evidence/shots/mock/SURF-009.png), which is the sole condition witness-worklist tests, so it counts as the 17th judgeable pair. It has NO build capture at all — the popover cannot be opened without activating MCPRouter, which this campaign never does — so it never enters capture-lineage's population, which is built from published captures. capture-lineage therefore reports 'JUDGED 16 of 16 judgeable (100%)' on a registry holding 17 judgeable surfaces. That is the defect's whole shape, and it is the campaign's own first failure mode occurring INSIDE a gate written to prevent it: a denominator built from what was captured rather than from what was enumerated reads 100% precisely when a surface was never photographed. The direction is the dangerous one — an uncaptured surface raises the percentage instead of lowering it. Nothing is concealed in this campaign's own record: SURF-009 carries a shotNote naming the constraint, its three cases (CASE-0004, CASE-0006, CASE-0109) are n/a with the reason, and evidence/shots/pairs.json carries shot:null. The defect is that a reader of the gate line alone would not know to look for any of it. Remains open-detector: the fix is in the skill's scripts, which are not edited from this repo.
subject.note: DETECTOR DEFECT, recorded so its number is not published as a product finding. `witness-worklist.py:90` is `judgeable = [p for p in pairs if p.get("reference")]` -- it tests the reference half and never the shot half. SURF-009 (Mac menu-bar popover) has `shot: null` and an explicit `reason: build half uncaptured` in pairs.json, and is still counted, so the script reported `pairs=20 judgeable=17 comparable fraction: 85%` where the honest figure is 16 of 20, 80%. The script already defends the mirror-image failure and its own comment says why: a campaign reported 20 judgeable pairs whose references were all unrendered .html paths, and it now demotes those to unjudgeable with a named reason. The shot side has no equivalent test. Consequence here is one point of over-report and no false verdict, because capture-lineage.py computes judgeable from captures that exist and reported JUDGED 16 of 16 -- the two gates disagree by exactly this surface, and the disagreement is what found it. A campaign relying on the worklist alone would carry an uncompared surface inside a comparable fraction. Filed against the skill's script rather than this repo, so it is not fixed here.
subject.text: witness-worklist.py counts a pair as judgeable on the reference alone, so a surface with no build capture inflates the comparable fraction.

subject.detail: Measured 2026-08-21, test-campaign 0.9.2. `ledger.md`'s header line reads `80 cases` and `73 pass · 3 fail · 0 skip · 4 n/a`; its table carries 72 rows. The eight absent cases are CASE-0145, 0146, 0147, 0148 (lane router-daemon) and CASE-0151, 0152, 0153, 0154 (lane swiftui). All eight pass. MECHANISM, exact. The writer at campaign.py:1218-1241 buckets every case with `by_surface.setdefault(c.get('surface', '—'), [])`, so a case whose `surface` is absent lands under the literal key `'—'`. It then emits rows with `for s in inventory['surface']: for c in by_surface.get(s['id'], [])`. `'—'` is not a surface id, so that bucket is never visited and its contents are never printed. Nothing warns; the count in the header comes from a different code path than the rows beneath it, which is why the two disagree without either being flagged. WHAT IS LOST. CASE-0145 through CASE-0148 are this campaign's four `effect-witness` cases — the rung that required building a recorder outside the product, and the most expensive evidence in the run. They are absent from the ledger entirely. A reader of ledger.md cannot learn that the campaign has an effect-witness rung at all. DIRECTION. The eight dropped are all passes, so the table under-states the work rather than over-stating it. That makes it the safer direction, and it does not make it safe: a reader counting 72 rows against a stated 80 meets an unexplained gap of exactly the kind this campaign is written to make impossible, and the campaign's own rule is that every sweep prints its denominator. SCOPE. Ledger-specific. evidence.html renders all eight (5 to 11 references each, measured by grep), so the HTML page is correct and only the markdown artifact is affected. Distinct from DEF-052, which is about the defect registry being absent from BOTH artifacts; this one is about cases, in one artifact, via a different mechanism. NOT FIXED FROM HERE: campaign.py lives in the installed skill cache, not this repo.
subject.title: campaign.py's ledger writer prints only cases filed under a surface, silently dropping 8 of 80 — including all four effect-witness cases

subject.text: Measured by J2 on 2026-08-29, by trying to actuate SURF-004's declared controls and finding four with nothing to press. The design of record's capability-delta sheet offers a two-way decision — `Promote 2.3.0` and `Keep 2.2.0`, recorded as `Promote the held update` and `Keep the installed version` in `evidence/design-controls.json` under state `sheet:capability-delta`. `app/Sources/MCPRouterUI/Boards/SkillSheets.swift` declares three buttons and all three are `Button("Done") { board.sheet = nil }`, so the sheet a user opens to decide about a held update can only be dismissed. `SkillsBoardModel` carries no write at all: no promote, no keep, no never-run. Two further declared controls have no counterpart either — `Never run` is a filter chip the design draws and `SkillPresentation.Filter` (`all | held | local | needsAttention`) has no case for, and `Reveal repo in Finder` appears nowhere under `app/Sources/`. This is the third shape in `references/inert-ui.md` seen from the other side: not a control whose handler does nothing, but a promised control the build never drew, which no amount of testing the build reveals. It surfaced only because the census gave the surface a denominator and J2 tried to fill it — SURF-004 reaches 2 of 21 actuated and the four are recorded in `inventory.json` under `controlsUnactuatable` rather than quietly dropped.

subject.text: Measured by K3 on 2026-08-29 while trying to fill SURF-026's denominator, and it is the SkillSheets shape (DEF-062) a second time: a button drawn with an empty closure. `Button(InsightsBoardCopy.analyseNow) {}` is the whole of the analyst's action. It is `.disabled(true)` with `analyseUnavailable` as its help and its accessibility hint, which is `DESIGN.md` §3.4's dim-with-a-reason rather than an inert control — the refusal is the product's, not the campaign's — and the reason is that `PRD.md` §6 specifies a session analyst and nothing under `app/Sources` implements one. Three further declared readouts — `Analyst cadence`, `Analyst model`, `Second-opinion model` — have no counterpart at all: the build draws the panel's empty state where the design draws its configuration. The fifth declared control on that panel, `Insights window`, is NOT part of this defect and is recorded separately as a refusal: the window is fixed at 24 hours because the call log rotates and what a router can answer for is whatever survived, so a control offering seven days on a machine holding two would lie about its own range. That reasoning is already in the board's own header comment, which is why it is a stated reason rather than a finding. Recorded rather than trimmed, so five of SURF-026's seven declared controls sit in the denominator with a sentence each.

subject.detail: `TypedEntryView` rendered eight styled boxes, a helper line and a submit button, and no input affordance of any kind — no TextField, no keypad, no focus state. `PairingCodeEntry` had carried `append(contentsOf:)` and `deleteBackward()` since it was written and nothing in the UI called either, so `.disabled(!entry.isComplete)` on the submit button could never become false. The typed path is the documented fallback for every camera state — the source cites A16 — and for `.restricted`, where iOS Settings is a dead end the user may not be able to clear, it is the *primary* recovery. So the one surface a user reaches by deliberately choosing it was the one that could not be completed. Fixed with a real `TextField` behind the boxes: it carries the system keyboard, hardware keys on iPad, paste and dictation, and it is what `app.textFields` resolves to on glass. Deliberately NOT `.textContentType(.oneTimeCode)` — that AutoFill reads codes out of Messages and Mail, and this code is read off the Mac's own screen, so it would offer suggestions that are always wrong. The boxes became decoration (`accessibilityHidden`) and the field is the single element labelled 'Pairing code', because `children: .ignore` on a display is right and on an editor strips the trait VoiceOver and XCUITest need. Approach checked against an out-of-family lane (grok-4.6, xhigh) before implementing; it named the same shape and the same reason for avoiding `.oneTimeCode`. Guarded by `PhoneSurfaceTests.testTypedEntryPublishesAFieldToTypeInto`, armed 20 Aug 2026.

subject.detail: **The recorded cause was wrong, and this replaces it.** It said the shutter fired during a board transition and named the fix as a settle in `capture-mac-glass.sh`. Measured 20 Aug 2026 from the accessibility dumps the same script already writes, one per board, beside the pictures: | board | window | AXSplitGroup | clipped | |---|---|---|---| | Servers, Activity, Cleanup, Inbox, Settings | 980pt | 980pt | — | | Checks | 980pt | 988pt | 8pt | | Skills | 980pt | 1044pt | 64pt | | Discover | 980pt | 1119pt | 139pt | Every window in the run is the same 980x620 and every capture is the same 2096x1376, so no capture rect is wrong and no shutter is early. What differs is the shell **inside** the window: on three boards `NavigationSplitView` lays out wider than the window and centres the excess — the split group's origin moves left by exactly half the overflow in all three cases (180→148 for 64pt, 180→110.5 for 139pt, 180→176 for 8pt), which is what makes the clipping symmetrical. That is why the sidebar's section headers read `unning` and `brary` while the nav rows beside them are whole: the headers sit at a smaller leading inset and fall off first, and the header's trailing controls — `Manage marketplaces.`, `Review 2.3.0…` — fall off the right by the same amount. So this is a product defect on three boards rather than a lane defect on two captures, and it is worse than recorded: Checks overflows too, by 8pt, which is small enough that nobody reading the picture saw it. The app declares no minimum window width anywhere, so nothing stops a user reaching this state — the campaign's 980pt window is an ordinary size, not a stress case. The consequence that made it a defect stands unchanged and is now better founded: a clipped capture is admissible for what it shows and silent about what it cut, so a reader cannot tell an absent control from a cropped one. Both witness verdicts that depend on these captures say in their method field that the right-hand controls were read from the accessibility dump instead. `capture-mac-glass.sh` now prints `board width: examined=14 overflowing=3` every run, with a line naming each board and its excess. Reported rather than enforced, because three boards overflow today and a known red in `make all` either blocks unrelated work or gets its assertion softened. NOT FIXED, and the fix is a decision rather than a repair. Either the shell declares a minimum window width at least as wide as its widest board — one line, guarantees nothing ever clips, and costs users on small screens a window they cannot shrink — or the three boards compress, which keeps small screens usable and is per-board column work across all three. Discover at 1119pt is the one that decides how much that costs. PARTLY CLOSED 20 Aug 2026, on `ai/x4`, and the part that is not closed is named rather than left to look finished. The mechanism turned out to be a chain rather than a board: each row's fixed columns report a hard minimum width, the detail pane sums them, `NavigationSplitView` reports that as its own minimum, and nothing ever reads it back — this app opts into no minimum window size and `windowResizability` defaults to `.automatic` — so the window proposes 980pt and SwiftUI **places** the oversized child with default centre alignment. The symmetry was the tell. Referred to the xAI lane (grok-4.6, xhigh) with the measured table; it named the propagation as the bug, called both listed fixes second-best, and its Q3 answer — placement plus `.automatic` resizability rather than any documented split-view overflow mode — is what the one-line fix then confirmed. FIXED: `ContentZone` carries `.frame(minWidth: 0, maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)`. Measured on the rebuilt app through the same accessibility channel: all eight boards read `split=980` inside a `window=980`, overflowing 0 of 8, where the same probe on the previous build read 3 of 8. The sidebar is whole again — `Running`, `Library` and the footer readout all render in full where they were `unning` and `brary`. The leading alignment is the deliberate half: it decides who loses when the content still does not fit, and the answer is never the navigation. STILL OPEN: the boards' content is still wider than the detail pane on those three, so the trailing chrome is cut at the pane's right edge — Discover's search field reads `Search the regis` and a body sentence loses its last word. That is one-edge clipping where it was two, and it is the conventional behaviour of a too-narrow window rather than a split view eating its own sidebar, but it is still content going missing without saying so. Closing it needs the three boards' columns to flex, which is a design decision about what Discover looks like compressed and is the owner's rather than mine. GUARDED two ways, and the two see different things. `capture-mac-glass.sh` now **fails** on any board whose split group exceeds its window, and refuses to pass on `examined=0`; all three arms were exercised on 20 Aug 2026 — red at 3 of 14, green at 0 of 14, and exit 1 with no dumps at all. `ShellDetailWidthTests` asserts the modifier in `ShellWindow`'s detail column so a revert is red in `make test` rather than on the next glass run. That test's own first version was a detector defect found by arming: it searched the raw source slice, and the modifier it looks for is named in the doc comment three lines above it, so deleting the modifier left the assertion green. Comments are stripped before matching now, and both halves were re-armed separately. CLOSED 20 Aug 2026, and the second half corrected the first half's diagnosis of *which* content was too wide. The brief written from the split-group numbers said three boards' table columns needed to flex. A pane-level probe — every leaf's right edge against the window's, read from the same dumps — says otherwise, and it says so only after the probe itself was fixed: the first version read the frame's **y** where it meant **x** and reported clipping on seven of eight boards, which the pixels flatly denied. The Settings capture is whole, and looking at it is what caught the field offset. A frame's last five fields are x, y, w, h and a flag; the split-group gate only ever compared widths, which is why it was right while the leaf probe was wrong. Corrected, the drivers are: - **Discover**: content wants 823pt against a 684pt pane. Not the table — cutting `nameColumn` from 216pt to 96pt moved the number by **zero**. It is the controls row: a `.fixedSize()` segmented picker measuring 567pt beside a search field pinned at 240pt. - **Skills**: 748pt against 684pt, same shape — a 516pt fixed picker and a 216pt pinned field. - **Checks**: not a content defect at all. Its real content ends at 1152pt inside a 1160pt pane; the only thing past the edge is `KeyClaimProbe`, the `#if DEBUG` test surface A21 names, overhanging by 4pt. It is absent from any build a user runs, and it is what the whole 8pt split-group excess on this board was. FIXED by giving each board a `searchMinWidth` of four units and declaring the field `minWidth:idealWidth:maxWidth:` rather than `width:`. The picker cannot give a point back — that is what `.fixedSize()` means, and it is right, because a segmented control has nowhere to put a truncated label — so the field is the only control in the row that can. It renders at its full width wherever there is room and shows about eight characters at the narrowest window this app is used at, which is less than anyone wants and more than nothing: it still takes focus, accepts a query and submits. Measured after: every board reads `split=980` in a `window=980`, and the only leaf past the pane edge on any of the eight is a 1pt scrollbar — plus the Debug key probe's 4pt on Checks. Before, Discover's rows and footnote sat at 1283pt against an edge of 1160. GUARDED by a second test in `ShellDetailWidthTests`, armed 20 Aug 2026: restoring `.frame(width: DiscoverBoardMetrics.searchWidth)` reddens all three of its assertions. It names the two boards rather than looping over every file, because those are the two the measurement covers — a third board growing this problem is a new measurement, not a case this test silently already made.

subject.detail: DETECTOR DEFECT in test-campaign 0.9.2, found 21 Aug 2026. attach-shots.py iterates every image under evidence/shots and assigns `hit['shot'] = rel` on each match, last write wins, with no preference for a build capture over a design render. This campaign keeps six directories under evidence/shots (16 root, 8 design-size, 16 fidelity, 9 ios, 17 mock, 11 mock-hidpi), so for SURF-001 the candidates in iteration order are SURF-001.build.png, SURF-001.shell.png, mock/SURF-001.png, mock-hidpi/SURF-001.full.png -- and the last one wins. MEASURED for SURF-001, SURF-002 and SURF-006: `--apply` would repoint each surface's `shot` from its build capture to `evidence/shots/mock-hidpi/SURF-00N.full.png`, which is the render of the DESIGN, not the build. That is the skill's own headline failure mode -- publishing a picture of one thing under the name of another -- arriving in a sibling of the plane built to prevent it, and it would do so while every other gate stayed green, because capture-lineage.py gates the 16 captures cited by CASES and the surface wall is a different population. The report compounds it: the UNCORROBORATED block prints surface ids (SURF-001 ... SURF-011) rather than the file each verdict is about, so a reader sees eleven surfaces apparently lacking provenance when in fact each surface's ACTUAL `shot` field points at a corroborated build capture and the complaint is about a mock render nobody intended to attach. Distinguishing the two costs a re-derivation of the matcher by hand. Recorded rather than patched, precedent DEF-048, DEF-051, DEF-052 and DEF-053. The campaign's standing refusal to run `--apply` here predates this and was based on the DEF-006 mis-wire; it now has a measured mechanism behind it. Separately closed while investigating: this campaign's design-size captures carried their provenance in a second manifest, evidence/shots/design-size/captures.json, in a different schema ({captures:[...]} against the root's bare list) that no gate reads. Its 8 entries were merged into the root manifest with `target` derived from the root's declared target for the same subject and corroborated by each capture's own windowTitleReadback -- Servers, Activity, Skills, Discover, Inbox, Checks, Cleanup, Settings, every one matching -- recorded at capture time, and each carries `targetDerivedFrom` saying so. That was the campaign's own inconsistency and is fixed here; it was not the cause of the 11. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-27 (G21) after `evidence/shots/captures.json` was made a derived file. The uncorroborated count is 12 and stays 12: SURF-001..011 and SURF-022. Eleven of them are this defect -- `mock-hidpi/` sorts last, so it is the row that decides each surface's `shotProvenance`. The mock rows in the manifest deliberately carry NO `target`; the address the channel was pointed at is recorded in full as `renderedFrom`, with an `attachHazard` field naming this defect. Measured both ways on this tree: writing that address as `target` instead drops the uncorroborated count from 12 to 1 and DISARMS `--apply`'s refusal, because `attach-shots.py` only checks the field is present and never compares it to the subject's route -- which is item 5 of X8's work order. So the report going quiet would have been this defect getting worse while looking fixed. The twelfth, SURF-022, is not this defect: see DEF-061.
subject.title: attach-shots --apply would attach the design mock render as the build's surface shot for 11 surfaces, and its report names the surface rather than the file

subject.detail: Measured 2026-08-21 against test-campaign 0.9.2 on app/Tests. The pass reports examined=1661 mutating=320 blind=88. Two structural errors and two idiom errors inflate that number. STRUCTURAL. (1) It scans every `func`, not every test. Restricted to swift-testing's own discriminator (a func whose nearest preceding annotation is @Test) the denominator is 1531, not 1661: 130 of the examined functions are not tests. (2) Its helper exclusion at vacuity-check.py:162 is file-scoped — a name is a helper only if called more than once in the file that declares it. A shared stub declared in TestSupport.swift and called from other files therefore reads as a test, so MemoryFileSystem's `write`, `removeItem` and `moveItem`, HTTPStub's `stop` and WatchTestSupport's `remove` are each counted as a blind test. 21 of the 88 are support-file functions. IDIOM, on the mutator side. (3) The lookbehind `(?<![A-Za-z0-9_])` cannot exclude a dot, so a Swift enum case constructor matches a mutator verb: `ServerRowAction.forServer(s, pendingAuth: nil) == .reset(.clearPlacard)` reports ServerPresentationTests::trippedOutranksHeld as mutating via 'reset', where `.reset` is the expected VALUE inside the assertion. 41 of 72 re-measured findings are dot-prefixed. (4) It takes the last mutator by source POSITION and calls everything after it the tail, which misreads three Swift constructs: a mutator inside the assertion (`await #expect(throws: Never.self) { try await store.delete() }` — nothing can follow it by construction), a mutator in a `defer` block (source-early, execution-last, so the whole test body reads as 'after'), and a mutator as the last statement of a loop body whose observation is the next iteration (CallbackLifecycleTests::stopReleasesTheSocket rebinds the port ten times; the read of cycle N is the start() of cycle N+1). SAMPLE. Of the 15 findings with zero assertions after the last mutator — the highest-yield stratum — 9 were read in full. Two (DiscoveryTests::servers, CapabilityPlateTests::install) are helpers. All 7 remaining are real tests that do observe after mutating, through idioms no reader verb names: `client.calls.last?.operation`, `seen.filter { ... }`, a rebind that throws. Precision on that stratum is 0 of 7. ARMED, two ways, evidence/arming/blind-mutation.arming.log. A probe @Test that mutates and never observes was added and removed: blind moved 88 -> 89 -> 88 and examined/mutating moved by exactly 1 each time. The check does bite; it is the false-positive rate that is at issue, not the sensitivity. NOT REMEDIED BY VOCABULARY. The reader side is deliberately loose because a false reader match suppresses a finding. Adding this codebase's read idioms (`calls`, `operation`, `filter`) would lower the number without improving what the pass knows, and the terms are generic enough to suppress true findings too. The 88 stands recorded as a worklist with its measured precision beside it rather than tuned to look better. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-27 by G22, which declared `testRoot` and gave this pass a corpus for the first time. THE 88 DOES NOT REPRODUCE. Vendored 0.9.2 over `app/Tests` today reports examined=2133 mutating=3 blind=3, against the 1661/320/88 above. The denominator moving up while `mutating` collapses 320 → 3 is not tree churn: 0.9.1 and 0.9.2 ship IDENTICAL DEFAULT_MUTATORS and DEFAULT_READERS, and neither list holds `reset`, `write`, `removeItem`, `moveItem` or `remove` — the verbs this entry's idiom argument turns on. So the 2026-08-21 sitting ran an expanded vocabulary passed on the command line, and `campaign.json` declares none, which makes 88 a figure no documented invocation returns. Its cited evidence, `evidence/arming/blind-mutation.arming.log`, has never existed on any branch of this repository (`git log --all -- '*blind-mutation*'` is empty), so the arming claim above is not checkable from the tree. The measured structural and idiom errors are not withdrawn; what is withdrawn is the population they were measured over. TODAY'S POPULATION, AND ITS PRECISION. With `testRoot: app` the pass reports examined=2179 mutating=3 re-read-after=0 blind=3, and 0.15.0 returns the same three findings from the same corpus. All THREE were read in full — 3 of 3, not a sample — and all three are false positives. Precision 0 of 3. A FOURTH CAUSE, NOT IN THE ORIGINAL ENTRY, AND THE ONE THAT PRODUCES TWO OF THE THREE. The body slice is `src[pos:end]` where `pos` is the start of the DECLARATION, so a test whose own name begins with a mutator verb matches itself. `WatchRestartTests::restartIsIssuedBeforeTheStagingWrite` and `::restartIsOwedBeforeTheWriteLands` contain no mutating call at all: the only `restart\w*\(` in each is `func restart…(` on its own declaration line. Both then read — `WatchWorld.read(scratch.logPath)`, `WatchState.load(path:)`, `WatchWorld.serverNames(in:)` — and assert on `state.mcpServersHash` and `state.restartPending`. The third, `PhoneStorageFailureTests::restartRechecksTheCamera`, does call `await model.restart()` and then asserts twice, on `model.step` and on `model.entry.characters`: property reads that no reader verb names, which is cause (4)'s shape rather than a new one. This cause survives into 0.15.0 unchanged. NOT ENROLLED IN A GATE, and `blindVocabulary` still not declared, for the reason the entry already gives. A related gap measured at the same sitting: pointed at `src/` — the TypeScript tree, which has no tests — the pass prints `corpus: … (0 file(s))` and `examined=0 mutating=0 blind=0` and contributes nothing to `--gate`. It reports its empty corpus and does not fail on it, so a mis-declared `testRoot` reads as a clean pass. VOCABULARY DECLARED 2026-08-29 by K4, and the entry's own 'NOT REMEDIED BY VOCABULARY' paragraph is narrowed rather than withdrawn. That paragraph reasons entirely from the READER side, and on the reader side it is still right: adding this codebase's read idioms lowers the count without improving what the pass knows, which is why the declared reader list stops short of `expect` and `require` -- swift-testing's assertion macros, 5781 and 383 occurrences, either of which would mark every test that asserts after mutating as re-reading and collapse the count to near zero while the pass learned nothing. THE MUTATOR SIDE WAS NEVER ARGUED, AND THAT IS WHERE THE PASS WAS BLIND. Measured over the same 2282 test bodies at `83e5380`: the nine snake_case defaults find 3 mutating call sites; a camelCase list derived from this corpus finds 481. So `blind=3` was a reading of 3 of 481, a recall of 0.6%, and the entry's `precision 0 of 3` was a precision over a population the instrument could barely see. `campaign.json` now carries `blindVocabulary` with `only: true`, 19 mutators and 34 readers, derived mechanically -- a verb is kept only where method calls on a receiver are at least half its corpus sites and its own `func` declaration lines at most a quarter, which is causes (3) and (4) of this entry turned into a selection rule. THE THREE FINDINGS ARE ADJUDICATED, and each clears for a different checkable reason rather than all three for one. `restartIsIssuedBeforeTheStagingWrite`: one fitted mutator, `WatchWorld.remove(scratch)` inside a `defer`, and four declared readers after it -- `load`, `read`, `parse`, `servers`. NOT blind, positively. `restartIsOwedBeforeTheWriteLands`: three fitted mutators, the last `WatchState(restartPending: true).save(`, with `load` after it. NOT blind, positively. `restartRechecksTheCamera`: ZERO fitted mutator call sites in its body. It was flagged only because `restart` is a shipped default and this entry's fourth cause -- the body slice beginning at the declaration -- made `func restartRechecksTheCamera(` match itself. `restart` fails the selection rule (1 method call against 3 declaration lines, of 5 sites), so it is not in the vocabulary and the finding is withdrawn. WHAT THAT DOES NOT MEAN: its real mutation `await model.restart()` is now invisible to the pass, and its reads are still the property comparisons `model.step` and `model.entry.characters` that no reader verb names. It is UNEXAMINED by this instrument, not clean, and that is this entry's ceiling stated once more rather than closed. ARMED, AND ENROLLED, which the entry recorded as missing. `planning/test-campaign/bin/blind-vocabulary-arm.py` runs on every `make lint`: two plants identical but for one line, each measured alone and again inside a `shutil.copytree` of the real corpus, requiring examined+1 mutating+1 blind+1 for the blind plant and examined+1 mutating+1 blind+0 for the reading one. The specificity arm is the half a sensitivity arm alone cannot give: a detector that flagged every mutating body would pass the first and say nothing. 6 of 6 as expected on `cache 0.16.0` and again on the `vendor/` pin via `--instrument`. The two disagree only on the denominator -- 2282 against 2277, the five arrow-style `it/test(` blocks 0.9.3 added block detection for -- and agree on blind=111. THE 111 IS A WORKLIST AND THE CAMPAIGN STILL PUBLISHES NO BLIND NUMBER. Nothing above touches the structural causes: the pass still examines every `func` rather than every `@Test`, its helper exclusion is still file-scoped, and a `defer` mutator still reads as source-early -- which is exactly why the first of the three findings above needed reading rather than counting. This entry stays OPEN; what it now carries is a measured recall beside its measured precision.
subject.title: vacuity-check's blind-mutation pass examines non-tests and mis-reads Swift idiom; 7 of 7 sampled findings are false positives

subject.detail: Measured 2026-09-03 (WE3) on LUKESFF, Windows 11, CPython 3.13, console codepage 1252. `campaign.py`'s loader is `return json.loads(p.read_text())` with no `encoding=`. `Path.read_text()` defaults to `locale.getencoding()`, which is cp1252 here. This campaign's `inventory.json` holds em dashes and middots, so: $ python vendor/test-campaign/.../campaign.py check planning/test-campaign UnicodeDecodeError: 'charmap' codec can't decode byte 0x9d in position 284168 exit 1 It is a traceback rather than a verdict, and `exit 1` is the same code the gate uses for 'not ready to report'. A caller reading the exit status alone cannot tell a campaign that failed its checks from one the checker could not open. `PYTHONUTF8=1` makes it run; with that set it reaches its checks and reports normally, which is how the rest of this session's `campaign.py` measurements were taken. SCOPE. Windows hosts only -- macOS and most Linux default to UTF-8, which is why the campaign never met this on the Mac. It is not confined to `campaign.py`: `vacuity-check.py`, `strict-check.py` and `attach-shots.py` in the pinned 0.9.2 read and WRITE with the same bare calls, so on this host `attach-shots.py --apply` would write `inventory.json` back in cp1252 and mangle every em dash in the register. That one is a data-loss path rather than a crash, and it is the reason this is filed at detector severity rather than as a nuisance.
subject.title: campaign.py reads the registry with no encoding, so on a Windows console it dies on the first non-ASCII byte and checks nothing

subject.detail: parity-gate.sh, 20 Aug 2026 on main at e5755d0. The suite lane's citation run of scripts/acceptance/parity-oauth.sh exited non-zero and recorded `control-auth-post-http fail — the Swift router never reached the token endpoint`. The dedicated oauth lane, later in the same gate, ran the same script and recorded ok over 21 checks. The gate reported the row DIVERGED and printed 81 of 83. WHY IT IS UNEXPLAINED, established 21 Aug 2026 from disk without re-running anything. The run survives as evidence/runs/parity-gate-2026-08-20-oauth-flake.log, written 20:39:30. Its line 163 is the whole of what the citation run reported: `FAIL scripts/acceptance/parity-oauth.sh the gate reported findings`, and the next line is the following `ok` row. The script itself does not fail that quietly -- its failure branch (parity-oauth.sh:308-329) prints the POST /auth status, the browser hop, the tail of the router log and the first 20 requests the provider saw. Every one of those bytes existed and was discarded by the caller: `parity-suite.sh`'s `run_script` sent both streams to /dev/null at the time. So this defect is not a run that left no diagnostic, it is a run whose diagnostic the harness threw away, and no amount of re-reading the log can recover it. The instrument was repaired in commit 21d559b at 20:41:28 -- one minute and 58 seconds after this log was written, in the same commit that recorded the defect -- so `run_script` now keeps the log and prints its last 20 lines inline. A recurrence would therefore arrive with the cause attached. That is what closes this: the next occurrence, not more thought about this one. It stays open because there is still no cause and no reproduction; what changed is that the reason it could not be diagnosed is now known and no longer true. One candidate mechanism examined and NOT adopted. The R9 lane reported (21 Aug 2026, via uds:/tmp/cc-socks/9881.sock) that a stale $TMPDIR/mcp-router-parity.lock had made a gate fail its manifest-check for a non-real reason. That is a different symptom -- a manifest-check failure before the comparison, against this defect's completed run that reached `control-auth-post-http` and recorded a row -- and parity-oauth.sh takes that same lock at line 126 and preflights every port at 143-145, so the two lanes inside one gate could not have overlapped. Recorded as ruled out rather than left unmentioned, so the next reader does not spend the lead twice.
subject.text: Observed once, in one of two whole-gate runs, and not reproduced by: a standalone run of `parity-oauth.sh`, a second standalone run of it immediately afterwards (which exercised the same port-reuse wait, 9s and 12s), a standalone run of `parity-suite.sh`, or a second whole `parity-gate.sh` on the same tree. The second gate reported 82 of 83, 0 DIVERGED, and its suite lane reported the citation clean. **What it is not.** The lane distinguishes an environment failure from a finding on purpose, and this was the finding branch: `record control-auth-post-http fail` at `parity-oauth.sh:329`, reached only when the reference side completed an authorization and the Swift side did not. An unbindable port exits 2 through `wait_for_ports_bindable` and records `blocked`, not `fail`, so the port-reuse race is ruled out by the code path that fired. **Why it went undiagnosed, and what changed.** `parity-suite.sh`'s `run_script` sent both streams to `/dev/null` and printed `the gate reported findings` — a verdict with no evidence under it. The bytes naming which guard failed had already been thrown away by the time anyone read the gate's summary. `run_script` now keeps the log, prints its last 20 lines inline and names the file it kept, armed 20 Aug 2026 against a deliberately failing citation. A recurrence will say which of the 21 checks went red. **Why the duplicate run stays.** `control-auth-post-http` is proven on the wire by its own lane and also cites the script, so the gate runs it twice. That is now documented in `parity-suite.sh` rather than deduplicated, because the duplicate is what caught this: a single run would have reported a clean 82 of 83 and nobody would have known. Both record under the same row id and a `fail` wins. **Burn-in, 20 Aug 2026: 8 standalone runs of the lane, all green, 21 checks each.** Three immediately after the failure and five consecutively afterwards, plus one clean whole gate. One failure in roughly ten whole-lane executions, cause unrecoverable because that invocation's stdout was discarded. A green burn-in does not close this: the original failure is uninspectable, so the runs measure only that the lane is not reliably broken. What would close it is a captured reproduction, or a stated gate met — several consecutive whole gates including the cold port-reuse path — decided as its own question rather than inferred from a streak, which is the `install-launchd-watch` mistake this repository already paid for once (G1: name a fix per term and fix a bound IN ADVANCE, never a green streak). Not a UI defect and not a blocker on the cutover count — CASE-0036's measurement is the second run — but it is an unexplained non-determinism in the router or the lane, and it is recorded rather than absorbed.
subject.title: the OAuth parity lane failed once inside a full gate and has not reproduced

subject.detail: REPAIRED FOR THIS INSTANCE, NOT FOR THE MECHANISM. 18 briefs now carry `reckon-sources` naming the rows that back-reference them (WIN3..WIN16, WIN19, WIN20, WIN22, WIN23), each with a `target-note` saying which field of which row names the brief. The other 6 - WIN1, WIN2, WIN17, WIN18, WIN21, WIN24 - keep `registry-target: none` with a REWRITTEN reason that concedes the false half and states what is still absent: no registry entity states which UI framework the client is built on, records a Windows native design floor, records the daemon's macOS-shaped assumptions in `src/`, records the Windows build and gate spine, describes a Windows keyboard model, or measures a contrast ratio against a Windows control fill. WHAT IS STILL OWED IS THE ARM. cell.dataShape: two claims inside one renotify window

subject.note: R26. The throttle withholds a REPEAT and never an ESCALATION. The brief asks that a recurring error not generate alert spam, and the naive reading -- one alert per server per window -- swallows the one transition that matters. Four things make a notice due: nothing has been said yet, the KIND changed, the EXPIRY moved, or the window elapsed. E13 runs with `renotifyAfterMs` set to a year so nothing can go out on elapsed time, watches `expiring` become `expired` one millisecond past the boundary, and then asserts the repeat after it IS withheld -- so the arm is the escalation rather than the throttle being broken.

R26. Reading the report does not consume the notice; claiming it does. That is why there are two routes rather than one: folding them together would make `GET /upstreams/auth-expiry` spend the notification a caller was about to be shown, so opening a settings pane would silence the next alert. It is the same rule this repository enforces on its own gates -- a check that mutates the tree as a side effect of checking is not a check. E16 asserts it on the monitor and E24 through the routes; the lane asserts it as `count:2` after two GETs.

cell.dataShape: a credential record with no expires_in

subject.note: R26. THE VACUITY CASE, and the reason this item exists in the shape it does. A token whose stored record declares no lifetime has no derivable expiry, and the tempting reading -- it has not expired, therefore it is fine -- is the class this campaign keeps finding: a state that reads healthy because nothing measured it. `AuthExpiryRecord.state` has NO path from a missing number to `valid`; it returns `unknown` and the wire carries `unknownReason` saying which half is missing (`no-lifetime-declared` when `expires_in` is absent, `unreadable-authorized-at` when the stamp is). Asserted at both planes: E5/E6/E17/E21 in the suites, and the lane reads `state`, `unknownReason` and the ABSENCE of any invented `expiresAt` off a record it planted itself. Not `expiresAt: null` -- absent, so there is nothing there for a careless reader to round to fine.

cell.dataShape: an authExpiry block below the floor

subject.note: R26. A configured value the router will not take is REFUSED and reported with its key, its value as written, the floor that rejected it and its scope -- never clamped. A clamp invents a number nobody wrote, so the file says 500 and the behaviour is 60000 with nothing anywhere saying which is real. `warnWithinMs`'s floor is this item's own vacuity rule and ZERO IS NOT ACCEPTED: at zero a token passes straight from valid to expired and `expiring` is unreachable, which is R27's `tripAfter >= 2` one item earlier. E2 asserts that in both directions -- under a zero window a token one millisecond from death reads `valid`, and under the resolved policy the same token reads `expiring`.

cell.dataShape: a credential re-authorised between two claims

subject.note: R26. *Resolving authentication immediately clears the warning status* -- the brief's third bullet, and it is a CLEAR rather than an age-out. A server that stops deserving a notice has its delivery record DROPPED, so the next thing that goes wrong is reported at once instead of waiting out a six-hour window. The lane proves it against a wall clock: it re-authorises the record from outside, claims, breaks it again, claims again, and the notice arrives seconds later under the default six-hour renotify. A throttle that merely aged out could not produce that. The absence half is paired -- a SECOND server is broken in the same step, so 'the re-authorised one is gone' is read off a reply that carries another server rather than off an empty one.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=package not installed
subject.note: A real MSIX, built, deployed and removed, with a recorder at each step that is not the thing that wrote it. MakeAppx packs and .NET's ZipArchive reads the OPC container back - so the identity assertion is made against the PACKED ARTIFACT rather than against the file on disk that was handed to the packer. `winget validate` is the winget client applying a schema this repository does not own. Add-AppxPackage deploys and Get-AppxPackage reports: Fledgeling.MCPRouter_0.1.0.0_x64__facmrsw33693e. THE INSTALL ARM IS WHAT TURNS A FILE INTO A PACKAGE. A manifest can pack cleanly, validate cleanly, and be refused at deployment for a capability, an architecture or a signature - and every static check in the world passes right up to that point. 'CLEAN UNINSTALL RULES' IS THE HALF WORTH READING TWICE. UninstallGuidance promises that uninstalling preserves %USERPROFILE%\.claude\mcp-router. That is a promise about what SURVIVES, and a promise about survival cannot be checked by any amount of reading - only by an uninstall that actually ran. The lane plants a marker, installs, removes, and requires both that the deployment stack reports the package gone and that the marker is still there. WHAT THE LANE PUTS BACK: a self-signed certificate is added to LocalMachine\TrustedPeople so an unsigned developer package can deploy at all, and removed in a finally block however the run ends. Verified afterwards: zero Fledgeling.* packages, zero witness certificates. A lane that left a trusted publisher behind would have changed what this machine will install, silently and for every future run. NOT SETTLED: that anyone can obtain the package. Nothing publishes it, the winget InstallerUrl is a deliberate example.invalid placeholder, and this lane asserts the placeholder is PRESENT so the manifest cannot be mistaken for a shipping one. DEF-083 carries the publishing step, which needs a signing certificate and a pull request into a third-party repository.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=one capability queued
subject.note: The toast itself, in the Action Center, read by a process that cannot raise one. DEF-082 filed this as unmeasurable and gave a reason: UserNotificationListener's userNotificationListener capability is only grantable to a packaged application, and MCPRouter.Shell is WindowsPackageType=None, so the row was said to be downstream of WIN19's MSIX. THE REASON WAS WRONG, AND IT WAS WRONG BEFORE WIN19 LANDED. Measured on this host from an ordinary unpackaged Win32 console process with no package identity at all - Package.Current throws InvalidOperationException, which the lane asserts rather than assumes - UserNotificationListener.Current resolves, RequestAccessAsync returns Allowed with no consent prompt, and GetNotificationsAsync returns the toasts that are really there. On the first run those included three raised by win22-toast-witness the day before, carrying the exact strings NotificationPresentation writes. No MSIX, no capability, no packaged identity. WHAT IS STILL NOT AVAILABLE UNPACKAGED, and it bounds this case: every member of UserNotification.AppInfo throws NotImplementedException 0x80004001 for a caller with no package identity, so the listener can say what a notification SAYS and when it arrived and cannot say who raised it. Attribution here is the payload text, which the product owns, inside a time window this run opened - weaker than a publisher identity, and recorded as such. THE RECORDER IS NOT THE WRITER AND IS NOT EVEN THE SAME PROCESS: app/windows/MCPRouter.Witness.ActionCenter shares no code with the shell and cannot raise a notification. The shell's toast-probe.json is carried as the writer's self-report and graded by nothing. THE PRESENCE CONTROL is a removal: the matched notification is taken back out through the listener and the Action Center is read a third time, and the recorder is required to say no about it.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=one capability queued
subject.note: The COM activator the Windows notification platform wrote, read out of the registry by a process that did not write it. The writer is AppNotificationManager.Register() inside the shell; the recorder is HKCU through PowerShell's registry provider, and nothing of this repository's sits between them. Four arms. BASELINE requires the AUMID key to be ABSENT before the shell launches, so what the other three read is this launch. The three EFFECT arms read the key, the CustomActivator CLSID it names, and that CLSID's LocalServer32 - which came back as MCPRouter.Shell.exe carrying the platform's own ----AppNotificationActivated: argument, a string this repository does not write anywhere. THE ACTIVATOR IS THE ARM THAT CARRIES THE ITEM. A toast outlives the process that raised it; when somebody presses Review an hour later, Windows COM-activates the LocalServer32 registered for that CLSID. Without it the toast still appears and pressing it does nothing, which is the failure that looks most like success and exactly what a screenshot of a notification would have certified. WHAT THIS CASE DOES NOT SETTLE: that a toast is drawn, and that a press re-activates the app. Both need UserNotificationListener, whose capability is only grantable to a packaged application; DEF-082 carries them and is downstream of DEF-073. The shell's own report that the platform accepted a Show is carried in the evidence as writerSelfReport and is graded by nothing, because a process reporting its own effect is the shape of claim DEF-072 was about.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=no task registered
subject.note: The Windows task scheduler holding a task the product registered, read by an API that did not write it. The writer is MCPRouter.Shell.Live's LogonTaskSupervisor driving schtasks.exe with the Task Scheduler XML it builds; the recorder is Get-ScheduledTask, the ScheduledTasks module over the scheduler's WMI provider - a different API, a different process and a different vocabulary for the same facts. The XML says RunLevel LeastPrivilege and the recorder answers RunLevel Limited, and nothing in this repository translates between them. The scheduler also normalised the interval this run asked for, PT60S, into PT1M, which is the plainest available evidence that the read did not come back through anything this code wrote. EIGHT ARMS, AND TWO ARE ABOUT THE INSTRUMENT. BASELINE requires the recorder to report the task ABSENT before registration - without it, a task left behind by an interrupted run makes every other arm pass over a run that registered nothing. SILENCE requires it to report absence again after removal, which is what separates a reader from an echo: a recorder that always answered yes would satisfy the six product arms by construction. The other six read the three claims LifecyclePresentation prints to the operator - triggered at logon, un-elevated, restarting on failure - plus the executable and port this run asked for, plus presence and removal. WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE, and the reason it is one case rather than the whole of REQ-035: nothing here logs the user out, so the trigger has never been watched to fire, and nothing here starts or kills a daemon, so the restart has never been watched to happen. DEF-081 carries those two. This case settles that the registration the product performs produces, in the Windows task scheduler, a task carrying the properties the product's own UI describes - which before 2026-09-02 was unmeasured entirely, and which DEF-074 recorded as a supervision model nothing performed.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=a supervised process that dies
subject.note: The half of WIN23's supervision promise that had never been watched: a daemon the Windows task scheduler starts, loses, and starts again. DEF-081 filed it as unmeasurable and named the blocker as a missing Windows daemon binary; the blocker was real and is gone - app/windows/MCPRouter.Witness.Daemon is a harness process that starts, records its own start and waits to be killed, so there is something for the scheduler to supervise. WHAT THE MEASUREMENT FOUND IS NOT WHAT THE ROW EXPECTED. The registration the product wrote carried RestartOnFailure with a 60-second interval and a count of 3, and it did not restart the daemon at all. Killed, watched 150 seconds, on the unified scheduling engine and the legacy one, for a run started by a trigger and one started on demand: four registrations, no restart. The same block DID restart, three times at exactly 60 seconds, a task whose Command named a file that does not exist - so the instrument can see a restart, and RestartOnFailure governs a task that fails to LAUNCH rather than one whose action launched and later died. DEF-320 carries that, and the product now writes a Repetition on the trigger alongside MultipleInstancesPolicy IgnoreNew. THE RECORDERS ARE TWO AND NEITHER WROTE ANYTHING: Get-ScheduledTaskInfo for the scheduler's own account of its runs, and Get-CimInstance Win32_Process for the process identity, which is what makes 'it came back' a different process id rather than a report from the thing that came back. The daemon's own run log is carried and graded by nothing. EIGHT ARMS, THREE OF THEM ABOUT THE INSTRUMENT: BASELINE requires both tasks absent and no daemon running, so nothing below is inherited from an interrupted run; CLAIM.repetition and CLAIM.ignorenew read the product's own unmodified logon registration back through the WMI provider; SILENCE requires both recorders to say no once the tasks are gone. ONE SUBSTITUTION, SAID OUT LOUD: a trigger repetition does not apply to an on-demand start - measured, twice - so the live task carries a TimeTrigger where the product writes a LogonTrigger, because this lane must not log the machine out. Every Setting, the repetition interval, the principal, the action and the instances policy are the product's own document. That the trigger fires AT LOGON is still unwitnessed and DEF-081 keeps it.

subject.cell: execution-plane=daemon · data-shape=a credential literal in an env value, a header value, a URL userinfo and a URL query
subject.note: Every CONFIGURED credential is absent from the bundle, and the document that omits it is a real one. The absence alone is the easiest unfailable assertion in this repository: it holds over an empty document, over a 404, and over a gatherer that never read the config. So it is asserted beside three things that must be PRESENT — a public canary planted in the same log line, the env key name, and the header key name — and beside `"value":"present"`, which proves a decision was taken about the value rather than the whole server having been skipped. Layer 1 is what this case pins: an env value, a header value and a URL's userinfo are never PLACED in the document, so no key name a config invents can smuggle one through. It follows Describe's own construction, which maps the pair arrays to their keys before anything else touches them (B10).

subject.cell: execution-plane=daemon · data-shape=a request on a method the ported token gate does not cover
subject.note: ControlAPIRequest.isMutating is POST || DELETE || PATCH, ported from src/control.ts, and PUT is not in it. No route served PUT before this family, so nothing was ever exposed — but this family's write was written as a PUT, and an untokened PUT /profiles/x measured 200 while the rest of the suite was green. The write is a POST instead, because widening a ported gate that parity-manifest-check.sh derives from the reference in both directions is not a thing to do for a verb. The lane asserts the 405 on the wire and ControlProfileRoutesTests C6 holds the invariant over PUT, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE for whoever adds the next route here.

F5. The incremental scan. Scanning an unchanged file twice must yield the same events as scanning it once and must not open it the second time; a file that shrank must be re-read from zero and say so in filesReread. The corpus is 59,476 files and 19.5 GB (measured 2026-08-29), so the watermark is what makes the reader answerable inside a request rather than an optimisation.

F5. With no reporter wired, GET /invocations answers 503 naming that the router was never pointed at a transcript corpus, not an empty window. ControlDeps' optional ports have shipped nil in RouterServiceDispatch twice with a green suite (control-registry-search, D-p1-a), which is a 503 on a whole family no unit test could see.

FLOW-006.02. The panel drew a document THE ROUTER SERVED, not M19's fixture: the titlebar names g17-capability, the package's own H1 and prose are on screen, all three tab controls are drawn, and 'trawl' — the fixture capability every previous dump and capture of this panel was a picture of, M23's included — appears nowhere in the tree. Checks G17-P1, G17-P2, G17-P3. Picture: evidence/g17-document/readme.served.png. The flow's whole shape in one relation: one package, three tabs, three different documents. The three frames' drawn text is pairwise distinct and all three titlebars name the same package — so the tab is what changed and the subject is not. Check G17-P8.

The three refusals are pairwise distinguishable in the words the panel actually drew: 'g17-no-package has no package to read' / 'README.md is too large to show here' / 'Not shown — this image points outside the package it came with.' J2. Every sidebar row is selected in turn and the effect is read in the RESTORATION STORE, which is a different channel from the one that struck: `ShellModel.selection`'s `didSet` calls `store.save(destination:)`, so a real selection leaves a value in a scratch `UserDefaults` suite that nothing in the test wrote, and that a relaunch reads. `model.selection == .servers` after `model.select(.servers)` was deliberately NOT used — it reads the property the call just wrote, which is the actuation side of the vacuous assertion (`references/inert-ui.md`, `detector-defects.md` §11). Each row is approached from a DIFFERENT destination, because `didSet` guards on `oldValue != selection` and a loop starting where the model boots would have the first row write nothing at all. The destination-collapse relation is asserted as a count rather than as seven separate greens: seven presses, seven DISTINCT persisted values, so a shell whose rows all led to one place fails on the cardinality. A second model built on the same store comes up where the last row left it, which is the read-back a relaunch actually performs. `Settings` is the eighth control and is not a destination: M15 moved it to a scene of its own, so the effect read is the installed opener firing exactly once AND the console's persisted destination not moving. Both halves, because an implementation that opened the scene and also selected a board would pass the first alone. LIMIT, stated rather than left implicit: a persisted destination proves the selection took. It does not prove a different board was DRAWN — SwiftUI's view tree is opaque to a SwiftPM test and `ContentZone`'s switch is unreachable from here. That half is CASE-0001's, on glass, and it is FAILING (DEF-058, DEF-059), so it counts nothing. This is the in-process half and says which half it is.

J2. `Keep warm` is driven and the effect is read on the REQUEST THE CLIENT RECORDED — `{"warm":true}` then `{"warm":false}`, the encoded bytes rather than the `ServerPatch` value, because a computed property or a `CodingKeys` mapping can put a key on the wire that no stored property shows. Both directions are asserted: `warm: false` clears the policy rather than stopping anything, and a control that only worked one way would pass on the first alone. The row redraws from the model either way, so the row is exactly the observable that cannot distinguish a working switch from an empty closure. The recorded request can.

K3. The accept path is the only route in the product by which something a remote device asked for becomes something that runs, so the reading that matters is the declaration itself: the name and command the MAC resolved, and `force == false`, which is what stops an item that arrived from a phone replacing the command line of a server the user already trusts. Four same-channel reads are refused, and the arm is why. With the write removed, `acceptState` still clears, `sheetItemID` still goes nil, the row still leaves `rows` and the badge still falls by one — because all four come from `record(.accepted(…))` after the call. A case asserting any of them would have stayed green over a control that told the router nothing.

K3. `Decline` is the one disposition that is entirely local, so it is read in two places at once. The rows the board draws lose exactly one row — asserted as an ordered identity against the survivors rather than as a count, and again through `waitingCount`, which is computed off the same array so the sidebar and the list cannot disagree. And the router is told nothing: no declaration and no removal reaches the recording client, which is a channel the press does not touch at all. That second half is the substance. A decline that quietly removed a server would satisfy every list assertion here and would be the destructive act `DESIGN.md` §8 reserves for the Servers board. The read refused is `board.dispositioned[item.id] != nil` — the dictionary the call just wrote, the same tautology as a segment reporting itself selected.

subject.note: A reference attempting to ESCAPE THE PACKAGE is refused rather than served. Fifteen assertions over one response. The strongest of them is not a reason code: the fixture plants a secret file outside the package, and the case asserts that the secret's path appears NOWHERE in the raw body — if anything escaped, the bytes are in the response and no status code hides that. Then exactly one image travelled and it is the one inside the package (`docs/inside.png`), and nine references are refused with the reason each earns and no more than nine: `../outside/secret.png`, `../pkg-escape-evil/secret.png` (a SIBLING package whose path is a string prefix of this one), `link-out.png` (a real symlink out), `linkdir/secret.png` (a symlinked DIRECTORY), `../../../../etc/passwd` -> escapesPackage; `/etc/hosts.png` and `~/secret.png` -> absolutePath; `https://example.invalid/secret.png` -> remote; `%2e%2e/outside/secret.png` -> notInPackage. M30 armed this check with three planted divergences and a fresh-context verifier attacked it with 23 adversarial references for zero escapes. That evidence is real and it lives in M30's record, where it was proved ONCE. This case exists so the property is checked on a schedule instead. Run against BOTH implementations over a real socket: `dist/index.js serve` and the shipped `app/.build/debug/MCPRouterCLI serve`, each on 127.0.0.1:8981 with a scratch MCP_ROUTER_HOME. M30 already proves this route in process — `ControlDocumentRouteTests.swift` calls the handler and asserts on the string it returns — which is a different claim from this one: this lets the kernel carry the bytes and reads what a client actually receives, which is what the campaign asks of every other route on this lane. subject.note: R22. The requirement is written as an honesty guardrail rather than a behaviour because the load-bearing half is a promise about what is NOT in the output, and this campaign's own history is that such a promise is satisfied trivially by producing nothing. Every case under it therefore pairs its absence with a presence: a public canary in the same log line, the key names, and a non-zero `occurrencesRemoved`. R25 (server configuration profile export with safe secret redaction) is the sibling and had NOT landed when this was built — checked at LEDGER.md, status To Do — so the redactor is new here rather than a second one. It is deliberately a general component under RouterCore/Diagnostics rather than private to the bundle, so R25 reuses it instead of writing a third.
subject.text: One action exports the router's recent log, every declared upstream with its live state and cached tool surface, and the recent tool calls — and no credential value leaves in it. A secret-bearing field is never placed in the document; every known secret value is removed from every string that does survive, in its literal, percent-encoded and base64 forms; a value too short to be scrubbed from free text is named rather than used; and the untokened preview carries counts and no content.

subject.note: R22. Every CONFIGURED credential is absent from the bundle, and the document that omits it is a real one. The absence alone is the easiest unfailable assertion in this repository: it holds over an empty document, over a 404, and over a gatherer that never read the config. So it is asserted beside three things that must be PRESENT — a public canary planted in the same log line, the env key name, and the header key name — and beside `"value":"present"`, which proves a decision was taken about the value rather than the whole server having been skipped.

R22. Layer 2, and the channel layer 1 structurally cannot reach. A credential arrives in a diagnostics export by more routes than the field it was configured in: an upstream that rejects a call and quotes the token back in its error text, a command line carrying `--token=`, a log line somebody wrote by hand. Those are strings the bundle has every reason to carry, and the only thing distinguishing the secret inside one is its VALUE.

R22. The needle floor, which is a correctness rule rather than a performance one. An env value of `1`, `true` or `dev` used as a scrub needle deletes every occurrence of that text from every log line in the bundle — the timestamps, the ports, the word `device`. The result READS as thorough redaction and is a corrupted document, and nobody looking at it can tell which.

R22. A secret does not always reach a log line as itself. It reaches it percent-encoded when it travelled in a URL and base64-encoded when it travelled in a `Basic` credential, and a scrubber that knows only the literal reports a clean bundle over both. Both out-of-family lanes raised this independently and it is the one addition of theirs taken wholesale.

R22. The preview is a GET and GET is UNGATED in this router — `ControlHandler.gate` reads the token only for POST/DELETE/PATCH, matching the reference, recorded there as a ported defect rather than quietly fixed. So the preview is written to one rule: it discloses nothing `GET /servers` does not already disclose. Category names, counts, key names, and the redaction plan.

R22. The verb IS the gate, and it is not describing a mutation. The bundle changes nothing. It is a POST because stage 2 of `ControlHandler.handle` gates the token on POST/DELETE/PATCH only, so the verb is the only thing deciding whether this router hands its whole diagnostic corpus — log lines included — to any unauthenticated caller that can open the loopback port, which per `ControlToken` includes a web page the user merely visits.
WIN10. The three tab labels carry counts, so their accessible names move with the data — a case matching them exactly will be brittle by construction and must match on role plus prefix.

subject.text: On Windows the router daemon is supervised by a Scheduled Task registered against the user's own logon: it starts in the interactive user session so it can reach local browser instances for OAuth and per-user harness configuration, it runs un-elevated, and it is restarted by the scheduler if it fails.

DETECTOR DEFECT in test-campaign, measured 2026-08-27 (G29) against the vendored 0.9.2 and the machine's 0.15.0, which carry a byte-identical `tie()`. SURF-028's route is `app://mac/servers/{server}/document` -- a family of addresses, one per server. `bin/g17-document-flow.sh` rendered its frames against three of them and recorded each target honestly. `tie()` normalises scheme, host, port, query and fragment away and then asks for string equality or a suffix match, so `mac/servers/g17-capability/document` against `mac/servers/{server}/document` fails all three tests and the gate reports UNTIED -- 'the recorded target does not resolve to the subject's route'. Nothing was pointed at the wrong thing. `references/capture-lineage.md` says resolution is 'deliberately loose on the parts a harness legitimately varies'; a `{server}` segment is exactly such a part, and it is the one case the looseness does not cover. THE FIX BELONGS UPSTREAM, and is not applied here. `vendor/README.md` pins the tree by checksum so the gates can be re-run from a clone, and a `tie()` that behaves one way in this repository and another way everywhere else stops being evidence -- the same reasoning that keeps X7 and X8 open. Referred out of family (gpt-5.6-sol, high effort, 2026-08-27) and it reached the same conclusion independently: patch upstream, cut a release, re-vendor and re-pin, rather than forking the pinned copy. The patch is one function: treat a route segment of the form `{name}`, `:name` or `*` as matching exactly one non-empty target segment, leaving literal segments, the source-file refusal and the normalisation untouched, and leaving the seeded swap red. WHAT THIS REPOSITORY DID INSTEAD, and why it is not a workaround. The three served frames are published by the FLOW-006 steps that rendered them, each carrying the concrete route its own capture recorded, and SURF-028 publishes none. That is the registry becoming more accurate rather than less: the surface is a template and has no single portrait, while a step is that surface at one address and can name it. Every frame is now filed at the address the channel was pointed at. The detector limit is unchanged and is what this row records.

The package lane's own instrument, and a relation across runs rather than a fact about one: the same source must give the same verdict on a loaded host and an idle one. It did not — `make test` reported 4 issues at a one-minute load average of ~700 and passed 1473 tests at load 46 minutes later (DEF-030). Every one of the four asserted after a fixed sleep or a 2–5 second deadline, so what they were measuring was the machine. Closed by replacing each deadline with a condition: `ShellTestSupport.waitUntil` and `ActivityReconnectTests.completes` keep a bound so a condition that never arrives fails rather than hangs, but at 30s rather than inside the noise; and `searchIsDebounced` waits for the debounce to fire and then holds a full debounce window of quiet, because the wait alone is satisfied by the first request and would pass against the one-per-keystroke defect it exists to catch. Armed 20 Aug 2026 three ways, each watched to fail with its own message — `.seconds(0)` on the shared waiter reads `no poll ran at all` and `five keystrokes issued 0 requests`, `.milliseconds(1)` on the completion bound reads `reconnect did not return while the feed stayed live`, and a `queryChanged()` inserted into the quiet period reads `a later request arrived`. The contention that triggered the original failure came from another project and is not reproducible on demand, so the arms are the proof rather than a repeat of the load.

DEF-011's last open half, the one the row was left open for: `Read first…`, which the design keys on `k.provenance` and which `CleanupBoardModel.Candidate` had no field to key on.
