subject.detail: Measured 2026-08-27 by G16 while enumerating SURF-026, and independently by G15. M15 made Settings a Scene and removed the case from `Destination`, and capture-mac-glass.sh still ran `axkit select Settings`. That select fails — `axkit: no sidebar row starting 'Settings'` — the app stays on whichever board the loop visited last, and the shutter filed THAT board's pixels under SURF-011: byte-identical to the Cleanup board on one loop ordering and to the Insights board on another. THE CAMPAIGN'S OWN INSTRUMENTS CAUGHT IT FROM TWO DIRECTIONS, which is the part worth keeping. glass-assert.py's raster uniqueness check went red because two cases shared a sha256; `--discriminate` reported the neighbouring board's predicate wrongly accepting SURF-011's dump, because that dump IS the neighbouring board; and the capture manifest's readback recorded the picture's target as the neighbour's route under subject SURF-011, contradicting its own filename. FIXED HERE, NARROWLY: the capture script now refuses to photograph a select that did not take, and says which board the window is actually showing. That is the script's own standing rule rather than a new one — it already declines to substitute a picture for the pairing sheet and the status item, and its header records the run that filed the Inbox board as SURF-010. The title and the dump are still written from what the app is really showing, so the failure stays visible downstream; what is withheld is the photograph, because a misattributed picture is the one artefact nothing downstream can correct. STILL OPEN, and deliberately not fixed here: 1. SURF-011 has no route to the Settings SCENE. It needs Cmd-comma or the app menu, not a sidebar select that cannot succeed. CASE-0016 and CASE-0111 fail until it does. 2. THE MENU MAP IS PRE-M22. Committed SURF-001.menu.txt binds Cmd-4 to `Discover`; the running app binds Cmd-4 to `Harnesses`, exactly as Destination.selectionDigit declares (activity 1, servers 2, skills 3, harnesses 4, discover 5, inbox 6, evals 7, cleanup 8, insights 9). glass-assert.py's SURF-001 `menu` dict is the old map, so CASE-0001 asserts five bindings this build does not have. Correcting it is editing an assertion to restore a green, which this campaign forbids — it is owed as its own item, from Destination.selectionDigit rather than by hand. WHY IT IS THE SAME FINDING AS G14'S, ONE LAYER DOWN. G14 found the surface LIST had stopped growing while the product did. This is the EVIDENCE not having been re-taken since the build moved: the committed glass artefacts were last written on 20 Aug by cef3729, before M22 added two destinations and renumbered four accelerators. In both cases a completeness gate reported clean because what it measured was a stale artefact rather than the product. CLOSED ON THE EVIDENCE SIDE, 2026-08-27 (G21/G29). The frame this defect produced was still published: `inventory.json` gave SURF-011 the shot `evidence/shots/SURF-011.build.png`, and at `519aebc` those bytes were the Insights board. `capture-lineage.py --gate` reported it UNTIED because the capture step's own row said `target: app://mac/insights` while the filename said SURF-011 -- the manifest was right and the wall was wrong. Two moves, both provable from git. The Insights frame is renamed `evidence/shots/DEF-059.insights-filed-as-SURF-011.png`, keeping every capture-time field, so the defect keeps its exhibit and no filename match can offer it to SURF-011 again. The Settings capture it overwrote is restored to `SURF-011.build.png` from `cef3729`, TOGETHER WITH ITS MANIFEST ROW from the same commit -- the last commit where those bytes and that row agreed (sha 3b5a26ef, `target: app://mac/settings`, readback `Settings`, 2026-08-20T11:32:58Z). Restoring the pair from one commit is a recovery of a capture-time record; restamping the row against the new bytes would have been the manifest-after-the-fact defect. What is NOT closed is the cause: `axkit select Settings` still fails, so the campaign still has no Settings capture newer than 2026-08-20 and the glass script still declines to take one. THE CAUSE NOW HAS A READER, 2026-09-02 (wa5). `axkit select Settings` still fails, and the campaign still has no Settings capture newer than 2026-08-20 -- unchanged. What has changed is that the age is no longer invisible: `bin/glass-build-gate.py` reports `evidence/shots/SURF-011.build.png` and `evidence/ax/SURF-011.*` as STALE against the build this tree would produce, so the lane cannot be green over them again without somebody re-taking them. `bin/capture-mac-glass.sh`'s refusal to photograph a select that did not take is the other half and is unchanged. Both halves of the remaining work -- a route to the Settings SCENE, and the re-capture -- are macOS work and are not attempted here. CLOSED 2026-10-19 on glass. capture-mac-glass.sh opens Settings with ⌘, (backgrounded), selects the Router pane in the Settings window's own source list, photographs that window as SURF-011 (target app://mac/settings), dumps the Security pane as a second dump of the same surface, and closes the window. glass-assert at the current build: checked=435 failures=0; --decoy SURF-011 reddens 6.
subject.title: `Settings` is no longer a sidebar row, so the glass capture filed a neighbouring board's pixels under SURF-011 — and the committed glass evidence predates M22

subject.detail: DETECTOR DEFECT in test-campaign 0.9.2, found 21 Aug 2026. attach-shots.py iterates every image under evidence/shots and assigns `hit['shot'] = rel` on each match, last write wins, with no preference for a build capture over a design render. This campaign keeps six directories under evidence/shots (16 root, 8 design-size, 16 fidelity, 9 ios, 17 mock, 11 mock-hidpi), so for SURF-001 the candidates in iteration order are SURF-001.build.png, SURF-001.shell.png, mock/SURF-001.png, mock-hidpi/SURF-001.full.png -- and the last one wins. MEASURED for SURF-001, SURF-002 and SURF-006: `--apply` would repoint each surface's `shot` from its build capture to `evidence/shots/mock-hidpi/SURF-00N.full.png`, which is the render of the DESIGN, not the build. That is the skill's own headline failure mode -- publishing a picture of one thing under the name of another -- arriving in a sibling of the plane built to prevent it, and it would do so while every other gate stayed green, because capture-lineage.py gates the 16 captures cited by CASES and the surface wall is a different population. The report compounds it: the UNCORROBORATED block prints surface ids (SURF-001 ... SURF-011) rather than the file each verdict is about, so a reader sees eleven surfaces apparently lacking provenance when in fact each surface's ACTUAL `shot` field points at a corroborated build capture and the complaint is about a mock render nobody intended to attach. Distinguishing the two costs a re-derivation of the matcher by hand. Recorded rather than patched, precedent DEF-048, DEF-051, DEF-052 and DEF-053. The campaign's standing refusal to run `--apply` here predates this and was based on the DEF-006 mis-wire; it now has a measured mechanism behind it. Separately closed while investigating: this campaign's design-size captures carried their provenance in a second manifest, evidence/shots/design-size/captures.json, in a different schema ({captures:[...]} against the root's bare list) that no gate reads. Its 8 entries were merged into the root manifest with `target` derived from the root's declared target for the same subject and corroborated by each capture's own windowTitleReadback -- Servers, Activity, Skills, Discover, Inbox, Checks, Cleanup, Settings, every one matching -- recorded at capture time, and each carries `targetDerivedFrom` saying so. That was the campaign's own inconsistency and is fixed here; it was not the cause of the 11. RE-MEASURED 2026-08-27 (G21) after `evidence/shots/captures.json` was made a derived file. The uncorroborated count is 12 and stays 12: SURF-001..011 and SURF-022. Eleven of them are this defect -- `mock-hidpi/` sorts last, so it is the row that decides each surface's `shotProvenance`. The mock rows in the manifest deliberately carry NO `target`; the address the channel was pointed at is recorded in full as `renderedFrom`, with an `attachHazard` field naming this defect. Measured both ways on this tree: writing that address as `target` instead drops the uncorroborated count from 12 to 1 and DISARMS `--apply`'s refusal, because `attach-shots.py` only checks the field is present and never compares it to the subject's route -- which is item 5 of X8's work order. So the report going quiet would have been this defect getting worse while looking fixed. The twelfth, SURF-022, is not this defect: see DEF-061.
subject.title: attach-shots --apply would attach the design mock render as the build's surface shot for 11 surfaces, and its report names the surface rather than the file

subject.detail: Found 20 Aug 2026 while building R8's gate against both routers. Against a fixture returning `-32603` with the message `Internal error: Authentication required`, the reference records `MCP error -32603: Internal error: Authentication required` and the Swift router records `[-32603] Internal error`. The upstream's own message is gone. CAUSE, cited exactly: modelcontextprotocol/swift-sdk 0.12.1, `Sources/MCP/Base/Error.swift:217-240`. The decoder reads the server's `message`, then maps the code — `-32700`, `-32600`, `-32601` and `-32602` each pass `unwrapDetail(message)`, and `-32603` alone passes `unwrapDetail(nil)`. `unwrapDetail(fallback)` returns `data.detail` when present and the fallback otherwise, so a server that answers -32603 with a message and no `data.detail` has its message discarded, and `Error.swift:91` renders `"Internal error" + (detail.map { ": \($0)" } ?? "")` as the bare canonical name. -32603 is the code servers use for an arbitrary application error, so it is the one that loses the most. TWO consequences: for the whole class of -32603 upstream errors the Swift router tells the user strictly less than the reference does; and R8's Swift half cannot detect a credential refusal at all, because there is no text left to match. This is a coverage gap in the parity suite as much as a defect in the SDK — no parity scenario had ever exercised a JSON-RPC error carrying a detailed message, which is why 82 proven rows never saw it. Remedies, none taken: report upstream and take a fixed release; pin a patched fork; or read the JSON-RPC error before the SDK types it, which needs a seam below the client.
subject.title: the Swift MCP SDK discards an upstream's error message for code -32603, so the router reports less than the reference does

subject.detail: parity-gate.sh, 20 Aug 2026 on main at e5755d0. The suite lane's citation run of scripts/acceptance/parity-oauth.sh exited non-zero and recorded `control-auth-post-http fail — the Swift router never reached the token endpoint`. The dedicated oauth lane, later in the same gate, ran the same script and recorded ok over 21 checks. The gate reported the row DIVERGED and printed 81 of 83. WHY IT IS UNEXPLAINED, established 21 Aug 2026 from disk without re-running anything. The run survives as evidence/runs/parity-gate-2026-08-20-oauth-flake.log, written 20:39:30. Its line 163 is the whole of what the citation run reported: `FAIL scripts/acceptance/parity-oauth.sh the gate reported findings`, and the next line is the following `ok` row. The script itself does not fail that quietly -- its failure branch (parity-oauth.sh:308-329) prints the POST /auth status, the browser hop, the tail of the router log and the first 20 requests the provider saw. Every one of those bytes existed and was discarded by the caller: `parity-suite.sh`'s `run_script` sent both streams to /dev/null at the time. So this defect is not a run that left no diagnostic, it is a run whose diagnostic the harness threw away, and no amount of re-reading the log can recover it. The instrument was repaired in commit 21d559b at 20:41:28 -- one minute and 58 seconds after this log was written, in the same commit that recorded the defect -- so `run_script` now keeps the log and prints its last 20 lines inline. A recurrence would therefore arrive with the cause attached. That is what closes this: the next occurrence, not more thought about this one. It stays open because there is still no cause and no reproduction; what changed is that the reason it could not be diagnosed is now known and no longer true. One candidate mechanism examined and NOT adopted. The R9 lane reported (21 Aug 2026, via uds:/tmp/cc-socks/9881.sock) that a stale $TMPDIR/mcp-router-parity.lock had made a gate fail its manifest-check for a non-real reason. That is a different symptom -- a manifest-check failure before the comparison, against this defect's completed run that reached `control-auth-post-http` and recorded a row -- and parity-oauth.sh takes that same lock at line 126 and preflights every port at 143-145, so the two lanes inside one gate could not have overlapped. Recorded as ruled out rather than left unmentioned, so the next reader does not spend the lead twice.
subject.text: Observed once, in one of two whole-gate runs, and not reproduced by: a standalone run of `parity-oauth.sh`, a second standalone run of it immediately afterwards (which exercised the same port-reuse wait, 9s and 12s), a standalone run of `parity-suite.sh`, or a second whole `parity-gate.sh` on the same tree. The second gate reported 82 of 83, 0 DIVERGED, and its suite lane reported the citation clean. **What it is not.** The lane distinguishes an environment failure from a finding on purpose, and this was the finding branch: `record control-auth-post-http fail` at `parity-oauth.sh:329`, reached only when the reference side completed an authorization and the Swift side did not. An unbindable port exits 2 through `wait_for_ports_bindable` and records `blocked`, not `fail`, so the port-reuse race is ruled out by the code path that fired. **Why it went undiagnosed, and what changed.** `parity-suite.sh`'s `run_script` sent both streams to `/dev/null` and printed `the gate reported findings` — a verdict with no evidence under it. The bytes naming which guard failed had already been thrown away by the time anyone read the gate's summary. `run_script` now keeps the log, prints its last 20 lines inline and names the file it kept, armed 20 Aug 2026 against a deliberately failing citation. A recurrence will say which of the 21 checks went red. **Why the duplicate run stays.** `control-auth-post-http` is proven on the wire by its own lane and also cites the script, so the gate runs it twice. That is now documented in `parity-suite.sh` rather than deduplicated, because the duplicate is what caught this: a single run would have reported a clean 82 of 83 and nobody would have known. Both record under the same row id and a `fail` wins. **Burn-in, 20 Aug 2026: 8 standalone runs of the lane, all green, 21 checks each.** Three immediately after the failure and five consecutively afterwards, plus one clean whole gate. One failure in roughly ten whole-lane executions, cause unrecoverable because that invocation's stdout was discarded. A green burn-in does not close this: the original failure is uninspectable, so the runs measure only that the lane is not reliably broken. What would close it is a captured reproduction, or a stated gate met — several consecutive whole gates including the cold port-reuse path — decided as its own question rather than inferred from a streak, which is the `install-launchd-watch` mistake this repository already paid for once (G1: name a fix per term and fix a bound IN ADVANCE, never a green streak). Not a UI defect and not a blocker on the cutover count — CASE-0036's measurement is the second run — but it is an unexplained non-determinism in the router or the lane, and it is recorded rather than absorbed.
subject.title: the OAuth parity lane failed once inside a full gate and has not reproduced

subject.detail: The lane built with CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO, so the app carried no keychain access group and SecItemCopyMatching returned -34018 errSecMissingEntitlement rather than errSecItemNotFound. PairingRecordStore maps the two apart correctly, so the phone's Settings surface rendered "Can't read this phone's pairing" on a device that had simply never been paired. That was recorded as DEF-X2-b, a suspected product defect. It is a lane defect: built with CODE_SIGN_IDENTITY=- the same assertion passes and the test proceeds 54 lines further. The Makefile now carries a SIGNED variable used by test-ios-glass alone, with the measurement in a comment beside it. The general lesson is the one the campaign keeps relearning — a harness flag can manufacture a finding that reads exactly like the product's own.
subject.title: the ios-glass lane built unsigned, and an unsigned build cannot read the keychain

subject.note: F7. `Analyse now` actuated, and the outcome read on a channel the press did not write. The board posts once and then draws what a SECOND `GET /insights` returned; the staging client answers that read differently before and after, so “the board redrew from the router” and “the board did nothing” are not the same picture. The same-channel reads declined are the button's own callback returning and `analysing` falling back to false. Both survive an empty body — which is exactly the control this item replaced.

F7. The same control from the router's side, and the strongest reading of it: `POST /insights/analyse` through `ControlHandler.handle`, then a separate `GET /insights` that reports the run. The POST's own 200 is not the oracle — the later GET is, and it is a different request through a different arm of the dispatch table.

F7. The three configuration menus the design draws and the build replaced with an empty state — `Analyst model`, `Second-opinion model` and `Analyst cadence`. Each patches exactly one member and leaves the other two nil, which is what stops a press on the cadence menu from re-asserting a model the user did not touch. Asserted as the three patch payloads the client received, in order.

F7. What the analyst read and what it refused to say. The corpus reports a positive `linesRead`, a named discard count and every store it did not open with the reason — including Cursor's, which is enumerated and deliberately unread. A recommendation naming an entry outside the candidate list, or a signal the run never counted, is rejected and COUNTED rather than dropped, so an engine that discarded everything is distinguishable from one that was handed nothing.

parity-gate.sh on main at e5755d0, 20 Aug 2026: **82 of 83 rows proven (4 of them by suite only, not by wire comparison), 0 DIVERGED, 1 blocked.** REQ-014's contract is the owner's cutover target of 82 of 83 with `fixture-registry-search` a standing exclusion, and that is what was measured. The two rows that stood between 80 and 82 closed the same day: `install-launchd-watch` by ai/p8, which made the `reran` term attributable — it had read yes on 2 of 6 decoy trials where no stimulus could reach the watched path — and `control-auth-post-http` by ai/p7, which built a real OAuth client and now agrees with the reference across the discovery cascade, the registration bytes, the PKCE parameters, the token exchange, the callback page, the credential file and the re-authorization branch. **The gate exits 1 and that is not this case failing.** It exits 1 while any row is blocked, deliberately, and the one blocked row is the standing exclusion the requirement names. The gate prints the distinction itself: `82 proven is at or past the target of 82. That is a count, not a licence`. Read as a pass on the requirement, not as a licence to flip the installer — that is the owner's call on R4-C's evidence, which this case does not make. **Armed, and one arm was not planned.** The mechanical arm is `parity-lane-selftest`, which runs every lane against a deliberately broken Swift router and requires each to go red; it ran green in the same `make all` that carried this tree, printing `every new lane went red against a broken router. The lanes can fail.` The unplanned arm is the first whole-gate run of the day, kept at `evidence/runs/parity-gate-2026-08-20-oauth-flake.log`: the same script on the same tree reported `81 of 83 rows proven … 1 DIVERGED … This is NOT a pass`, so the aggregate verdict is live rather than a constant. That run's cause is unexplained and is recorded as DEF-033 rather than absorbed into this note.

The R19-INT merge that did happen is `ff05efd4`, 2026-08-24, "Merge R19-INT: Stale manifest snapshot clobbers concurrent write (gap-fix 4 verified at 79d40ee)".

cell.dataShape: two claims inside one renotify window

subject.note: R26. The throttle withholds a REPEAT and never an ESCALATION. The brief asks that a recurring error not generate alert spam, and the naive reading -- one alert per server per window -- swallows the one transition that matters. Four things make a notice due: nothing has been said yet, the KIND changed, the EXPIRY moved, or the window elapsed. E13 runs with `renotifyAfterMs` set to a year so nothing can go out on elapsed time, watches `expiring` become `expired` one millisecond past the boundary, and then asserts the repeat after it IS withheld -- so the arm is the escalation rather than the throttle being broken.

R26. Reading the report does not consume the notice; claiming it does. That is why there are two routes rather than one: folding them together would make `GET /upstreams/auth-expiry` spend the notification a caller was about to be shown, so opening a settings pane would silence the next alert. It is the same rule this repository enforces on its own gates -- a check that mutates the tree as a side effect of checking is not a check. E16 asserts it on the monitor and E24 through the routes; the lane asserts it as `count:2` after two GETs.

cell.dataShape: a credential record with no expires_in

subject.note: R26. THE VACUITY CASE, and the reason this item exists in the shape it does. A token whose stored record declares no lifetime has no derivable expiry, and the tempting reading -- it has not expired, therefore it is fine -- is the class this campaign keeps finding: a state that reads healthy because nothing measured it. `AuthExpiryRecord.state` has NO path from a missing number to `valid`; it returns `unknown` and the wire carries `unknownReason` saying which half is missing (`no-lifetime-declared` when `expires_in` is absent, `unreadable-authorized-at` when the stamp is). Asserted at both planes: E5/E6/E17/E21 in the suites, and the lane reads `state`, `unknownReason` and the ABSENCE of any invented `expiresAt` off a record it planted itself. Not `expiresAt: null` -- absent, so there is nothing there for a careless reader to round to fine.

cell.dataShape: an authExpiry block below the floor

subject.note: R26. A configured value the router will not take is REFUSED and reported with its key, its value as written, the floor that rejected it and its scope -- never clamped. A clamp invents a number nobody wrote, so the file says 500 and the behaviour is 60000 with nothing anywhere saying which is real. `warnWithinMs`'s floor is this item's own vacuity rule and ZERO IS NOT ACCEPTED: at zero a token passes straight from valid to expired and `expiring` is unreachable, which is R27's `tripAfter >= 2` one item earlier. E2 asserts that in both directions -- under a zero window a token one millisecond from death reads `valid`, and under the resolved policy the same token reads `expiring`.

cell.dataShape: a credential re-authorised between two claims

subject.note: R26. *Resolving authentication immediately clears the warning status* -- the brief's third bullet, and it is a CLEAR rather than an age-out. A server that stops deserving a notice has its delivery record DROPPED, so the next thing that goes wrong is reported at once instead of waiting out a six-hour window. The lane proves it against a wall clock: it re-authorises the record from outside, claims, breaks it again, claims again, and the notice arrives seconds later under the default six-hour renotify. A throttle that merely aged out could not produce that. The absence half is paired -- a SECOND server is broken in the same step, so 'the re-authorised one is gone' is read off a reply that carries another server rather than off an empty one.

cell.dataShape: no monitor, and the wrong verb, token and content type

subject.note: R26. With no monitor both routes answer 503 NAMING the missing capability, the shape `/harnesses`, `/extensions`, `/caches` and `/upstreams/health` use -- an empty report would be indistinguishable from a router holding no credentials at all. Beside it the wire refusals: 405 on the wrong verb for each path, 401 untokened, 415 with no content type, and a 404 rather than a 405 on `/upstreams/auth-expiryx`, because claiming a prefix collision would turn a typo into an answer that reads as 'the method is wrong'.

cell.dataShape: five upstreams, four planted records, one stdio server

subject.note: R26. THE PAIRED ABSENCE, and the load-bearing case. The claim is that the expiry is DERIVED from files the router already wrote rather than asked of the upstream, and half of that claim is an absence: nothing was spawned. An absence asserted alone is satisfied by a feature that does nothing, which is REQ-035's recorded lesson. So the lane never asserts it alone. It reads the daemon's child count off the process table -- zero, and zero running the stdio fixture's own script -- in the same run in which it REWRITES a planted credential record between two requests and requires the reported `expiresAt` and `state` to move with it. Zero children beside a report that follows the file is the claim; zero children alone is not.

subject.note: The surface DENOMINATOR reconciled against the product rather than against itself. R1 every id in DestinationCatalog.All has a surface row; R2 every Label is a declared control on the shell surface; R3 every requirement sourced from app/windows/ that has a case reaches a surface that exists; R4 every Windows surface declaring controls says where the list came from, and every control it names appears verbatim in the files that source names. Typing a row into inventory.json cannot make R1, R2 or R4 pass. It found two real things on the tree it was written against: SURF-045's controlsSource named a path that does not exist (LogonTaskSupervisor.cs is under Lifecycle/), and SURF-030 declared a control called 'NavigationView pane' that appears in no source file at all. WHAT IT DOES NOT CHECK: that a declared control is drawn, reachable, or does anything - that is control-census.py's actuated count and the UIA lane behind it - and that a board's list is COMPLETE, because affordances built in a DataTemplate or in code-behind carry no literal a static reader can see. Every such row says so in its controlsSourceNote and the count is a floor.

subject.note: WHAT THIS ROW SPEAKS FOR, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It measures the NODE reference only. `swift` and `xcodebuild` are absent on this machine, so nothing here is a Swift test result and this case must not be read as coverage of `AuthRoutes.promote`; the Swift side of REQ-019 is still carried by `ControlApproveDispatchTests` and this campaign has not run it. Three arms over the shipped `handleControl` out of `dist/`: a writable home answering 200 with `pending` gone from disk; the same call with the save's temp path occupied by a directory, answering 500 with the errno message and `pending` still on disk; and the occupation removed, answering 200 again. The denial is the filesystem's own `EISDIR` at exactly the step that makes the change durable - not a mocked `FileSystem` - and the lock sidecar and the manifest read are left working on purpose, because a denial that also stopped the lock would produce a 500 carrying the LOCK's sentence and prove nothing about the save. ACLs were tried first and are recorded in the lane's header as a control that did not arm: `icacls <file> /deny <user>:(D,WD,AD,WEA,WA)` and `icacls <dir> /deny <user>:(DC)` both apply, read back as DENY aces, and `renameSync` over the target succeeds anyway on this machine. An ACL that is set and does not bite produces a green arm that never armed, which is why the temp-path occupation replaced it. What it found: the reference answers 500, so Swift's pre-R21 200 was a divergence and R21's change closed it (DEF-442), while the error BODIES still differ (DEF-441). `deps.liveReload` and `deps.manifest` are stubs - they are the announcement collaborators the 200 path calls after the write - and the route, the lock, `loadManifest` and `saveManifest` are the shipped ones.

Node's `POST /servers/:name/approve` against a manifest write the filesystem refuses answers `500` with `{"error":"<the errno message verbatim>"}` - the run recorded `{"error":"EISDIR: illegal operation on a directory, open '...\\manifest.json.tmp-4752'"}` - and leaves `pending` on disk. subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=one capability queued
subject.note: The toast itself, in the Action Center, read by a process that cannot raise one. DEF-082 filed this as unmeasurable and gave a reason: UserNotificationListener's userNotificationListener capability is only grantable to a packaged application, and MCPRouter.Shell is WindowsPackageType=None, so the row was said to be downstream of WIN19's MSIX. THE REASON WAS WRONG, AND IT WAS WRONG BEFORE WIN19 LANDED. Measured on this host from an ordinary unpackaged Win32 console process with no package identity at all - Package.Current throws InvalidOperationException, which the lane asserts rather than assumes - UserNotificationListener.Current resolves, RequestAccessAsync returns Allowed with no consent prompt, and GetNotificationsAsync returns the toasts that are really there. On the first run those included three raised by win22-toast-witness the day before, carrying the exact strings NotificationPresentation writes. No MSIX, no capability, no packaged identity. WHAT IS STILL NOT AVAILABLE UNPACKAGED, and it bounds this case: every member of UserNotification.AppInfo throws NotImplementedException 0x80004001 for a caller with no package identity, so the listener can say what a notification SAYS and when it arrived and cannot say who raised it. Attribution here is the payload text, which the product owns, inside a time window this run opened - weaker than a publisher identity, and recorded as such. THE RECORDER IS NOT THE WRITER AND IS NOT EVEN THE SAME PROCESS: app/windows/MCPRouter.Witness.ActionCenter shares no code with the shell and cannot raise a notification. The shell's toast-probe.json is carried as the writer's self-report and graded by nothing. THE PRESENCE CONTROL is a removal: the matched notification is taken back out through the listener and the Action Center is read a third time, and the recorder is required to say no about it.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=one capability queued
subject.note: The COM activator the Windows notification platform wrote, read out of the registry by a process that did not write it. The writer is AppNotificationManager.Register() inside the shell; the recorder is HKCU through PowerShell's registry provider, and nothing of this repository's sits between them. Four arms. BASELINE requires the AUMID key to be ABSENT before the shell launches, so what the other three read is this launch. The three EFFECT arms read the key, the CustomActivator CLSID it names, and that CLSID's LocalServer32 - which came back as MCPRouter.Shell.exe carrying the platform's own ----AppNotificationActivated: argument, a string this repository does not write anywhere. THE ACTIVATOR IS THE ARM THAT CARRIES THE ITEM. A toast outlives the process that raised it; when somebody presses Review an hour later, Windows COM-activates the LocalServer32 registered for that CLSID. Without it the toast still appears and pressing it does nothing, which is the failure that looks most like success and exactly what a screenshot of a notification would have certified. WHAT THIS CASE DOES NOT SETTLE: that a toast is drawn, and that a press re-activates the app. Both need UserNotificationListener, whose capability is only grantable to a packaged application; DEF-082 carries them and is downstream of DEF-073. The shell's own report that the platform accepted a Show is carried in the evidence as writerSelfReport and is graded by nothing, because a process reporting its own effect is the shape of claim DEF-072 was about.

subject.cell: execution-plane=windows-host - data-shape=a supervised process that dies
subject.note: The half of WIN23's supervision promise that had never been watched: a daemon the Windows task scheduler starts, loses, and starts again. DEF-081 filed it as unmeasurable and named the blocker as a missing Windows daemon binary; the blocker was real and is gone - app/windows/MCPRouter.Witness.Daemon is a harness process that starts, records its own start and waits to be killed, so there is something for the scheduler to supervise. WHAT THE MEASUREMENT FOUND IS NOT WHAT THE ROW EXPECTED. The registration the product wrote carried RestartOnFailure with a 60-second interval and a count of 3, and it did not restart the daemon at all. Killed, watched 150 seconds, on the unified scheduling engine and the legacy one, for a run started by a trigger and one started on demand: four registrations, no restart. The same block DID restart, three times at exactly 60 seconds, a task whose Command named a file that does not exist - so the instrument can see a restart, and RestartOnFailure governs a task that fails to LAUNCH rather than one whose action launched and later died. DEF-320 carries that, and the product now writes a Repetition on the trigger alongside MultipleInstancesPolicy IgnoreNew. THE RECORDERS ARE TWO AND NEITHER WROTE ANYTHING: Get-ScheduledTaskInfo for the scheduler's own account of its runs, and Get-CimInstance Win32_Process for the process identity, which is what makes 'it came back' a different process id rather than a report from the thing that came back. The daemon's own run log is carried and graded by nothing. EIGHT ARMS, THREE OF THEM ABOUT THE INSTRUMENT: BASELINE requires both tasks absent and no daemon running, so nothing below is inherited from an interrupted run; CLAIM.repetition and CLAIM.ignorenew read the product's own unmodified logon registration back through the WMI provider; SILENCE requires both recorders to say no once the tasks are gone. ONE SUBSTITUTION, SAID OUT LOUD: a trigger repetition does not apply to an on-demand start - measured, twice - so the live task carries a TimeTrigger where the product writes a LogonTrigger, because this lane must not log the machine out. Every Setting, the repetition interval, the principal, the action and the instances policy are the product's own document. That the trigger fires AT LOGON is still unwitnessed and DEF-081 keeps it.

subject.cell: execution-plane=daemon · data-shape=a request on a method the ported token gate does not cover
subject.note: ControlAPIRequest.isMutating is POST || DELETE || PATCH, ported from src/control.ts, and PUT is not in it. No route served PUT before this family, so nothing was ever exposed — but this family's write was written as a PUT, and an untokened PUT /profiles/x measured 200 while the rest of the suite was green. The write is a POST instead, because widening a ported gate that parity-manifest-check.sh derives from the reference in both directions is not a thing to do for a verb. The lane asserts the 405 on the wire and ControlProfileRoutesTests C6 holds the invariant over PUT, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE for whoever adds the next route here.

F5. A run bracketed by two version boundaries carrying different versions is counted toward NEITHER. The oracle is that the version's run total does not move, and the same test removes the later boundary and requires it to move, so the assertion is watched being able to change its answer. Without the second half this passes against an implementation that credits every historical run to the installed version, which is the defect the whole item exists to refuse (spec-F5.md 2.2).

F5. The serialised key set of an InvocationEvent is exactly ts, kind, name, harness. Driven from a fixture transcript line that carries a cwd naming a project and an args carrying prompt text; neither may appear in the output. InvocationEvent.wireKeys is asserted alongside, so a fifth member added later reddens this rather than shipping. The privacy claim in spec-F5.md 3 is worth what fails when it stops being true.

F5. The incremental scan. Scanning an unchanged file twice must yield the same events as scanning it once and must not open it the second time; a file that shrank must be re-read from zero and say so in filesReread. The corpus is 59,476 files and 19.5 GB (measured 2026-08-29), so the watermark is what makes the reader answerable inside a request rather than an optimisation.

subject.evidence: vacuous
subject.note: R26. It inherits R27's rule (REQ-029) and meets it by not needing it: a health probe of a stdio upstream IS a child process, so R27 defaults background probing off and never lets a scheduled sweep cold-start. An expiry needs no probe at all, so this feature arms no task, holds no timer and spawns nothing — which is why it is ON by default where health probing is off. The vacuity rule is `warnWithinMs`'s floor of 60000 with zero REFUSED: at zero a token passes straight from valid to expired, `expiring` is unreachable, and the promise 'you are told before it stops working' would hold only because nothing can enter the state it names. R27's tripAfter floor of 2 is the same rule one item earlier. The `mobbin` lesson is carried into the notification rather than rediscovered: with a refresh token held, no command is offered, because telling its owner to re-authorise sends them round a loop that cannot succeed.
subject.text: The router says when an upstream's credential is running out or has been refused, before a tool call fails on it — and it can say that it does not know. Expiry is DERIVED from what the router already holds (`authorizedAt` + `expires_in` in the record it wrote when the flow settled), never asked of the upstream, so nothing is spawned to answer the question. A token whose record declares no lifetime reads `unknown` carrying the reason, and there is no path from a missing number to `valid`. A configured value the router will not take is reported as refused with its scope rather than clamped in silence. Repetition is throttled and escalation is not: a warning becoming an expiry, and an expiry moving because the credential was replaced, go out at once, and re-authorising CLEARS the warning rather than ageing it out.

The sheet's pixels: `SURF-007.provenance-sheet.png`, 633476 bytes, sha d48520a1a99d, window-scoped off the CGWindowID the launched pid owns, recorded in `evidence/shots/captures.json` with the `cleanupSkills` scenario that produced it and the title read back off the running app. The claim is that this surface exists as drawn output rather than as a view struct: an AXSheet at 512×416 inside the window, with the copy the case above enumerates. It does NOT claim agreement with the design of record, and here that is the point rather than a caveat — the design's version of this sheet states four things the router cannot observe, so agreement with it would be the defect.

The document response crossing a real kernel socket, seen by a party that is not the router. The six cases above read status codes and bodies back through urllib, which proves the route answered but takes the router's own word for how the bytes travelled; this takes the kernel's. `bin/witness-document-socket.sh` starts the SHIPPED router against a scratch home, then holds a socket open with a real `GET /servers/constructed-served/document` written into it while lsof(8) samples the socket table. Before: 1 LISTEN row on 8983 owned by the pid the shell launched, 0 on the decoy. During: 4 ESTABLISHED rows, 1 of them owned by the router pid — the ACCEPTED half, which is the half that proves the process took the connection rather than merely reserving the port; 0 on the decoy. The 589 bytes read straight off that socket begin `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` and contain the fixture's read me sentinel, so the connection lsof saw is the one that carried this route's document. After the process is killed: 0 LISTEN rows. The server is CONSTRUCTED and labelled so: 0 of the 21 upstreams on this machine declares a package directory, so this route 404s noPackageDirectory for all of them and no real package here reaches this outcome.

NO PICTURE IS FILED HERE, AND THE REASON IS A MEASUREMENT RATHER THAN A SHRUG. `screencapture -x -l<CGWindowID>` against this window returns whatever surface the window server last composited, and against a LIVE launch that is behind everything that is nothing: window chrome, a title, and not even the sidebar. It exits 0 while doing it. The first two runs of this lane filed those frames. The cold and stale pictures came back byte-identical to each other — sha 84a469099e7c, 267622 bytes both — while their accessibility trees differed by 26 rows, so the pictures agreed about a state the app was not in and nothing in the capture channel said so. That is the defect `bin/capture-mac-glass.sh` already refuses in its own form, one plane over. The cause is measured. A FIXTURE launch photographs correctly, because `FixtureControlAPIClient` has its data at the first render and the first paint therefore carries the board — which is why nine years of this campaign's glass captures had never met this. A live launch does not, and the window never recovers: watched for 16 seconds at 2-second intervals, the same dump that reports a 980x620 window reports its sidebar at y=-537 with a height of 1964 on every single sample. Hide-then-unhide, a navigate-away-and-back reselect and a resize were each tried and each left the surface byte-identical. So `bin/paint-check.py` refuses the frame — the sidebar's rectangle is not inside the window's, which is an exact invariant of a laid-out window rather than a threshold — and the harness deletes it and records why. The state itself is not unmeasured: CASE-0197 holds it in the AX plane, over the same run. What is missing is the evidence that it reached the SCREEN, and that is stated rather than substituted.

subject.note: Each of the shell's three top-level unhandled-exception handlers made to fire on purpose, and the line it wrote read back out of shell-startup.log by a process that did not write it, after the process that did had exited. THIS CASE EXISTS BECAUSE REGISTRATION IS NOT FIRING. DEF-079 was raised on sixteen launches that wrote no `unhandled:` line including eight that terminated at 0xC000027B, and it stayed open through the fix - two more handlers registered - because none of the three had been observed catching anything. App.xaml.cs takes `--fault <ui|appdomain|task|dispatcher>`, compiled out outside DEBUG and inert unless passed; win-shell-unhandled-witness.ps1 launches the shell once per kind. FOUR ARMS. BASELINE is a launch with NO --fault and requires its region of the log to hold `launched` and no `unhandled:` line, which is what makes the three EFFECT lines the injection's rather than startup's; and every arm reads only the bytes appended after its own launch, so a line an earlier run left behind cannot satisfy one. The three EFFECT arms then require, each after its own fault, `unhandled: [xaml]` for a throw on the UI thread inside XAML's dispatch of OnLaunched, `unhandled: [appdomain terminating=True]` for a throw on a non-UI foreground thread, and `unhandled: [unobserved-task]` for a faulted task nobody awaits after a collection and WaitForPendingFinalizers. All four held. WHAT THIS CASE DOES NOT SETTLE, and what has since moved. The DispatcherQueue route ran here as an UNGRADED probe while DEF-085 was open. subject.detail: Three consecutive runs, same build, same booted iPhone 16 Pro, no product change between them: run 1 failed 3 of 5, runs 2 and 3 failed 4 of 5. The case that moved is `tapping 'X' did not produce a navigation bar titled 'X'` — green for all five tabs in run 1, red on the first tab in runs 2 and 3. The only edit between run 1 and run 2 was adding XCTAttachment captures to a different test, so the code under assertion did not change. A plausible mechanism is DEF-008: the tab button's accessibility identifier is the SF Symbol name while its label is the tab title, so `buttons["Discover"]` resolves on one attribute or the other depending on which the tree publishes first. Not diagnosed further here — this campaign records the instrument's reliability rather than repairing another branch's test. Consequence: the lane's outcome-rung claims are recorded inconclusive, because green twice is the campaign's own bar and this lane did not clear it. CLOSED 20 Aug 2026. Diagnosed from run 3's exported App UI hierarchy: at the failure the navigation bar's identifier was 'Settings' and the Settings tab carried Selected, so the opening tap had never landed. Run 1 passed because a freshly installed app launches on Discover, making its first selectTab a no-op; runs 2 and 3 restored to Settings and tapped a tab bar that existed but was not yet hittable. Existence is not hittability. `selectTab` now waits on a `hittable == true` predicate and retries the tap up to three times against the tab button's own `isSelected`, which is the tab bar's answer to 'which tab am I on'. Green twice since, across all three affected tests. DEF-008 was not the mechanism.

subject.text: CAUSE FOUND AND FIXED 20 Aug 2026; this record replaces one that said the cause was unknown and named machine saturation as a candidate. The candidate was wrong. The process-wide accessibility engine was OFF, so SwiftUI's `_UIHostingView` built its accessibility container and vended an EMPTY element array — `accessibilityElements == []`, not nil — and every label assertion in the target read empty and reported its own honest verdict, `nothing was measured, so this proved nothing`. That is indistinguishable, from inside the suite, from a product that renders no copy. A probe settled it: calling `_AXSSetAutomationEnabled(true)` took the same hosted view's published element count from 0 to 1. THE ENGINE HAD BEEN ON BY ACCIDENT — something else on this machine had switched it on — which is why this suite was green for months while depending on ambient host state no file in this repo controls, and why it went red with no change to the branch. THREE CHANGES ARE THE FIX, and the third was found only because the first two were not enough. (1) `PhoneSurfaceTests` resolves `_AXSSetAutomationEnabled` out of `/usr/lib/libAccessibility.dylib` (falling back to `AccessibilityUtilities.framework`) via dlopen/dlsym and calls it once per process, before the first `host()`. (2) The walker reads `accessibilityElements` first, because SwiftUI publishes through the array and leaves `accessibilityElementCount()` at 0 — measured on iOS 26.5, where one hosted `Text` reported `accessibilityElements.count == 1` and `accessibilityElementCount() == 0` in the same breath, so reading only the indexed API walked past every element SwiftUI had. Those two took `make test-ios` from 52 failures to 0 — and then `make all`, run immediately afterwards on the same device, came back with 39. (3) THE STATE IS DEVICE-SCOPED AND THE CALL LANDS ON THE NEXT PROCESS, NOT THIS ONE. On a device left in the disabled state, the run that re-enables it fails a DETERMINISTIC set of 15 test cases — identical set, measured three times, verified with `comm` in both directions — and the run after it, with no change to anything, is clean. The 15 are exactly the cases that host a `ScrollView`; the tests that pass alongside them are geometry, counts and negative assertions, all of which an empty tree satisfies, so the green half of that run was vacuous too. `test-ios` therefore runs a throwaway single-test process before the graded one and discards its exit code. MEASURED END TO END: three consecutive runs with the call mutated to `(false)` drive `MCPRouter-Unit` into the disabled state (54 failures each, the whole suite red, which is correct for a dead engine); the very next `make test-ios`, with the warm-up in the recipe, is 36 tests and 0 failures in 1.4s. THE INSTRUMENT CHECK IS ITSELF INSTRUMENTED. `testTheAccessibilityEngineCanBeSwitchedOn` blocks on a probe that hosts `ScrollView { Text }` and reads it back through the same walk every other assertion uses, with a 20s deadline. Two narrower probes were built first and both were wrong in opposite directions, which is why the shape is stated rather than assumed: a bare `Text` read either way reports the engine live at t=0 of a run in which 15 cases went on to read empty, and a `ScrollView` read through the accessibility-container path alone reports the engine dead on a device where all 35 other tests pass. A probe that answers differently from the thing it stands for answers a different question. On a dead engine the deadline fires and the case fails with `no hosted Text published a label within 20s`, measured. ARMED THREE WAYS. (a) Renaming the symbol to `_AXSSetAutomationEnabledXXX` on a device whose engine is already live fails exactly one test — the instrument check — and leaves the other 35 green, which is correct for that arm and proves only the resolution assertion. (b) With the call mutated to `(false)`, the first run on `MCPRouter-Arm`, a device created for the arm, recorded 53 failures across 36 tests: that is what proves the other 35 depend on the engine. (c) The first run ever taken on `MCPRouter-Arm2`, a device whose engine had never been live, is 36 tests and 0 failures, so a fresh device needs no warm-up and only an explicitly disabled one does. Both arm devices were deleted afterwards; `make test-ios IOS_UNIT_DEVICE=<name>` recreates either. TWO HARDENING CHANGES from the investigation are kept and neither is the fix: `test-ios` creates and owns `MCPRouter-Unit` instead of sorting booted devices first — the exact picker DEF-020 condemned, still live in this recipe — and the walk retains every element it visits so `ObjectIdentifier` is unique among live objects as its use assumes. A third, waiting on a product surface's tree over a two-second deadline, was written, measured to change nothing, and removed: it cost 130 seconds a run and bought no measurement. The wait that IS kept differs from it in the one way that matters — it waits on a probe whose answer is known, so a timeout is a fact about the instrument rather than about the view. THE DEPENDENCY IS ON A PRIVATE SYMBOL, in the test target only, never linked into the app; the instrument check fails loudly if a future runtime renames it, so this target goes red rather than quietly empty. Carried as CASE-0126.
subject.title: the iOS unit lane read an empty accessibility tree because the engine was off

subject.text: Measured 20 Aug 2026. `make test` failed with 4 issues at a one-minute load average of ~700 and passed all 1473 tests in 179 suites at load 46, on the same source, minutes apart. The four were `ActivityReconnectTests` (`a reconnect over a feed that stays live releases its guard`), `DiscoverBoardTests` (`client.searchQueries.count` reading 1 where the baseline said 2), and `SettingsAndMenuBarTests` twice (`model.trackerState` still nil). An earlier run at the same load failed only the first, so the set was not stable either — which is what separated this from a product defect. A suite that reports a defect the product does not have is the failure this campaign has already paid for once, in DEF-029, where a dead instrument read as a dead product for ten consecutive runs. CLOSED by making each wait a condition rather than a deadline, at three sites: 1. `ShellTestSupport.waitUntil` — ceiling 5s → 30s. It returns the moment the condition holds, so a passing test pays nothing for the larger bound; the bound exists only so a condition that never arrives fails instead of hanging. Five seconds was inside the scheduling noise of a contended host, which is the whole finding. 2. `ActivityReconnectTests.completes` — 2s → 30s, same argument. The defect it bounds is a call that *never* returns, so it exhausts any budget and a generous one costs only the time a genuine hang takes to report. 3. `DiscoverBoardTests.searchIsDebounced` — a fixed sleep replaced by two waits, because the claim has two halves and one sleep proved neither on a slow host. First a bounded wait for the debounce to fire at all; then a full debounce window of quiet with the count still at one, which is what rules out one request per keystroke. The second is a real quiet period rather than a deadline, so load cannot shorten it into a false pass — the wait on its own is satisfied by the *first* request and would pass against exactly the defect this test exists to catch. Armed 20 Aug 2026, all three, each watched to fail with its own message: `waitUntil` at `.seconds(0)` reads `no poll ran at all`, `the poll died with the scene that started it` and `five keystrokes issued 0 requests`; `completes` at `.milliseconds(1)` reads `reconnect did not return while the feed stayed live`; and a `queryChanged()` inserted inside the quiet period reads `a later request arrived: five keystrokes issued 2 requests in total`. The original trigger is not reproducible on demand from here — the load came from another project's Rust test binary, two node processes and `lsdiagnose` — so the fix is proven by the arms rather than by reproducing the contention.
subject.title: four async package tests asserted on a deadline the machine could miss

subject.text: Measured 20 Aug 2026 on two different worktrees the same afternoon. A fresh `git worktree` has no `node_modules` and no `dist`; `parity-selftest` is the last target `make all` runs, and its own environment check therefore fires only after lint, both builds, 1483 package tests, the iOS lane and the on-glass lane have all passed. Both runs came back `exit=2` on a tree where nothing was wrong with the code — roughly forty minutes each, twice. It is a lane defect rather than a product one, and the shape is familiar: the gate was honest (it said `the MCP SDK is not installed. Run npm install.` rather than skipping) and it was honest at the wrong moment. A check that can only fail on the environment belongs where the environment is checked. CLOSED by moving both checks into the `tools` target, which `all` runs first: `node_modules` must exist, and `dist/index.js` must exist because without it `parity-lane-selftest` SKIPS, and a skip is not a pass. Each names the command that fixes it. subject.text: CleanupBoardRow carries three treatments for a skill row — the `Read first…` substitution when SkillChecks.originUnchanged fails, the skill-kind `Remove…` drawn disabled because the router removes servers and never files on disk, and the candidacy reason — and none of them had a rendered path in any configuration of the product. Release reaches the branch only if a real user happens to hold an orphaned skill. Fixed in-campaign by adding a Debug-only `cleanupSkills` scenario and two SkillFixtures.uninstalled rows, kept separate from `populated` because SURF-004's on-glass predicate asserts the count populated publishes. No view code was touched and no assertion was weakened. Now photographed by CASE-0138/CASE-0139 and guarded in the harness by CASE-0144.

subject.source: app/Sources/MCPRouterKit/Control/Scenario.swift; evidence/runs/make-test-3.log (clean build, 1512 tests in 188 suites); app/Scripts/enum-layout-stamp.py; Makefile target enum-layout-stamp; evidence/runs/make-test-4.log
subject.text: Adding a 14th case to `Scenario` made `make test` fail with 31 issues, two of which cannot be true of the source: `Expectation failed: (… → .live) == (.live → .fixture(…cleanupSkills))` in ShellClientFactoryTests and TriageSourceGuardTests, both asserting a Release-posture guard that returns .live unconditionally. `git stash` of the two changed source files → 19 tests pass; unstash → the same failures return, which reads as a real regression. It is not. `Choice.live` is encoded in the spare inhabitants of `Scenario`'s tag, so a new Scenario case shifts that encoding, and stale MCPRouterUI object files compiled against the old layout compare a value that no longer means what they think. `rm -rf app/.build` then rebuild: 5/5 pass, then 1512/1512. The hazard for this campaign is the mirror case — a stale build can as easily produce a green — so any test evidence taken across an enum change is taken from a clean build. MITIGATED 2026-08-20: `app/Scripts/enum-layout-stamp.py` hashes the ordered case list of every enum in the package (212 of them) and removes `app/.build` when that hash moves; `make test` now depends on it. The stamp is the case lists rather than the source, so it holds still for an ordinary edit and for a `switch` over the enum — the false positive a naive grep for `^\s*case` would hit — and moves for an added or renamed case. Armed on all four: comment SAME, switch statement SAME, added Scenario case MOVED, renamed Scenario case MOVED, restore back to baseline. The SwiftPM behaviour itself is unchanged and still upstream; what is fixed is this repo's exposure to it.
subject.title: an incremental Swift build after adding an enum case reports impossible test failures

subject.source: planning/test-campaign/evidence/shots/pairs.json; planning/test-campaign/inventory.json; witness-worklist.py output before and after
subject.text: `evidence/shots/pairs.json` is what `witness-worklist.py` reads, and it had drifted from `inventory.json`. It listed 17 pairs against a 20-surface registry, so SURF-018, SURF-019 and SURF-020 were never offered for judging at all despite having both a mock reference and an attributed build capture. Four more pairs named a build half that was absent or wrong: SURF-010's capture existed and was cited by two cases while the pair said none, SURF-012/013/014 pointed at nothing while the iOS lane's captures sat in `evidence/shots/ios/`, and SURF-001 pointed at `SURF-001.build.png`, which is byte-identical to `SURF-002.build.png` (sha f221cce5) because the shell is photographed from the Servers board — the case had already been moved to the distinct sidebar crop `SURF-001.shell.png` and the pair map had not. Four iOS pairs also carried a `conditionsNote` describing a macOS `screencapture`, and a `reason` of `build half uncaptured` beside a build half that existed. Repointed by hand from `inventory.json` rather than by `attach-shots.py --apply`, which stem-matches and would re-create the DEF-006 mis-attributions. The comparable count is now 16 of 20 pairs with both halves, 3 with no design of record by construction, and SURF-009 with no build half for the reason its cases already carry.
subject.title: the witness pair map under-reported what had been photographed

subject.detail: CLOSED 2026-08-20. The cause was two independent framing errors, both invisible because the gate could not run to report them. The design references came from `obscura fetch --screenshot`, which captures at a fixed 1280x720 dpr1 viewport with no viewport flag, so every reference was clipped rather than merely small - the bottom row of one carried 578 non-background pixels of 640 sampled. And the build captures were 980x620 against the design's 1156x680 window, aspect 1.581 against 1.700, which no crop reconciles. Fixed by rasterising the design through CDP with `Emulation.setDeviceMetricsOverride` at 1280x900 dpr2 (readback asserted `[1280, 900, 2]` before any capture), re-photographing the eight Mac boards at the design's own 1156x680 with a setframe readback guard, and cropping both halves to the window's own content box. prescan goes from framingComparable 0/16 to 8/8, aspectRatioOfRatios 1.0 and scaleRatio 1.0 on every pair (evidence/runs/prescan-fidelity.json). Eight verdicts written: 2 pass, 5 fail, 1 unoracled.
subject.text: The campaign names design-review and be-my-witness as gates and has never run either, and the reason was never measured — it read as a skip. It is not. be-my-witness 0.2.0's deterministic prescan over all 16 pairs that hold both halves reports isEvidence 16/16, settled 16/16, framingComparable 0/16, proceed 0/16. Not a dead predicate: the scale ratios differ per lane (0.466x on the SURF-001 sidebar crop, 1.64x on the Mac boards, 0.942x on the phone) rather than returning a constant. Every reference was rasterised at a 1280x720 dpr-1 viewport, inside which prototype.html draws a fixed artboard rather than filling the frame, so rendering larger pads rather than enlarges. Re-rendering the reference does not fix it either: the design's Mac window is #win at 1156x680, aspect 1.700, and the build's is 980x620, aspect 1.581. The build half crops exactly — scale=(2096-1376)/(980-620)=2.0, margin=(2096-980*2)/2=68, content rect (68,68,1960,1240), precisely 2x the AX frame — but no crop reconciles two different window shapes. What would make them comparable is re-capturing the app at the design's window size, which means driving the app again and photographing a window shape the product does not use. Left unresolved deliberately: the structural and lexical differential in evidence/differential.md is the comparison that is valid here, and it ran.
subject.title: the rendered-quality gate has never been able to run, and nothing said why

subject.detail: `evidence/shots/captures.json` is the only manifest `capture-lineage.py --gate` reads, and two lanes write it: `capture-mac-glass.sh`, and `scripts/acceptance/name-glass-attachments.py`, which merges the iOS lane's rows up from `evidence/shots/ios/captures.json`. The Mac script wrote `json.dumps(rows)` — its own rows, whole file — so whichever lane captured last erased the other's lineage without saying anything. Measured 2026-08-20 on v0.9.1's new lineage plane: the parent held 16 Mac rows and none of the 9 iOS ones, and the gate reported 6 iOS captures UNSOURCED — 'the only thing binding this picture to SURF-012 is its filename', which is the correct verdict on a manifest that had been overwritten. The pictures were always right and their provenance was always recorded; it was recorded into a file that was then replaced. Fixed by merging on `path` in both writers, and the 9 rows were restored from the lane's own capture-time record rather than reconstructed.
subject.title: two capture lanes wrote one manifest and the last one deleted the other's provenance

subject.detail: `campaign.py` keeps defects in `inventory.json` under a `defect` list, and `add` assigns the next id from that list. `defects.in.json` is an input file. Twelve defects found in the sittings of 19 and 20 Aug were written straight into the input file with hand-written ids taken from that file's own length, which had stopped tracking the registry at DEF-006. The result: DEF-007 through DEF-018 each named one defect in the registry and a different one in the staging file, and neither file said so. Visible symptom, and the only reason it was caught: `RUN-2026-08-20.md` contains 'DEF-011 is the finding worth acting on ... Cleanup's' at line 96 and 'DEF-011 - the rendered-quality gate has never been able to run' at line 481, in one document, meaning two unrelated things. This is `capture-lineage`'s failure mode moved from pictures to identifiers: a name binding to two subjects with nothing checking the binding. Fixed by renumbering the twelve staged defects to DEF-034..DEF-045, merging them into the registry, and rewriting the fifteen references that meant the staged numbering. Every renumbered record carries `stagedAs` naming its old local id, so a reader meeting the old number in an untouched artifact can resolve it. The remaining 74 references were checked one at a time and meant the registry defect they already named. A fourth lesson, from the third instance's cleanup rather than from the collision itself. Reconstructing the concurrent session's two entries welded `text: ""` and `note: ""` onto both, and the first renumbering pass then used `"text" in d` to tell the two writers' entries apart -- so the artifact defeated the discriminator that would have caught it. Both authors independently read the empty values as harmless because they carried no content. The hazard is shape, not content: a membership test reads a key's PRESENCE, and an empty string defeats `"text" in d` exactly as thoroughly as a populated one would. `campaign.py add` injects only `id`, `status`, `evidence` and `armed`, so that key-shape occurred on exactly the two reconstructed entries and was traceable; the keys were stripped and the pass re-run discriminating on `title`. Recorded because "empty therefore harmless" is a reasonable-sounding wrong answer that both sessions gave.
subject.note: SECOND INSTANCE, 20 Aug 2026, in the case registry rather than the defect registry, and it landed the same way. A helper reported `next case id: CASE-0145` while cases.json already held CASE-0149 and CASE-0150; campaign.py's own `next_id` is max+1 and would have said CASE-0151, so the number that was trusted did not come from it. `add` takes an explicit id through `setdefault` and therefore appends a second entry rather than refusing, so CASE-0149 and CASE-0150 each came to name two cases -- an iOS Settings structural case against REQ-005 and a RouterCore write-failure case against REQ-019 -- and the `set` calls that followed wrote onto the pre-existing pair. Caught by an evidence-existence audit rather than by any gate: the new cases printed `3 evidence` where two were supplied. Restored from `git show HEAD:` (both pre-existing entries are byte-identical to HEAD again, verified by dict comparison) and the new pair renumbered to CASE-0153 and CASE-0154. The registry is sparse -- 74 gaps between 1 and 152 -- so a free-looking number is not evidence that it is free, and only max+1 is. THIRD INSTANCE, the same evening, and this one had two writers rather than one. A second Claude session working the same campaign allocated DEF-047 and DEF-048 at about 23:30 (the SDK -32603 message discard, and a detector defect in vacuity-check.py's blind pass) and committed planning/test-campaign as a directory in 6bdeea4, which also swept up this session's in-progress registry edits. This session allocated DEF-047 and DEF-048 for different defects minutes later, from a read taken before that commit landed. Resolved by renumbering THIS session's pair to DEF-049 and DEF-050 -- the later allocation moves, and the session that moves is the one that can enumerate its own references, which is the only reason the choice is safe rather than arbitrary. The peer's entries were not edited. Note for anyone reading the mechanism: `add` assigns from the registry list, so two writers holding a stale read get the same number, and no gate in the campaign detects it. The detection here was a peer message, and before that an evidence-existence audit; neither is a gate. campaign.py could refuse an explicit id that already exists -- `add` currently takes one through `setdefault` and appends a duplicate instead.
subject.title: the campaign's own defect ids named two different defects each, because the staging file numbered from its own length

subject.text: Measured by R27 on 2026-08-29 against the daemon on a scratch home. A server whose command exists and exits immediately (a shell that returns 17) is acquired for the full startupTimeoutMs and then reported as 'did not initialize within Nms': with the budget at 3000ms the probe took 3.15s wall clock. A server whose command does NOT exist fails in 0.01s, because the spawn itself throws. So the cost is specific to a child that spawns and dies, and the reason is that the handshake races connect() against a timer with no third branch for 'the process exited' - nothing watches the child's termination during startup. NOT FIXED HERE, and the reason is a boundary rather than effort. The race lives in StdioUpstreamTransport, which is the reference-diffed startup path R2 owns and R4 compares; adding an exit branch would change how this router reports a failure the reference reports differently, which is a parity decision and not a health-check one. R27's own bound is deliberately narrower - probeTimeoutMs covers the tools/list request so that 'the child never started' and 'the child answered too slowly' stay different answers - which means the budget that governs this arm is the upstream's startupTimeoutMs, and that is stated on the record rather than hidden. WHAT IT COSTS TODAY: a manual probe of a crash-looping stdio upstream blocks for the default 60s, and the caller has no way to shorten it except by setting that server's startupTimeoutMs. scripts/acceptance/r27-health.sh sets 1500 on its flaky fixture for exactly this reason, and says so. 2026-10-19 — FIXED IN BOTH ROUTERS by merge 02d764b0 (Merge ai/stdio-exit). A child that exits before initializing now fails at once, naming its status, instead of waiting out startupTimeoutMs. Unit evidence: RealProcessStartupTests (app/Tests/RouterCoreTests/RealProcessStartupTests.swift) and test/stdio-exit.test.ts. Verified 2026-10-19: the `Real child processes — startup` suite passed under `swift test`, and `node --test` on test/stdio-exit.test.ts passed. Status is fixed · in-test. No campaign re-run is recorded against this row, and the R27 wall-clock probe has not been run again against it.
subject.title: A stdio child that starts and then exits is not noticed, so acquisition waits out the whole startup budget

subject.source: app/Sources/RouterCore/Control/Describe.swift transportMembers; app/Sources/RouterCore/Control/ControlHandler.swift gate; src/control.ts is the reference half
subject.text: Found while building R22's redactor, filed rather than fixed. `Describe.row` emits `command` and `args` RAW, and `ControlHandler.gate` reads the token only for POST/DELETE/PATCH, so the complete command line of every stdio upstream is readable by anything that can open the loopback port. The same function is careful in the adjacent case — it emits `envKeys` and `headerKeys` and never a value, with B10's reasoning attached — so argv is the one credential-carrying position on that route that is published whole. It matters because argv IS a credential channel: `--token=`, `--api-key=` and a connection string with an inline password are ordinary MCP server invocations, and R22 scrubs args for exactly that reason. The exposure predates R22 and is not made worse by it: the bundle's args go through the value scrub, and this route's do not. NOT FIXED HERE, and the reason is a parity decision rather than effort. `GET /servers` is reference-diffed — `control-servers-get` in planning/parity/surface.tsv, verdict `proven` — so redacting args moves a surface R4 compares byte for byte, and the ungated GET is itself a ported defect this repository records rather than silently repairs. Closing it means changing both routers or declaring a divergence, and that is the owner's call. 2026-10-19 — FIXED IN BOTH ROUTERS by merge 74d15306 (Merge ai/argv-redact), whose subject records that GET /servers stops publishing secret-bearing argv. Unit evidence: ArgvRedactionTests (app/Tests/RouterCoreTests/ArgvRedactionTests.swift) and test/argv-redact.test.ts, with parity vectors in argv-redact.json. Verified 2026-10-19: the `ArgvRedactionTests` suite passed under `swift test`, and `node --test` on test/argv-redact.test.ts passed. Status is fixed · in-test. No campaign re-run is recorded against this row.
subject.title: GET /servers discloses every stdio upstream's full argv to an unauthenticated local caller

subject.evidence: scripts/windows/run-shell-selftest.ps1 exits 2 `NOT-RUN: no selftest.json after 180 s`. shell-startup.log records two launches, 08:09:47.250 and 08:13:14.882, each followed by `loaded at rasterization scale 1.5` and nothing further. Exactly one capture is written, destination-discover.png at 103 KB - a real drawn board - and `discover` is the FIRST entry in DestinationCatalog.All. The process is gone afterwards: Get-Process MCPRouter.Shell returns nothing. Reproduced on a clean rebuild, scripts/windows/build-shell.ps1 exit 0.
subject.title: The Windows shell self-test never completes: one destination captured, no report after 180 s

subject.evidence: Selecting Harnesses, Cleanup or Inbox through SelectionItemPattern.Select() leaves the window title, the caption band and the ENTIRE control-view tree byte-identical to the destination before it - the lane's fingerprint over the tree's accessible names is unchanged, which is why it is recorded as a COLLAPSE rather than as an empty board. The pane item itself does take the selection: SelectionItemPattern.Current.IsSelected reads True on all three. So the highlight moves and nothing behind it does. Order-independent: a reverse sweep, where every destination has a different predecessor, fails on exactly the same three. Six others - Discover, Servers, Activity, Checks, Insights, Settings - pass in both directions, so the harness, the actuation and the oracle all work.
subject.title: Three destinations select in the pane and never open their board: Harnesses, Cleanup, Inbox

subject.evidence: app/windows/MCPRouter.Shell/Shell/ShellWindow.xaml:91 declares the <muxc:NavigationView> with x:Name="Nav" and no AutomationProperties.Name. The ten items INSIDE it are named - ShellWindow.xaml.cs:267 sets each NavigationViewItem's AutomationProperties.Name from DestinationCatalog, and :293 names the pane-footer Settings item - so the omission is the container's alone.
subject.title: The shell's NavigationView pane carries no AutomationProperties.Name

subject.evidence: shell-lane.ps1 Start-Shell walked the root element's children and returned the FIRST whose ProcessId matched. A WinUI process publishes several top-level windows, and on one run the first match was a Microsoft.UI.Content.PopupWindowSiteBridge hosting a tooltip. Every subsequent read was scoped to that popup: the window title read as the empty string, no element carried the accessible name of any destination and none carried the automation id Nav, so 8 destinations came back `unoracled`, 3 rows failed and the pane read as unaddressable. The dump written in the same second - which walks by process id rather than through that handle - holds a complete healthy tree with all ten pane items. Recorded in the transcript of that run.

subject.evidence: run-shell-lane.ps1 registered a fixed task name, MCPRouter-WINSHELL-AutomationPlaneLane. Two runners in separate worktrees called it seconds apart; `schtasks /Create /F` overwrote, and the first runner's `schtasks /Run` then printed "ERROR: The system cannot find the file specified" because the winner had already deleted the task on its way out. That wrapper sat for its full 900 s and reported NO VERDICT with an empty lane.log.
subject.title: Two shell-lane runs on one machine registered the same scheduled task and deleted each other's

subject.evidence: Four claims about the ambient surface have no instrument on this machine. (1) AmbientPresentation.TrayToolTip is carried into the icon through NIM_MODIFY and Shell_NotifyIconGetRect returns a rectangle, never the tip, so the tip's text is the application's own account of itself. (2) A notification-area click is delivered to a window procedure and there is no out-of-process way to press it here - already recorded on DEF-101. (3) settings.ambientIcon.explorerRestart.baseline shows the reader can say no with nothing owning the icon, but nothing distinguishes a restored tray entry that is live from one the tray answers for out of HKCU\Control Panel\NotifyIconSettings, which is why DEF-300's arm passes with the re-add watchdog removed. (4) Nothing in the build constructs AmbientFlyoutView: it renders from the model it is handed rather than from literals now, but no operator can open it and no arm reads it.
subject.title: Nothing on this host can read a notification-area tooltip, press its icon, or tell a restored tray record from a live one - and the ambient flyout is not mounted at all

subject.evidence: Across eight runs of scripts/windows/uia/shell-lane.ps1 on 2026-09-03 the shell terminated mid-run in five of them, and never on the same subject twice: on selecting Cleanup, on selecting Discover, on selecting Servers, during the Settings board's removal arms, and three times during the ambient arms in one run. Every launch wrote `handlers: xaml=True, appdomain=True, unobserved-task=True, dispatcher-guard=True` to shell-startup.log and not one of the deaths wrote an `unhandled:` line - so all four routes DEF-079 and DEF-085 added were armed and none of them saw it. The lane records each death honestly (a destination row reads CRASH, a control row reads unoracled) rather than reporting the empty tree that follows as a finding about a board. IT IS NOT THE AMBIENT POLL THIS ITEM'S NEIGHBOUR ADDED. Deaths were observed on builds with the poll deliberately removed (planning/evidence/WIN-SHELL/arming/def-301-planted-lane.txt, three deaths in one run) as well as on the shipping build, and the last three runs of the shipping build were 10-of-10, 10-of-10-with-one-crash, and 10-of-10 clean. That is the whole of what is known about the cause.
subject.title: MCPRouter.Shell terminates intermittently while a destination is being read, with nothing in any of the four unhandled-exception routes

subject.evidence: CAUSE FOUND AND FIXED, 2026-09-03. shell-lane.ps1's Start-Shell stopped stale shells with `Get-Process 'MCPRouter.Shell'`, which names every process of that name on the MACHINE. Two runners in a fleet wave run this lane from two worktrees at once, so each one's Start-Shell terminated the other's shell partway through its sweep. The victim reported a destination CRASH at whichever destination it happened to be reading - which is why the four deaths landed on four different destinations, why none left an `unhandled:` line in shell-startup.log, and why none produced an Application Error or Windows Error Reporting event: nothing faulted, the process was killed. Four deaths in eleven runs on 2026-09-03, on BOTH trees - the DEF-302 branch and, after stashing app/windows back to main's and rebuilding clean, main's own. THE OTHER RUNNER WAS THEN SEEN DIRECTLY: with the fix in place the lane logged `leaving a shell that is not this lane's subject, pid=40292 at C:\Dev\mcp-router\.worktrees\wd1-ambient-truth\...\MCPRouter.Shell.exe` - a second runner's shell, live in the same interactive session, exactly the process the old code would have killed. run-shell-lane.ps1's own header already records the same collision one level up, on the scheduled TASK NAME, from 2026-09-02.
